Their 2026 study compares core developers, who sit near the center of a project, with peripheral developers, who contribute less often. Earlier work showed that the two groups adopt AI tools at different rates.

The authors study how that gap plays out now that coding agents can act on their own. The question matters because agents are changing how teams divide work and review code. If core and peripheral developers use agents in unlike ways, project leads may need unlike rules and support for each group.
arxiv-2601-20406:
S. Elgammal studies whether the High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider could reveal a torsion field, an extension of gravity in Einstein-Cartan theory. The analysis uses privately simulated data matched to the collider's planned setup, with proton collisions at high energy. It focuses on pairs of muons with large mass.

The key variable is an angular distribution measured in the Collins-Soper frame. A torsion field would distort that distribution in a characteristic way. Case studies of this kind tell experimenters which signals to hunt for when the upgraded collider turns on. They also show how strong a signal must be to stand out.
arxiv-2601-20606:
Xinyu Wang and five colleagues present WFR-MFM, a one-step inference method for dynamic unbalanced optimal transport. Reconstructing how a system evolves from limited observations is fundamental in single-cell biology. There, unbalanced optimal transport models transport and mass change together, since cells divide and die as they move through states.

Existing approaches simulate trajectories at inference time, which makes inference a bottleneck at scale. A one-step method removes that simulation loop. Faster reconstruction would let biologists trace how cell populations develop across far larger datasets. The point is speed. A one-step read can stand in for a long run that few labs can pay for. It turns a slow step into a fast one, and that is no small thing.
arxiv-2601-20806:
Jiangen He and Wen Lou map how library and information science schools organize their research. Their 2026 study is the first full empirical map of its kind, they report. It covers schools across the United States. The team analyzed more than fourteen thousand publications. They came from over twelve hundred faculty members at forty-four institutions, across the years 2013 to 2024.

The authors used word embeddings and topic modeling to sort the work. They found sixteen distinct research themes. Those themes group into three broad dimensions. They are Library and Knowledge Organization, Human-Centered Technology, and Computing Systems. The map shows how each school's structure and portfolio fit together. It gives the field a clear view of where its strengths now lie.
arxiv-2601-21006:
Michael Jones and five co-authors fuse simulation and experiment to read fusion shots. Their 2026 paper concerns inertial confinement fusion, or ICF. A mix of physics-based simulation and experiments was key to reaching ignition in ICF. Both sides produce mixed outputs: scalars and images. Only part of the simulated data is available in real shots. That gap makes inference about a shot hard.

The authors propose a joint diffusion approach to multi-modal inference. Diffusion models can fill in missing views in a principled way. Trained across both data worlds, the model can infer hidden values. Better inference helps physicists tune the next shot. The work joins plasma physics with machine learning.
arxiv-2601-21106:
Annesh Pal and three co-authors make a flexible clustering model scale to wide data. Their 2026 paper studies Dirichlet process mixture models, or DPMMs. These models estimate the number of clusters from the data itself. They draw that number from an infinite choice of partitions. That freedom makes them a robust alternative to parametric mixtures. The catch is cost: inference in high dimensions is heavy. Two key parameters are usually fixed by hand.

The authors let both the concentration parameter and the variance be unknown. Their adaptive model learns them from the data. Collapsed variational inference keeps the computation tractable. Scaling such models matters for modern datasets with many features. The paper targets clustering that adapts its own complexity. It serves analysts who cannot guess cluster counts in advance.
arxiv-2601-21206:
Yu Guo and Rong-Xin Miao study a web of linked theories in holography, the idea that a bulk world can be described by a theory on its edge. Their setup joins several such edge theories through branches of a curved gravity model. Each branch carries its own coupling strength.

Using a classic theorem recast for holography, the authors prove a junction rule on the joining surface. That rule leads to conservation laws at the nodes of the web. The work also links the setup to parallel worlds that a signal could pass through. It gives a cleaner picture of how linked holographic systems share energy and information.
arxiv-2601-21306:
Wei-Di Chang, Mikael Henaff, Brandon Amos, Gregory Dudek, and Scott Fujimoto question a basic belief about model-based reinforcement learning. The usual story blames weak long-term forecasts and piling errors for poor results. Planning by search, on that view, should fix a learned policy.

The authors find that search can hurt results even when the model is highly accurate. Swapping a learned policy for search is not a plug-and-play upgrade. Something about the search itself clashes with how the policy was trained. The finding urges care: a good world model does not guarantee that planning on top of it will help.
arxiv-2601-21506:
Joonhee Lee, Hyunseung Shin, and JeongGil Ko design a navigation system for indoor robots that pairs speed with understanding. Classic mapping methods locate a robot reliably but need detailed maps. They also cannot read the signs and room numbers that guide people indoors.

Vision-language models can read those cues but often react too slowly for a moving robot. The authors combine both strengths in a dual-process design. A fast process keeps the robot moving safely, while a slower one reads the scene for meaning. The pairing targets hospitals, offices, and malls, where robots must move quickly and still find the right door.
arxiv-2601-21706:
Nan Lin, Yanbo Wang, and Jacco Heres unify generative tasks for smart meter data under one flow-based model. Meter data underpin planning and running the distribution grid. Privacy rules often make the real data unavailable, and what is collected can be corrupted or too coarse.

A generative model can fill those gaps with realistic synthetic series. Flow matching gives one frame for tasks like imputation, upscaling, and scenario creation. Grid planners could then test plans against rich synthetic demand without touching private records. The unified design also cuts the need for a separate tool per task.
arxiv-2601-21806:
Walter Wreszinski revisits one of the oldest puzzles in quantum mechanics, the EPR paradox. The paradox was meant to show that quantum theory must be incomplete if it respects locality. Locality is the idea that distant objects cannot instantly affect each other. Generations of debate followed about what the theory really says.

In his 2026 preprint, Wreszinski draws out a principle he finds implicit in a 1935 paper by Schrödinger. Using it, he argues for a proof that the EPR-locality paradox does not arise within the Copenhagen interpretation. He shows the point already with the simplest case, an entangled pair of two spin one-half particles. The claim, if it holds, would settle a long conceptual dispute about where the paradox actually lives.
arxiv-2601-22006:
Vasily Bokov, Lisa Kohl, Sebastian Schmitt, and Vedran Dunjko ask how little quantum computing is enough. Quantum machine learning is often sold as a promising use for quantum computers, backed by proofs of possible advantage. The authors invert the usual question: how small a role can the quantum device play while the advantage survives?

Their 2026 preprint studies learning under quantum priors, where most of the work is classical and the quantum part is minimal. Proving advantages in that lean setting matters because near-term quantum hardware is scarce and error-prone. If a small quantum contribution still provably helps, useful quantum learning could arrive years earlier than designs that need a full quantum pipeline.
arxiv-2601-22206:
Shi Bo and AmirEmad Ghassami study imitation learning when the student cannot see the world cleanly. In offline imitation, an agent learns from recorded expert behavior. Trouble starts when part of the state that drove the expert's decisions is observed only through noisy measurements, and the distribution shifts before deployment.

Those flaws create spurious links between states and actions. Standard behavioral cloning then converges to systematically wrong behavior, whether it uses the raw measurements or ignores them. The authors' 2026 preprint develops causal imitation learning that corrects for measurement error and distribution shift. The problem is practical: robots and medical policies alike learn from sensors that never report the true state.
arxiv-2601-22506:
Kaili Sun and four co-authors show a surface that emits heat waves with a twist that flips by side. Metasurfaces are thin, patterned sheets that steer waves of many kinds. Their 2026 preprint reports Janus chirality: the emitted heat's spin turns one way on one face, the other way on the back.

Getting such coherent, two-faced emission from one device is a hard feat. The team show it in a real build, not just on paper. Control of heat glow's spin could serve sensing, signaling, and heat control. The work opens a new knob for thermal design.
arxiv-2601-22906:
P. H. Cezar and a team of astronomers report gas observations of six nearby quasars. These are type-2 quasars, bright galactic centers partly hidden from view, drawn from the QSOFEED sample. Using a near-infrared instrument on a large telescope in the Canary Islands, they took long-slit spectra of each one.

The spectra trace warm molecular gas plus atomic gas at low and high ionization. Such gas shows how quasar energy pushes back on its host galaxy, a process called feedback. Feedback helps explain how galaxies and their central black holes grow together.
arxiv-2601-23006:
Junyou Su and a team of co-authors pick better training data for fine-tuning language models. Training on full datasets is costly, and extra data often adds little. Existing selection methods are tied to one domain: what works for general instructions fails on reasoning, and the reverse also holds.

Their method, InstructDiff, uses differential entropy to judge data in a domain-adaptive way. Smarter selection could cut training bills while keeping quality high. It also makes fine-tuning feasible for smaller teams with narrow, specialized data. Domain-adaptive selection is the aim, since instruction data and reasoning data reward very different selection strategies.
arxiv-2601-23206:
Morten I. K. Munk, Arturo Valdivia, and Paolo Burelli generate dynamic game content with small language models. Large models promise rich, changing game worlds, but they suffer narrative incoherence and high running costs. Their size also forces cloud access, which offline games cannot assume.

The proof of concept shows small models can produce high-quality content locally. On-device generation keeps games playable without a connection and cuts server bills. It also keeps player data on the machine, a privacy plus for studios. Small models answer the offline problem directly, since they can run on the player's own machine without cloud access.
arxiv-2602-02406:
Tung Quoc Le and 2 co-authors give the first general guarantees for tuning several hyperparameters at once by learning from data, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Hyperparameters are the settings chosen before training, and data-driven tuning automates that choice. Performance can depend on those settings in jagged, implicit ways, so past theory covered only a single setting.

The framework strengthens tools from real algebraic geometry to handle structured loss functions with many settings. It yields sharper generalization guarantees, meaning bounds on how well tuned choices transfer to new data. The authors also prove a matching lower bound and extend the analysis to validation loss under weak assumptions. Examples include weighted group lasso and weighted fused lasso, two sparse modeling methods. The results put a common practice on firm statistical ground.
arxiv-2602-02506:
Boris Ivetić and 1 co-author work out heat and motion statistics on a space where momentum itself is curved, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Snyder space encodes noncommutativity, the failure of position labels to commute, through that momentum-space curvature. The authors use an approach that does not depend on one realization, built on momentum-space invariants.

They derive changed partition functions and heat quantities for the Maxwell-Boltzmann, Bose-Einstein, and Fermi-Dirac statistics, in both normal and ultra-fast regimes. Curvature brings temperature-linked fixes that push energy, entropy, and energy density below standard values. Applied to the early universe, the changed radiation density alters the Friedmann rules that govern cosmic growth. Big Bang nucleosynthesis, the making of the lightest atoms, then bounds the Snyder deformation setting tightly. A mapping extends the bounds to the generalized uncertainty principle, yielding some of the strongest current constraints.
arxiv-2602-02706:
In a 2026 paper, Rachel Ulrich and 5 co-authors rescue ionospheric readings from an instrument aboard the International Space Station that many workflows would partly discard as noise. The electrostatic analyzer experiment flew from March 2023 to April 2024, spanning the maximum of solar cycle twenty-five. It sampled the topside ionosphere at mid and low latitudes in situ.

Their statistical workflow estimates the instrument noise floor, handles irregular time-based sampling, and extracts real ionospheric signals. Instead of thresholding away noisy spectra, the method learns a rival noise model and fits the reading surface with a scaled Gaussian process approximation. Values normally rejected are recovered. Plasma settings derived from the spectra inform space-weather effects on satellite navigation and radio communication. Data coverage grows substantially, enabling noise-assisted monitoring of ionospheric variability through a solar maximum.
arxiv-2602-03006:
Ziyang Yu and 1 co-author distill a large model's reasoning into a graph of small predictors in a 2026 paper. Running large language models for classification at scale is slow and costly. Standard distillation copies only final labels, discarding the teacher's intermediate reasoning and hiding where student errors come from in the training data.

Their framework, GCP, asks the teacher for reasoning as a graph of intermediate concepts. The student mirrors that graph with its own concept predictors. A graph-aware strategy picks which examples to label next, weighing concept uncertainty, diversity, and centrality. Targeted retraining updates only the most influential concept modules. Tests on eight classification benchmarks showed better performance under limited labeling budgets, with more interpretable training dynamics.
arxiv-2602-03206:
Formulas for suprema and infima in generalized ordered vector spaces are proved by Tomas Chamberlain, together with 1 co-author. Their setting uses an algebra called L, assumed Dedekind complete, meaning suprema of bounded sets exist. The objects are module homomorphisms, maps preserving the algebraic structure, that are order bounded between partially ordered modules with a decomposition property studied in functional analysis.

The target is a Dedekind complete vector lattice over the same algebra, satisfying one additional mild condition. Chamberlain's team proves the Riesz-Kantorovich formulas in that generality. Those formulas compute the least upper bound and greatest lower bound of such homomorphisms pointwise. The result extends classical lattice theory, where the formulas are central tools for order bounded operators on vector lattices.
arxiv-2602-03306:
Only some vector dimensions matter for a given query, and Zhanyu Wu, with 2 co-authors, learns to predict which ones. Dense search represents queries and documents as high-part vectors, but for a given information need many dimensions are redundant. Feedback-based masking figures importance noisily at test time, while supervised adapters learn one global transformation shared by all queries, ignoring per-query differences in what makes documents relevant.

Their system first builds oracle importance spreads from supervised relevance labels. A predictor then learns to map a query vector to those label-distilled scores. At use, the predictor alone selects a query-aware subset of dimensions for similarity computation, with no feedback step. Tests across several retrievers and benchmarks beat full-part, feedback-based, and adapter earlier methods.
arxiv-2602-03506:
Transformers can write down mathematical formulas that fit data, but nobody knew which internal circuits do the work. Arco van Breda and Erman Acar open that black box in a 2026 article on symbolic regression models. They introduce PATCHES, an evolutionary algorithm that searches for compact circuits inside the model and checks them for correctness.

PATCHES isolates 28 circuits, giving the first circuit-level characterization of a symbolic regression transformer. A causal evaluation framework scores the finds for faithfulness, completeness, and minimality. Mean patching with performance-based scoring proves most reliable at finding real circuits. Popular shortcuts like logit attribution and probing mostly capture correlations, not causes, the authors warn.
arxiv-2602-03606:
Bekenstein's bound caps how much entropy can fit in a region, given its size and energy. Stefan Hollands and 2 co-authors prove a version of it for wave packets in a 2026 paper. They take a Klein-Gordon wave packet localized in a region of width 2R. Its entropy, they show, stays below a constant times the radius and its energy.

The result holds in a wider framework of local, Poincaré covariant nets of standard subspaces from quantum field theory. The authors also set up a variational problem that sharpens the bound when the packet is not fully localized. Their general bound agrees with recent numerical work on the one-particle modular Hamiltonian. Versions of entropy balance and ant formulas for wave packets round out the paper.
arxiv-2602-03706:
A quantum measurement is not just a look; it can pump energy into the system being measured. Robert Czupryniak and 3 co-authors build a general theory of engines powered entirely by such measurements in a 2026 paper. Their central object is the quantum vacuum bending function, which captures how interactions lower a system's ground-state energy.

The striking claim is universality. Work, efficiency, and every other thermodynamic observable depend only on the shape of that ground-state energy landscape, not on microscopic details. Work fluctuations follow the landscape's curvature, tempered by a model-dependent factor and a generalized fluctuation relation. Exactly solvable models and simulations confirm the theory across single and many-body systems.
arxiv-2602-04006:
Networks built from interpretable pieces are Jusheng Zhang and 4 co-authors' answer to black-box deep learning. Their 2026 paper proposes the Rational-ANOVA Network, which decomposes a function into main effects and sparse pairwise interactions, following functional ANOVA. Each piece is a learnable rational function, a ratio of polynomials.

A strictly positive denominator prevents poles and blow-ups while still capturing sharp transitions. The low-order structure keeps the model readable and data-efficient. Rational pieces also extrapolate beyond the training range better than polynomial ones. Benchmarks on controlled functions and image classification test whether interpretability and accuracy can advance together.
arxiv-2602-04106:
A blue LED without gallium or indium would ease supply pressure on lighting. Ilteris K. Turan and 2 co-authors compute the electronic structure of calcium tin nitride, CaSnN2, in a 2026 paper. Advanced quasiparticle methods, including ladder diagrams in the screened interaction, give its band structure and exciton properties.

The material shows a direct band gap matching blue light. Symmetry analysis of the valence bands reveals a catch: the top band favors light polarized along one axis, awkward for emission from the usual crystal face. Other faces avoid the problem. Effective masses and crystal field splittings complete the design picture.
arxiv-2602-04506:
Guihyun Han, Minkyu Park, and S. H. Rhim study a magnetic material whose electric responses can be tuned by stretching it, in a 2026 paper on Mn3Al. The material is a compensated ferrimagnet, where opposed magnetic parts nearly cancel out.

First-principles work varied both strain and chemical potential, which sets how electrons fill energy levels. At one setting, three topological features appeared at once: Weyl points, nodal lines, and gapped nodal lines. The anomalous Hall effect, a sideways voltage, grew strongly under tensile strain. The linked Nernst effect, a sideways response to heat, changed sign near the Fermi level. The authors tie these shifts to changes in Berry curvature.
arxiv-2602-04706:
Yike Sun and 3 co-authors clean up wasted vocabulary in language model tokenizers in a 2026 paper. Tokenizers split text into pieces learned from data. Some pieces survive into the final vocabulary even though they are almost always merged into larger pieces during actual use.

The authors call these leftovers intermediate merge residues. They waste vocabulary space and may increase vulnerability to odd or adversarial inputs. Their method, LiteToken, simply removes the residue tokens. Because the tokens are rarely emitted, pretrained models often work with the trimmed tokenizer without further training. Experiments showed less token fragmentation, fewer parameters, and better robustness to noisy or misspelled inputs. Overall performance stayed intact.
arxiv-2602-04806:
Hayden Monk and Darryl Z. Seligman derive formulas for how a close pass by a massive body can fling a small object out of its star system, in a 2026 paper on orbital mechanics. Interstellar visitors found in recent years have made those ejection paths key to grasp.

Working in the restricted three-body setting, the authors map orbital elements before a pass to those after it, in closed but approximate form. Ejection works best once the small body's orbital eccentricity passes a threshold. The final eccentricity is driven mainly by one velocity part tied to the perturber's motion. Simulations backed the formulas as a good first pass. Uses cover our solar system and two exoplanet systems with known giant planets.
arxiv-2602-05506:
Computer science students now lean on large language models for many course tasks, and instructors are still deciding where to draw the line. Xinrui Lin, Heyan Huang, Shumin Shi, and John Vines study both sides across five scenarios: writing, quizzes, programming, project work, and looking up information. Their user studies cover sixteen students and six instructors, and they sort the observed uses into seven main intents.

Conflict between student practice and instructor norms varied sharply by task. Generating writing and solving quiz problems clashed clearly with norms, while revising text and checking quiz answers drew broad agreement. Project work fell in between. The authors note that instructors are shifting from bans toward recording model use as part of grading. They close with design guidelines for campus AI tools, such as guardrails that keep students engaged and comprehension checks that turn low-conflict uses into chances to learn.
arxiv-2602-06106:
Whether people wipe down shared gym gear or shared work tools is a cooperation puzzle, studied by Alexander Feigel and Alexandre V Morozov. Each user can clean before or after use, pay a cost, and lower the risk for the next person. Some users free-ride on the cleaning of others.

The pair built an evolution-style model tuned with real-world values. Cleaning spread when its cost fell, when social rewards for cleaning rose, and when rule-breaking was watched. Surprisingly, raising infection costs through punishment mattered less for keeping a fully cooperative group stable. The model shows sudden flips between clean and dirty norms, matching patterns seen in shared facilities.
arxiv-2602-06306:
Special curved spaces called Fano manifolds admit highly symmetric metrics, and Satoshi Nakamura studies a weighted version of the constant scalar curvature condition on them. The weighted metrics, introduced by Lahdili, depend on two weight functions. Nakamura builds a third weight from the pair and links the two kinds of special metric.

Under positivity and curvature conditions on the weights, he proves that a weighted constant scalar curvature metric exists exactly when a matching soliton metric exists. He also explains how the soliton arises naturally from Sasaki geometry, through a circle bundle over the manifold. There, the soliton on the base gives rise to a transverse Mabuchi soliton tied to the bundle's Reeb field.
arxiv-2602-06806:
Silpa Vadakkeeveetil Sreelatha, Dan Wang, Serge Belongie, Muhammad Awais, and Anjan Dutta introduce RAIGen, a tool for finding rare traits that text-to-image models seldom show. Earlier bias work either fixed fairness groups in advance or looked for traits that dominate outputs. Both miss minority traits that are still stored in the model but rarely drawn. RAIGen needs no preset minority groups.

It uses a sparse autoencoder with a nested shape and a new score that mixes how rarely a neuron fires with how distinct in meaning it is. Neurons flagged this way reveal seldom-shown traits in their most strongly firing images. The tool found traits beyond standard fairness groups in Stable Diffusion, scaled to a larger model, and enabled boosting of rare traits during generation, supporting checks across model types.
arxiv-2602-07006:
Alokesh Manna, Neil Spencer, and Dipak K. Dey develop a statistical model for forensic footwear evidence. Shoe prints from crime scenes can identify a shoe's make and model, but thousands of identical shoes exist, so investigators look for accidentals, the cuts and scrapes a sole accumulates through wear. Some accidental patterns are common, others highly distinctive, and quantifying a pattern's rarity measures the strength of the evidence.

The authors build a hierarchical Bayesian model framed as a latent Gaussian model, which scales efficiently to large collections of annotated prints through integrated nested Laplace approximations. Spatially varying coefficients capture how tread patterns relate to where accidentals appear. On held-out data the model beat existing methods, improving accuracy and reliability in forensic shoe print analysis and giving courts a better-grounded measure of how distinctive a print really is.
arxiv-2602-07306:
Serving large language models across many GPUs is throttled by synchronization: tensor parallelism splits matrices but forces devices to coordinate constantly.  Chong Wang and ten co-authors restructure the computation with the Parallel Track Transformer, which minimizes cross-device dependencies.

The design cuts synchronization operations up to sixteenfold against standard tensor parallelism while keeping model quality competitive. Integration into TensorRT-LLM and vLLM brings faster first tokens and faster per-token times.  Inference builders get an architectural change rather than another tuning trick, aimed at the communication bottleneck that limits multi-GPU scaling.  The gains hold across both serving stacks tested, suggesting the restructuring generalizes rather than tuning one system.
arxiv-2602-07606:
A classic theorem says large twin-free graphs must contain a large matching, co-matching, or half-graph as a semi-induced subgraph. Those three patterns define eight graph classes by which indices stay bounded.  Jan Dreier and two co-authors completely classify the parameterized complexity of Independent Set, Clique, and Dominating Set across all eight classes.

Drawing tractability and hardness results from the literature and filling the remaining gaps, they show Independent Set is fixed-parameter tractable whenever the half-graph and co-matching indices are bounded. They also construct classes that separate other cases.  Parameterized complexity teams get a finished map for three canonical problems across a natural family of graph classes.
arxiv-2602-07706:
Medical AI models often squeeze patient data into a few narrow patterns, which hurts reuse on new tasks. Yuanyun Zhang and six co-authors propose dense feature learning, a training approach that shapes the geometry of medical embeddings directly instead of chasing one prediction target.

The method rewards balanced, well-spread, and mutually distinct features using only linear-algebra rules, with no labels and no attempt to rebuild the input. Tests on hospital records over time, clinical text, and combined patient data show steadier features and better results on later tasks. The paper suits readers building reusable representations for health data rather than one-off predictors.
arxiv-2602-08406:
Designing solar absorbers from MXene metasurfaces means predicting light spectra that are expensive to compute with full-wave solvers. Shujaat Khan and two co-authors offer a deep-learning shortcut that predicts 102-point absorption spectra from small metasurface patterns. Their arXiv paper combines transfer learning with multi-channel refinement and smoothing.

A pretrained MobileNetV2 backbone is fine-tuned for the task, while parallel convolutional channels sharpen features and Savitzky-Golay smoothing trims high-frequency noise. The model beats standard and deformable convolutional baselines, reaching an average error of 0.0227 and an R-squared of 0.9563. Readers get a fast, accurate tool for nanophotonic design iteration.
arxiv-2602-08806:
Kelvin-Helmholtz instability ripples the edges between flowing plasmas in space, from solar-wind interfaces to jets and disks. Shishir Biswas and four co-authors analyze its rare-gas version, where uneven pressures arise and the Chew-Goldberger-Low rules replace MHD. Their arXiv paper mixes math and sims.

Growth rates and magnet effects peak in the MHD limit. In the large slow-down rare-gas limit, energy sent into tilt leaves less for bending field lines, so currents, magnetic islands, and gusts all weaken. Readers get a side-by-side look across regimes, with lessons for churn and merging in the heliosheath.
arxiv-2602-09106:
William B. Johnson and one co-author introduce a quantitative version of Steinhaus' property (S) for Banach spaces, called uniform property (S). A space has the property when, for any two distinct unit vectors and any perturbation size, the largest gap in perturbed norms stays above a positive function. That function depends on perturbation size and vector separation. The modulus is computed exactly for atomless L-one spaces.

The class proves stable under ultrapowers and Bochner L-one constructions, and includes all Gurariĭ spaces and Banach lattices of almost universal disposition. Each Banach space fits isometrically inside a non-strictly convex space of the same density with uniform property (S). An explicit renorming of l-one spaces is given, settling several open questions in ZFC about property (S) geometry.
arxiv-2602-09306:
Shared step-by-step suggesting keeps user data on devices, but split, noisy, same-like local logs cap model quality. Thi Minh Chau Nguyen and five co-authors bring LUMOS, a setting-split build that uses an on-device language model as a local meaning maker, instead of sharing slopes or helper settings. From each user past, the model builds three matching forms: future-leaning runs, meaning-same rewordings, and taste-clashing what-ifs as telling negatives.

Those built runs enter a three-view rival tuning inside the shared spine, deepening picture learning without baring private facts. Across three public tests, LUMOS always beats rival hub-run and shared baselines on hit-rate and ranking quality at cutoff 20. The design shows how local making can cure shared data thinness privately.
arxiv-2602-09606:
Automated traffic now exceeds human traffic on the web, and a growing share is explicitly malicious, with evasive bots faking users, solving captchas, and mimicking human patterns. Ghalia Jarad and Kemal Bicakci explore a gentler protocol-level defense in their 2026 paper: telling bots from users by TLS fingerprints using the JA4 technique, which encodes handshake parameters.

Two gradient-boosted classifiers were trained and tested on a dataset of real JA4 fingerprints after feature extraction. The CatBoost model performed best, with near-perfect discrimination, F1, and accuracy scores, while XGBoost ran nearly as well. Feature analysis flagged specific JA4 components, including handshake bytes and counts of ciphers and extensions, as most influential. Future work aims at newer protocols and added device features to resist advanced evasion.
arxiv-2602-09906:
Some equations change character as their solutions change, turning singular in one range and degenerate in another. A 2026 paper led by Simone Ciani, with four co-authors, studies nonnegative solutions to doubly nonlinear equations in exactly that mixed regime. The goal is local Hölder continuity, a precise way of saying solutions cannot jump or spike wildly on small scales.

The authors introduce a new technique that handles both the singular and degenerate cases up to certain Barenblatt numbers. Their proof rests on a new integral Harnack estimate linking two averaged norms, a result they note stands on its own. The work gives analysts a single route through a regime that previously had to be split apart.
arxiv-2602-10306:
A 2026 paper by S. S. Podkorytov, sole author, describes how homotopy similarity relations and finite-order invariants behave under composition. The setting is the function from maps of X into Y to maps of X into Z, induced by a map from Y to Z. That inducing map is strongly r-similar to the constant map.

The paper traces both structures through the induced function, recording how composition with a nearly constant map reshapes similarity relations and finite-order invariants alike. The composition viewpoint unifies the two behaviors in one setting, giving a compact account of maps, invariants, and induced functions under homotopy similarity.
arxiv-2602-10506:
Wei Chen and nine co-authors model graph domain adaptation as a steady process in a 2026 paper. Recent methods chop adaptation into discrete steps, building intermediate graphs or aligning in stages. Real graph structures, however, evolve continuously and nonlinearly, so fixed-step approximations miss the actual transformation.

Their method, DiffGDA, treats the journey from source to target graphs as a spread process governed by random differential rules. Structure and semantics evolve jointly along steady paths rather than jumping between checkpoints. The paper argues this steady framing captures the true motion of domain shift better than stepwise alignment. It reports stronger transfer results for graph tasks where the shift itself is gradual and intertwined.
arxiv-2602-11206:
Spiking networks promise energy-fast, brain-like computing, but spikes do not differentiate. Jose Marie Antonio Miñoza, writing alone, offers UltraLIF, a frame that replaces surrogate gradients with ultradiscretization from tropical shape. A soft maximum converges to hard thresholding as a learnable heat falls.

Two neuron models follow: UltraLIF from leaky integrate-and-fire motion, and UltraDLIF from diffusion building gap-junction coupling. Both train by standard backpropagation with no forward-backward mismatch, and theory gives convergence to classic motion with bounded, non-vanishing gradients. Tests on six benchmarks beat surrogate-gradient rivals, most clearly in single-timestep settings on neuromorphic and time data.
arxiv-2602-11906:
Proving that one logical theory conservatively extends another often hinges on largeness notions that measure how much combinatorial structure a set contains. Quentin Le Houérou and one co-author introduce a variant of parameterized largeness and obtain polynomial bounds, using a tree partition theorem based on Milliken tree theorem. Through forcing interpretation, any proof of a universal statement in the stronger theory can be translated into a proof in the weaker theory. The cost is only a polynomial increase in size.

The result concerns Ramsey theory for pairs and weak König lemma, theories whose relationship has been studied through conservation results. The polynomial size bound turns a qualitative conservation claim into a quantitative one: translations exist and they do not blow up proofs uncontrollably. For reverse mathematics, that precision matters, since the cost of moving between theories is itself informative.
arxiv-2602-12006:
Optimal control of mean-field random systems needs a maximum principle, and Peng's version for McKean-Vlasov equations lacked a clean proof. Johan Benedikt Spille and one co-author present a novel approach whose main step adds a third adjoint equation, a conditional McKean-Vlasov backward stochastic differential equation. That equation handles the pairing of squared terms containing two independent copies of the first-order variational process.

The construction extends Peng's principle from standard random equations in full, giving a proof the authors describe as conceptually consistent. Beyond its own clarity, the approach should prove useful for extensions to common-noise cases and endless cases, where mean-field control theory continues to expand.
arxiv-2602-12206:
Citation graphs map how research links together, but the OpenAIRE graph is huge: over 200 million works and over 2 billion citations, about 2.5 terabytes uncompressed. Joakim Skarding led this work with one co-author, Pavel Sanda, shrinking that graph so ordinary computers can use it. The processed version fits in 16 gigabytes of memory while keeping the full link structure.

The data also come in a simple format for easy handling, plus a Python pipeline to process future OpenAIRE releases. A larger version adds more fields, such as titles and author lists. For researchers without cluster access, the work turns a daunting dump into a usable map of scholarly citation.
arxiv-2602-12406:
Selecting many objects at once in extended reality starts with two steps: switching into multi-selection mode, then picking each intended object. Mohammad Raihanul Bashar led this work with three co-authors, testing how eyes, hands, and voice serve each step. Four mode-switching methods were compared, from pinch variants to voice, and three subselection methods, all combining gaze with dwell, pinch, or voice.

DoublePinch paired with Gaze plus Pinch performed best overall, while SemiPinch performed worst. Voice mode-switching helped, but Gaze plus Voice subselection was less favoured, since repeated vocal commands felt tedious. The findings give empirical guidance for designing multi-selection in XR, where speed must be balanced against fatigue and the feel of repeated commands.
arxiv-2602-12506:
Reinforcement learning fine-tuning has boosted vision-language models on reasoning tests, yet those models still suffer weak visual grounding, hallucinations, and over-reliance on text cues. Rosie Zhao led this work with seven co-authors. They show that simple, set textual changes, such as misleading captions or wrong chain-of-thought traces, cause large drops in robustness and confidence.

Effects grow stronger when chain-of-thought consistency is counted, across open-source multimodal reasoning models. Closed models show similar failure modes but keep markedly greater robustness and reasoning consistency. That gap suggests open-source fine-tuning practice, not an inherent task limit, is at fault. Analysis reveals an accuracy-faithfulness trade-off. Fine-tuning raises benchmark accuracy while eroding the reliability of accompanying reasoning. Adversarial augmentation helps robustness but does not alone prevent faithfulness drift. Faithfulness-aware rewards can restore alignment, though pairing them with augmentation risks shortcut strategies.
arxiv-2602-12606:
Relational deep learning learns directly on relational stores, modelling items and links across linked tables. Justin Gu led this work with ten co-authors, giving RelBench v2, a major growth of the RelBench benchmark. Four large relational data sets are added, spanning scholarly publications, business resource planning, buyer sites, and medical files. That grows the benchmark to 11 data sets with over 22 million rows across 29 tables.

New auto-complete jobs require models to guess missing field values within tables while following time limits, growing beyond forecast jobs built from SQL queries. External tests are also added, including Temporal Graph test event streams, ReDeLEx access to over 70 real-world stores, and 4DBInfer data sets and jobs. Tests show relational models steadily beating single rivals on auto-complete, forecast, and suggestion, showing the value of modelling relational structure directly.
arxiv-2602-12806:
Text fed to language models is usually scrubbed of names and other identifiers, but scrubbing specific items does not guarantee that a person cannot be re-identified. Nataša Krčo and three co-authors introduce RAT-Bench, a benchmark that judges anonymisation tools by re-identification risk rather than by item removal alone. Using United States demographic statistics, they generate synthetic texts carrying varied direct and indirect identifiers, spanning several domains, tongues, and difficulty levels.

An attacker model then tries to infer attributes from the scrubbed text, and the risk is reported for the United States population, accounting for how identifiers differ in power. Even the best tools fall far short of perfect, especially with non-standard direct identifiers and indirect clues. Language-model-based anonymisers trade better privacy for higher compute, and work well across languages, pointing to concrete design lessons.
arxiv-2602-12906:
Rings and gaps in protoplanetary discs are thought to trace dust traps and forming planets, but many extended discs had never been resolved sharply enough to check. Quincy Bosschaart and three co-authors present high-resolution ALMA observations of 26 previously unresolved extended discs within 200 parsecs, completing the sharp sample for nearby star-forming regions. Seventeen discs show clear substructures, while nine look smooth, compact, or ambiguous.

Combined with literature data across 730 discs, the team finds nearly all extended discs carry substructures: about 91% overall, rising to about 98% after correcting for highly inclined systems where structures hide. Substructures appear more often in larger, massive discs around higher-mass stars, and structured discs hold onto their dust over time. The result supports dust traps, possibly carved by giant planets, as a near-universal disc feature.
arxiv-2602-13006:
Quantum thermal averages are hard to compute straight, but an strong standard likely can mimic them as an ordinary ensemble average. Vijay Ganesh Sadhasivam and two co-authors build such a likely next Feynman and Hibbs, with a twist: quantum fluctuations are treated around where the path starts rather than around its centre. Instead of fully tuning the likely variationally, they explore approximate functional forms chosen for number toughness.

The closed-form likely that results is exact in both the standard and harmonic limits. Tests against exact position distributions for quartic, Morse, and double-well potentials in one dimension show good agreement where harmonic support holds. For practitioners, the method offers a practical shortcut: quantum thermal expectations from standard-style sampling, without the full machinery of path-integral mock run.
arxiv-2602-13206:
Large AI models collaborating at the mobile edge promise better services under tight resources, but model complexity clashes with limited compute, memory, and communication. Peichun Li and four co-authors survey joint AI in mobile edge networks, covering system design and uses in transportation and healthcare. They organise recent resource-lean techniques into spatial and time groups.

Spatial techniques cover mixture of experts, federated tuning, hierarchical diffusion, and patch-based diffusion. Time techniques cover routing fitting, split learning, speculative decoding, and cascading fitting. Building on that survey, the authors propose a multi-stage diffusion system that elastically distributes large making models across mixed edge resources. Tests show gains in leanness and adaptability for making data, supporting joint AI as a practical edge paradigm.
arxiv-2602-13806:
Rebuilding dynamic scenes from casual videos matters for scalable robot learning, yet four-dimensional rebuilding from a single camera remains highly ill-posed. The key insight is that real-world motion shows multi-scale order from object level down to particle level. A multi-scale dynamics mechanism splits complex motion fields, and Gaussian sequences with multi-scale dynamics represent dynamic 3D Gaussians through layers of multi-level motion.

That layered structure greatly reduces ambiguity and promotes physically plausible dynamics. Multi-modal priors from vision foundation models add complementary guidance, limiting the solution space and improving rebuilding fidelity. The approach enables accurate, globally consistent 4D rebuilding from monocular casual videos, with large improvements on dynamic novel-view synthesis benchmarks and real-world manipulation data. Can Li leads the work with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14206:
Mona Azadkia and one co-author study a 2026 arXiv estimator for Chatterjee's dependence coefficient. The coefficient runs from 0 to 1, hits 0 exactly under independence, and hits 1 when Y is a measurable function of X. It matches an earlier coefficient of Dette, Siburg, and Stoimenov for continuous marginals.

The paper analyzes the kernel-type estimator's asymptotics and local power. Under independence, a non-degenerate central limit theorem holds after centering, at rate root n over h1. Under Gaussian-copula alternatives with correlation tending to zero, second-order expansions trace how power behaves. The work sharpens the statistical footing for a widely used dependence measure.
arxiv-2602-14306:
Sylwia Zielińska-Raczyńska and one co-author study a 2026 arXiv problem in pulse propagation through Rydberg exciton media. Short pulses travel through a Cu2O crystal holding Rydberg excitons, modeled with density matrix formalism and finite-difference time-domain methods. Saturation effects under Rydberg blockade take center stage.

The paper explores not only absorption bleaching but also power-dependent shifts in the medium's dispersive properties. Exciton lifetime and coherent population oscillations shape the dynamics in key ways. A two-pulse pump-probe setup is also examined, with results matching recent experiments well. The work clarifies how blockade physics governs fast light pulses in exciton media.
arxiv-2602-14406:
Fathima Ameen and three co-authors introduce a 2026 arXiv dataset of conversations on Truth Social. Argument mining and stance detection help explain how opinions form and clash online, but most public resources cover Twitter and Reddit, leaving alt-tech platforms understudied. TruthStance fills that gap with threads from 2023 to 2025.

The dataset holds 24,378 posts and 523,360 comments with reply-tree structure preserved. A human-annotated benchmark of 1,500 instances covers argument mining and claim-based stance detection, with inter-annotator agreement reported, and evaluates language-model prompting strategies. Using the best configuration, the team released model-generated labels for 24,352 posts and 107,873 comments, enabling analysis of stance patterns across depth, topics, and users.
arxiv-2602-14506:
Kutay Tire and three co-authors probe a 2026 arXiv use of transformers for quadratic programs and choice-making. Linear focus can provably crack free quadratic programs by chopping matrix values row by row and mimicking gradient descent rounds. Adding multilayer perceptrons widens the trick: one transformer block can crack l1-penalized quadratic programs via loop soft-thresholding, and l1-capped quadratic programs with an added feedback loop.

That theory spurs Time2Decide, a method that boosts a time series base model by feeding it plainly the co-move matrix between variates. For portfolio tuning, framed as an l1-capped square plan, Time2Decide uniformly beat the base base model. It also beat the old forecast-then-tune plan, showing co-move-aware transformers can lift choice-making past forecasting alone.
arxiv-2603-01506:
Jianqiang Ren, Lin Liu, and Steven Hoi build a way to turn one photo into a moving 3D head in this 2026 work. Fast, detailed head avatars matter for games, film, meetings, and virtual worlds. A single model should also serve both weak and strong hardware without losing key detail.

Their method, OMG-Avatar, stores the head as Gaussian blobs at several levels of detail. A transformer reads broad face traits, while sampled points add local detail, joined with depth cues to keep overlaps sane. Head and shoulders are built apart, then merged, which fixes a weak spot of older face models. The build takes a fraction of a second, and tests beat prior tools on rebuild quality, acting control, and speed.
arxiv-2603-01806:
Xiong Zhang, Hong Peng, Zhenli He, and colleagues spot anomalous nodes in networks without any labeled examples. Their 2026 work targets bad actors in social and review graphs, such as fake accounts and banned users. A recent method boosts links among normal nodes while cutting links of odd nodes, yet its fixed cutoff misfires.

Their model, GCTAM, splits the cutoff step into contextual and global parts that work together. Contextual truncation lowers the affinity of likely anomalous nodes based on local cues. Global truncation raises affinity among normal nodes, using high-order links the old method ignored. Wide tests on large real graphs show wins over peer methods on most tasks. Gains stand out on two famous review data sets, and the method still finishes on the largest sets where rivals fail.
arxiv-2603-02306:
Adrian Fraser simulates a mixing process inside stars in this 2026 paper. Fingering convection stirs chemicals in star zones where heavy material sits above light material. It matters in red giants and possibly in polluted white dwarfs. Past three-dimensional simulations could not reach the extreme settings found in real stars.

The gap is set by one ratio, comparing viscosity with heat spread, which is tiny in stars. Fraser runs simulations spanning old settings down to true stellar values. A standard mixing model stays consistent with simulations across that whole range. So clashes between that model and observations cannot be blamed on the old gap. Extra physics, not simulation limits, must explain the mismatch.
arxiv-2603-02806:
Jonas von Berg, Adalbert Fono, Massimiliano Datres, and colleagues prove that steady classifiers need to be much bigger than their data. Their 2026 paper defines stability as the average distance from a data point to the model's decision boundary. A larger margin means small input changes rarely flip the answer.

Their bound improves as stability grows, and it needs no smoothness assumptions, covering jagged classifiers too. A direct consequence follows: a model that merely fits its training points with about as many parameters as points must be unstable. Real robustness therefore demands heavy overparameterization. Experiments back the theory, with stability rising alongside model size and tracking test accuracy, while older norm-based measures said little.
arxiv-2603-03206:
Cullen Anderson, Narmeen Oozeer, Foad Namjoo, and colleagues test how poisoned examples can hijack an AI model's steering. Contrastive steering finds a trait direction by comparing the model's inner signals on paired examples. It then shifts those signals along that line at runtime. Safety teams use it a lot, yet nobody had checked how it holds up when the example set is rigged.

A modest share of rigged examples leaves steering mostly intact. Past a clear threshold, though, attackers can plant strong unwanted side effects on purpose. A look at the shapes of distinct attack types points to guards. The weak step is a plain average over many signals. Swapping in a robust form of that average cancels most of the harm.
arxiv-2603-03506:
A M Guzman and M C McDonald hunt for a pattern in detector noise that should exist across columns if it exists at all. Their hunt appears in an instrument report for Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. Read noise in bias frames already grows with row number, because dark current builds during readout. Their report checks the column direction for the Wide Field Channel's four amplifiers, across different maintenance periods called anneal cycles.

No column dependence appears. Read noise in the physical prescan regions sits about half an electron lower than in the science arrays, exactly where no readout dark accumulates. Three follow-ups round out the study. Read noise shows no visible trend across an anneal period. Two amplifiers show a brief linear decline across their first science columns. And masking unstable hot pixels lowers the noise of their columns.
arxiv-2603-03606:
Satabdi Das and four colleagues ask blind and visually impaired people what would make photo sharing feel safe. A shared image can accidentally expose sensitive or embarrassing content its owner cannot see, risking privacy and relationships. Their 2026 study tests image obfuscation filters as a pre-sharing shield, with twenty blind and visually impaired participants judging filtered images of varying sensitivity.

Pixelation was the least preferred filter. Other preferences shifted with image type and with the audience, family, friends, or strangers, so no single filter wins everywhere. Across audiences, participants felt more comfortable sharing filtered images than unfiltered ones. The authors turn those patterns into design guidelines for sharing tools that warn and protect without taking control away from the person sharing.
arxiv-2603-03806:
Hanpeng Liu and four colleagues teach a vision model to read many images as one long book, with separators between chapters. Mamba, a state-space architecture, processes sequences causally and efficiently, which suits autoregressive pretraining, but vision versions were stuck with short sequences. Their 2026 method, STAR, inserts an identical separator token before each image, marking where one picture ends and the next begins.

That simple device quadruples the usable input sequence length while keeping every dataset image at its original size. Pretrained the long way, their STAR-B model scores competitively on the standard ImageNet classification benchmark, at the top of the Vision Mamba class. The authors argue the gain comes from finally exploiting the architecture's strength, long-range dependence across a genuinely long visual sequence, rather than from any added parameters.
arxiv-2605-00006:
Mrinal Kanti Roychowdhury gives an explicit study of optimal quantization on a sphere, the problem of placing a limited set of points so they best represent the whole surface. Working with geodesic distance on the unit sphere, he analyzes three highly symmetric discrete models in full analytic detail. The aim is benchmark cases where the optimal answer can be written in closed form rather than only computed.

The models place points evenly on the equator, on two small circles at matched latitudes north and south, and on a single small circle. For each, he derives the optimal quantizers and mean-square errors, proving that optimal cells form unbroken arcs with midpoint representatives. Curvature is shown to reduce distortion on a single circle while keeping the standard decay rate. The results clarify how curvature changes quantization on curved spaces.
arxiv-2605-00406:
Huw Price proposes a deflationary reading of the famous Bell correlations in quantum physics. Experiments inspired by John Stewart Bell's work show linked particles behaving in ways widely taken to prove the world is nonlocal. That reading sits in tension with relativity, unless realism about an independent world is abandoned. Price points to a familiar statistical effect instead: selection bias.

How a sample is selected from a larger population can create correlations between unrelated variables, or hide real ones, and preselection through preparation of the starting state is a known source. Price argues that the selection in standard two-particle Bell experiments is exactly such a preselection, and that it has been overlooked in this setting. On his account, the correlations are selection artefacts, and neither relativity nor realism needs to fall.
arxiv-2605-00506:
Tom Utting, Mario Giulianelli, and Arabella Sinclair model how speakers choose what to say in dialogue as a cost-sensitive choice among alternatives. Some alternatives serve the speaker's fixed goal, while others are merely plausible in context. By separating the two sets, the authors can read the same cost measure as speaker-oriented or listener-oriented, and ask which cost speakers actually seem to minimize.

They generate both kinds of alternative sets with language models, then test production choices in open-ended dialogue under strict and probabilistic versions of cost minimization. Minimizing surprisal, roughly how unexpected an utterance is, relative to the goal-directed alternatives gave the strongest account of what people said. Rival costs based on even information spread or on length predicted more weakly and less consistently. The study offers alternative-conditioned optimization as a principled frame for studying the pressures that shape natural speech.
arxiv-2605-00606:
Surendra Kumar Gour and Malay K. Nandy propose a route to the universe's matter-antimatter imbalance that needs no supersymmetry. Their engine is a complex scalar field whose own coupling terms plainly break a global symmetry. Three sample forms are studied, each making tangled source terms in the field's rules of motion.

Starting from a fully even start, those source terms build a real charge density: the asymmetry is created by the motion, not inserted. At late times the density falls in just the way needed to leave a constant baryon-to-photon ratio, a freeze-in by motion. One family of potentials works across a wide range of scalar masses. Another needs masses too light to be believed. A third gives an asymmetry that does not depend on the mass at all. If the charge passes well to plain matter, the route can match what is observed.
arxiv-2605-01206:
Ryoi Ohashi, Hiroki Isobe, Ryota Nakai, and Kentaro Nomura study tunneling duality in fractional quantum Hall states, focusing on the Read-Rezayi state. Point-contact geometries allow either quasi-particles or electrons to tunnel, and the two descriptions should be dual. Treating non-Abelian edge operators requires new tools, so the authors introduce a phase-shift instanton that incorporates phase factors from primary fields into the instanton gas framework.

Using that method, they reformulate the Moore-Read duality and obtain an explicit dual description for the three-level Read-Rezayi state. Quasi-particle tunneling phase shifts map strong quasi-particle tunneling to weak electron tunneling. In the strong-coupling regime, nonlinear conductance is evaluated analytically and universally follows a quartic voltage scaling for both states, reflecting a topological constraint on the tunneling particle.
arxiv-2605-01306:
Mohamed Sy's doctoral dissertation joins laser spectroscopy, a method that reads gases from the light they absorb, with machine learning to spot many gas species at once in harsh settings. Standard tools fail when spectra overlap, noise is high, or some species in the mix are unknown.

Sy tests five linked tools. A denoising network cleans shock-tube signals from fast fuel breakdown tests. One framework flags unknown species without full calibration, and a blind method rebuilds both amounts and spectra from mixed data alone, checked on blends of up to eight gases. A derivative-based step pulls out weak species hidden under broad ones. A final tool gives certified labels for organic vapors. Each method is checked in real experiments, pointing toward fast, sturdy gas sensing for engines, air monitoring, and plant safety.
arxiv-2605-01406:
Ayaka Murakami and Kouichi Takemura find closed-form special solutions of the q-Heun equation, a difference equation that plays the role for q-series that Heun's equation plays for ordinary differential equations. Exact solutions of such equations are rare and prized, since they anchor both theory and computation.

The pair start from solutions of polynomial type, answers that end after finitely many terms. Applying q-integral transformations, operations that act like integration in the q-world, they turn those seeds into new solutions of the same equation. Each new answer is written as a finite sum of q-hypergeometric functions, the q-versions of the classic special functions. The construction adds to the short list of cases where the q-Heun equation can be solved in named functions, a step toward a fuller map of its solution space.
arxiv-2605-01506:
Detao Bai and six co-authors build one encoder that takes in sight and sound together, the way people do. Current omni-modal models use separate encoders and a lopsided diet. Video is sampled at a frame or two per second against audio many times denser, so motion detail and cross-sense timing are lost.

Their OmniEncoder runs a single Transformer backbone that embeds both streams at a matched 25 frames per second in one shared space. Three devices make it work: a token template that tags what is what, a position scheme tuned for mixed streams, and a shifting time window that keeps cost sane. Against a strong split-encoder baseline on the same token budget, the unified model gains a lot on smooth visual tasks. Those tasks include sign language and fine sports actions, and the model holds its own on audio-visual tests.
arxiv-2605-01706:
Ghazal Danaee and four co-authors make active learning for brain scans fair as well as cheap. Labeling medical images costs expert hours, so active learning picks the most useful scans to label next; standard picks chase raw uncertainty and can quietly leave one demographic group badly segmented.

Their weighted entropy strategy bends the uncertainty score by each group's current performance on the labeled set, so weak groups get labeled first. A masked, scaled entropy, confined to the target region, keeps organ size differences from faking uncertainty. On synthetic brain images with a planted bias in one structure, a 3D U-Net is trained under several strategies. The fairness-aware picks cut group disparity sharply against both random and standard sampling, from balanced and lopsided starts alike. The authors count the study among the first on fair active learning for segmentation.
arxiv-2605-02106:
Terry Dorsey and Kevin Huggins argue that AI should be built around memory, not just model weights. Current systems do well through large models, retrieval, and static training sets. Yet they struggle to keep a lasting record of past work. They also struggle to place that record in time, track its source, or explain it.

Their Dynamic Gist-Based Memory Model treats past experience as a clear, lasting structure. A user can inspect that structure and read it in new ways over time. Memory becomes a core base for reasoning, not a side store. The paper lays out that shift and describes how gist-based records change as new interactions arrive.
arxiv-2605-02306:
Chang Liu and colleagues revisit Gaussian filtering for state estimation, using information geometry as the lens. Exact Bayesian filtering works only for linear Gaussian systems. Nonlinear cases rely on approximations, such as extended and unscented Kalman filters. The tutorial frames prediction and update as inference over state distributions.

Their new filter refines the mean and covariance step by step. It uses natural gradient descent on the manifold of Gaussian laws. That respects the family's own geometry and keeps the covariance positive definite. The paper serves as a tutorial as well as a method paper. It highlights basic questions about Gaussian filtering that the geometric view makes clear.
arxiv-2605-02406:
Benjamin Kraus and colleagues build an ultra-stable, transportable ultraviolet laser for an aluminium quantum logic clock. Optical clocks need such a laser to probe a narrow clock transition precisely. Their system reaches a fractional frequency instability near two parts in ten thousand trillion, using an ultra-stable cavity with crystalline mirror coatings and a frequency quadrupling chain of two single-pass doubling stages.

Acceleration sensitivity, measured on all three axes, is among the lowest recorded for transportable systems. A further trick partly cancels photo-thermal noise against photo-birefringence noise. That cancellation mitigates noise from optical power fluctuations inside the cavity at lower Fourier frequencies, a key limit for portable clock lasers that must leave the lab.
arxiv-2605-03006:
Valentin O. Deliyski, Galin N. Gyulchev, Daniela D. Doneva, Petya G. Nedkova, and Stoytcho S. Yazadjiev model direct images of thin disks around rotating black holes with added scalar hair. A massive scalar field changes the paths of light near the horizon, so it should also change the pattern of polarized light from the disk.

Their main finding is a shift in the twist of the polarization vector, which was largest for the least scalarized cases they studied. That result points to local path effects, not total field strength. With vertical fields at steep viewing angles, the twist direction can also flip.
arxiv-2605-03306:
John M. Hitchcock shows that languages needing exponential-size circuits are typical inside symmetric exponential time, in the resource-bounded category sense. Category here measures largeness through a game, extending classic results that placed the same circuit class as small inside a larger space class.

Hitchcock defines smallness against single-valued strategies for the symmetric class and turns a known range avoidance algorithm into a winning game strategy. That makes the exponential circuit class meager there, so its complement, languages that truly need huge circuits, is comeager and thus typical. The note ties circuit lower bounds to descriptive largeness.
arxiv-2605-03406:
Dae Woong Ham, Stefanus Jasin, and Xuejun Zhao ask how researchers should decide when a sequential hypothesis test has seen enough evidence to reject. Group sequential tests check the same hypotheses at several stages as data arrive, spending a type-1 error budget across checks. Classical spending rules are valid, but which is fastest was unclear.

The authors optimize the rejection criterion directly, under the same error controls, using sample average approximation combined with mixed-integer linear programming. Their optimal approach dominates classical Lan-DeMets, Pocock, and O'Brien-Fleming procedures in their comparisons. A striking pattern emerges: optimal solutions usually spend the error budget aggressively early. They also apply the method to a recent empirical study.
arxiv-2605-04206:
Katja Froehlich and five co-authors present a way to find dryland sites where native plants might regrow and survive without long-term watering. Their case study is Saudi Arabia, where many past planting efforts have relied on costly irrigation in a water-scarce land.

Using climate records, satellite data, and expert-chosen reference sites, they build a climate score and map it across the country. Sites where the climate looks good but plants are still sparse are flagged. The screening then narrows the search to thirteen priority places. Nearby healthy ecosystems serve as targets for what regrowth could reach.
arxiv-2605-04306:
Fritz Lekschas and Nezar Abdennur present a tool for exploring high-dimensional data by touring through two-dimensional views of it. Any single flat view loses information, so tours animate a path through many views, but older tools limit how freely a user can steer that path.

Their interface mixes preview images, smooth scrubbing along paths between views, direct manual control, and a wandering automatic tour in one place. It renders millions of points with graphics hardware, runs in a web browser, and works with Python and JavaScript. They show it on text, image, and single-cell data.
arxiv-2605-04406:
Tushar Das and three co-authors propose a learnable geometry for the symmetric positive definite matrices that appear throughout machine learning, from covariance data to medical imaging. Networks using these matrices have relied on fixed geometric rules, much like hand-crafted features, which limits what they can express.

Their metric is built from a spline-based transformation that is constrained to stay monotone, avoiding the folding and gradient failures of looser designs. Two versions, acting on spectra or on a matrix factorisation, can approximate any suitable transformation and contain earlier pullback metrics as special cases. The result is a geometry that adapts to data instead of being chosen in advance.
arxiv-2605-04606:
Yichen Li, Qiankun Liu, and Ying Fu propose an unsupervised object detector that knows what categories it is finding, without using any hand-labelled training data. One-shot detectors need labelled examples, while general unsupervised methods propose boxes but cannot say what kind of object each box contains.

Their method uses unlabelled reference images. A similarity score between a predicted object and the references guides learning. It pushes the model toward features tied to each class, through a loss designed for that purpose. The same framework can also run in a category-blind mode when no references are available. Number-based and visual tests on both modes show the approach works. It narrows the gap between label-free detection and labelled-data accuracy.
arxiv-2605-05106:
Lakshita Jindal and Kavita Jain study how defects correlate with each other when a quantum system is driven across a phase transition in finite time. The Kibble-Zurek mechanism predicts average defect counts from the slowing dynamics near the critical point. Correlations between defects, described here as kink-kink correlations, need more than that basic picture.

Working with the one-dimensional transverse-field Ising model under an algebraic quench, the pair examine the correlation at the end of the drive. For faster-than-linear quenches the correlator depends only on the Kibble-Zurek length, while slower quenches bring in an extra length scale from phase differences between low-energy modes. The work tests which features of earlier linear-quench results are universal.
arxiv-2605-05206:
Xiaoyu Wu and five co-authors study outlier tokens in diffusion transformers used for image generation, a few tokens with unusually large values that attract heavy attention while carrying little local information. The phenomenon was known in vision transformers but not in generative models. The authors find it in both the encoder and the denoising transformer of modern pipelines.

Simply masking the large tokens does not help, suggesting the real problem is corrupted local patch meaning rather than extreme values alone. Their Dual-Stage Registers add register tokens at both stages, trained where possible and created at test time otherwise. Across image benchmarks the intervention reduced outlier artefacts and improved generation quality.
arxiv-2605-05606:
Many real systems are only glimpsed through sparse, noisy measurements. Yu Wang and Arnab Ganguly infer the hidden paths and parameters of stochastic differential equations from such data. Classical smoothing methods suffer from path degeneracy and scale poorly, so the authors take a variational route.

They describe the posterior equation through a backward score, a gradient field defined by a Kolmogorov equation, and learn it with neural networks. A likelihood objective then tunes the model parameters in an EM-style loop. On nonlinear test systems, the method stayed accurate with very few observations and scaled better than Markov chain Monte Carlo.
arxiv-2605-05806:
Retrieval-augmented generation bolts a search engine onto a language model, and the seam between them causes mismatches. Elad Hoffer and six co-authors ask whether an attention-based model can retrieve from its own representations instead. Their framework, INTRA, lets decoder attention score pre-encoded evidence chunks and reuse them directly as context.

Retrieval and generation become one mechanism, and context encoding is amortized across queries. On question-answering benchmarks, INTRA beat strong engineered retrieval pipelines on evidence recall and final answer quality. The work suggests the retriever was inside the model all along.
arxiv-2605-05906:
Axion-like particles could be the dark matter, and if they decay into photons, the sky should faintly glow at radio frequencies. Wen-Qing Guo proposes hunting that glow by cross-correlating radio intensity maps with the galaxy distribution from the 2MASS Redshift Survey. Ambient radiation, from the cosmic microwave background and an extragalactic radio backdrop, stimulates the decay and boosts the signal.

The survey covers the local universe, within redshift a tenth. Guo builds the theoretical framework for the cross-correlation, including those stimulation effects. A detection, or its absence, would probe micro-electronvolt-scale axion-like dark matter in a new way.
arxiv-2605-06106:
Mathis Degryse and three co-authors close a gap in the theory of learning augmented online bidding. In online bidding, an algorithm raises bids step by step for tasks such as resource allocation and clustering. The learning augmented version also hears predictions from an oracle, and quality is judged by consistency when predictions are good versus robustness when they are bad.

The authors derive matching upper and lower bounds on the best consistency for each robustness level above a stated threshold. Their key device is the bidding function, an abstraction that unifies how randomized bidding strategies are designed and analyzed. That device simplifies proofs that earlier work had left open. They also apply randomized bidding to the incremental median problem, showing the method works in a practical clustering setting.
arxiv-2605-06306:
T. Congy and G. A. El build an exact framework for the statistics of random nonlinear wave fields ruled by solitons. Their setting is the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation in a regime where typical wave fields are dominated by soliton pulses. Such integrable turbulence appears in water waves, nonlinear optics, and superfluids, yet predicting its intensity distribution from first principles has been an open challenge for the field.

The authors state a soliton gas resolution conjecture for the long time evolution of slowly varying random starting states. A random analogue of the inverse scattering transform then links the spectral density of the soliton gas to the probability density of wave intensity. The resulting full integral formula matches direct computer simulations closely across several regimes. The framework gives random wave statistics a firm exact footing.
arxiv-2605-06406:
Y. I. Izotov, N. G. Guseva, D. Schaerer, and R. O. Amorin present telescope observations of eleven compact star-forming galaxies with extremely high oxygen line ratios. Such galaxies are candidate sources of leaking Lyman continuum radiation, which can ionize gas between galaxies. The sample sits at low redshift and has low oxygen abundance and small stellar mass.

Using Very Large Telescope spectra, the team derives helium and oxygen abundances plus ratios for nitrogen, neon, sulfur, chlorine, argon, and iron. They also measure gas velocity spreads from many lines. Most lines agree closely, while helium lines run broader, likely tracing inner regions shaped by massive stars and scattering.
arxiv-2605-06506:
Omar Momen and Sina Zarrieß question a reported link between language model surprisal and how novel a metaphor feels. Surprisal measures how unexpected a word is in context and is often used as a stand-in for predictability. It is also tightly tied to how frequent a word is, which may be the real driver.

Using two frequency measures and surprisal from eight Pythia model sizes across many training checkpoints, they find word frequency predicts metaphor novelty more strongly than surprisal does. The surprisal link peaks early in training, then fades as its tie to frequency grows. Settings once read as optimal for predictability may mostly reflect word frequency.
arxiv-2605-06606:
Marco Zaccheddu and six co-authors image the internal structure of the proton using AI inside a Bayesian framework. Transverse momentum dependent distributions describe how quarks spread inside a proton, but pulling them from data is an inverse problem with hidden blind spots. Their flexible pixel-based method puts the distributions on a grid and fits them jointly with the evolution kernel that governs energy dependence.

A hybrid of normalizing flows and Metropolis-Hastings sampling explores the high-dimensional posterior exactly and fast. Closure tests of rising hardness check the method, and a singular value analysis exposes null parts that data cannot constrain. The result is three-dimensional partonic imaging with honest error bars.
arxiv-2605-06906:
Shang-Ling Hsu, Mark Tenzer, Cyrus Shahabi, and Khurram Shafique rethink pretraining for human mobility data, whose structure language-style recipes ignore. Visits are joint events of place, time, and activity; users keep persistent signatures; and people sharing places create cross-user signal. The authors state these as three axioms for a broader class they call multi-entity spatiotemporal event streams, which also covers authentication logs and health records.

Their TraXion framework designs objectives and architecture jointly to satisfy the axioms. One checkpoint per dataset beats task-specific baselines on anomaly detection, recommendation, and prediction tasks across six mobility datasets. Applied unchanged to enterprise authentication logs and intensive care mortality prediction, the same recipe matches or beats prior specialized work.
arxiv-2605-07206:
Wei Xiong and four co-authors show one magnetic material phase that displays two kinds of topological boundary behavior at once. Their setting is a two-dimensional antiferromagnet lacking certain mirror symmetry, modeled with a spin-density-wave mass term. Which behavior appears depends only on how the crystal is cut.
