A voluntary, low-cost program that mixes public and private money was needed, the act says. Working with willing owners since 1987, the program had already helped cut endangered species listings, according to the findings.
plaw-109-295-2006:
Homeland security for fiscal 2007 is funded by Public Law 109-295, approved October 4, 2006, covering the Department of Homeland Security for the year ending September 30, 2007. Appropriations acts in this style attach detailed orders to the money, and this sample shows that pattern at once.

Title I funds departmental management. The Secretary's office receives ninety-four million four hundred seventy thousand dollars, but five million is held back until a full port, container, and cargo security plan reaches Congress. That plan must require screening all incoming cargo and double the share now inspected. Ten million more waits for a multi-year Secure Border Initiative plan. Later titles fund the department's many agencies in the same itemized way.
plaw-109-296-2006: Livestock price reporting continues under Public Law 109-296, approved October 5, 2006, reauthorizing the Livestock Mandatory Reporting Act of 1999. The authority now ends September 30, 2010, instead of September 30, 2005. The act also rewrites swine reporting terms in the Agricultural Marketing Act. A base market hog becomes a barrow or gilt with no discounts taken from, and no premiums added to, its base price. A boar is defined as a sexually intact male swine, and the packer of sows and boars definition is narrowed by plant and year.
plaw-109-297-2006: An Alaska dam project gets more time from Public Law 109-297, approved October 5, 2006. It concerns Federal Energy Regulatory Commission project number 11480, licensed under the Federal Power Act. Despite the deadline in section 13 of that act, the Commission may stretch the time to start building. It may do so if the license holder asks and after notice. The stretch may run for three straight two-year periods beyond four years after the license issued. Good faith, due diligence, and the public interest must still be shown.
plaw-109-298-2006: Public Law 109-298, approved October 5, 2006, is the Wyoming twin of the Alaska hydroelectric extension beside it in this batch. It covers Federal Energy Regulatory Commission project number 1651 under the Federal Power Act. The Commission may extend the license holder's time to begin construction for three straight two-year periods. Here the periods run from the end of the extension originally granted, a wording difference from the Alaska act. The same tests apply: licensee request, notice, good faith, due diligence, and the public interest.
plaw-109-299-2006: Wichita, Kansas, water supply gains a new federal piece in Public Law 109-299, approved October 5, 2006, authorizing the Equus Beds Division of the Wichita reclamation project. The Secretary of the Interior may help fund and carry out the Equus Beds Aquifer Recharge and Recovery Component. That component is part of the city's Integrated Local Water Supply Plan. Running, maintaining, and replacing the division is the sole duty of the City of Wichita, and federal design or building money waits until plans satisfy federal law.
plaw-109-300-2006: Alaska enters the naming series with Public Law 109-300, approved October 5, 2006, for Ward Cove. The facility at 7172 North Tongass Highway is known and designated as the Alice R. Brusich Post Office Building. The act uses a headed section named for Brusich, with designation and references as subsections. References to the Ward Cove facility in United States laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records are deemed references to the Alice R. Brusich Post Office Building. No facts about Brusich appear in the text.
plaw-109-301-2006: Two people share an Alaskan naming act in Public Law 109-301, approved October 5, 2006. The facility on Lindbald Avenue in Girdwood, with no street number given, is designated the Dorothy and Connie Hibbs Post Office Building. Oddly, the section heading in the sample reads Connie Hibbs Office Building, dropping both Dorothy and the word Post, though the designation itself is correct. References to the Girdwood facility in federal records are deemed references to the Dorothy and Connie Hibbs Post Office Building.
plaw-109-302-2006: Manassas, Virginia, is honored in Public Law 109-302, approved October 5, 2006, designating the facility at 8801 Sudley Road as the Harry J. Parrish Post Office. The act's headed section gives the designation, then a references rule without quotation marks around the name in one sentence, a small printing quirk. References in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records to the Sudley Road facility are deemed references to the Harry J. Parrish Post Office. The measure is honorary only.
plaw-109-303-2006: Copyright royalty judging gets technical fixes in Public Law 109-303, approved October 6, 2006. It amends title 17 to correct the Copyright Royalty Judges program set up by a 2004 reform act. One change is punctuation, adding a comma in a list of section numbers. A larger one sets a deadline rule. If the last day for an action with the Judges falls on a weekend, holiday, or other non-business day, the action may be taken the next business day. It counts as on time.
plaw-109-304-2006: Shipping law is gathered into one clean code title by Public Law 109-304, approved October 6, 2006. It completes the codification of title 46, United States Code, Shipping, as positive law. The purpose section says the act reorganizes and restates laws then sitting in the appendix to title 46. Codifiers aimed to match Congress's original intent while removing unclear wording, contradictions, and other faults. The contents run through eight subtitles of title 46, the Maritime Administration, maritime security changes, matching changes to other laws, transition rules, and repeals.
plaw-109-305-2006: Railroad pensions keep a clear payer under Public Law 109-305, the Railroad Retirement Technical Improvement Act of 2006, approved October 6, 2006. It amends the Railroad Retirement Act of 1974 on continued payment of railroad retirement annuities by the Treasury. The rewritten sentence is short: the Secretary of the Treasury shall serve as the disbursing agent for benefits payable under the act, under rules the Secretary chooses to set. That single fix is the sample's whole substance, beyond the short title.
plaw-109-306-2006: Washington's Kennedy Center receives added funding authority from Public Law 109-306, approved October 6, 2006. It amends the John F. Kennedy Center Act to authorize more money for the performing arts center for fiscal year 2007. Two figures are set. For upkeep, repair, and security, nineteen million one hundred thousand dollars is authorized for that year. For capital projects, twenty million dollars is authorized for fiscal year 2007. In both places the act rewrites the year list so 2007 stands as its own item, instead of sharing an earlier line.
plaw-109-307-2006: Training young doctors in children's hospitals is funded again by Public Law 109-307, approved October 6, 2006, reauthorizing a payment program in the Public Health Service Act. The program pays children's hospitals that run graduate medical education programs. The sample extends it to fiscal years 2007 through 2011. Funding lines for those years are set at one hundred ten million dollars in one paragraph and two hundred twenty million dollars in another. One internal figure also changes, from twenty-six to twelve, in the payment formula the act amends.
plaw-109-308-2006:
Pets are written into disaster planning by Public Law 109-308, the Pets Evacuation and Transportation Standards Act of 2006, approved October 6, 2006. It amends the Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act.

State and local emergency plans, to win approval, must take into account the needs of people with household pets and service animals before, during, and after a major disaster or emergency. The federal emergency director's own preparedness work must also include plans of that kind, under the section the act amends next. The law answers a hard lesson of Hurricane Katrina, when many people would not leave home without their animals.
plaw-109-309-2006: One map date changes in Public Law 109-309, approved October 6, 2006, a technical correction to the Ojito Wilderness Act. In the definition section of that New Mexico wilderness law, the date October 1, 2004 is struck and January 24, 2006 is inserted. The date belongs to the official map of the wilderness. Nothing else in the Ojito act is touched: no boundary, acreage, or rule in the sample changes. Short laws like this keep the legal record pointing at the right version of a map.
plaw-109-310-2006: East Greenwich, Rhode Island, closes this batch with Public Law 109-310, approved October 6, 2006. Its wording differs slightly from most naming acts here: it designates the Post Office located at 5755 Post Road, rather than the facility of the Postal Service, as the Richard L. Cevoli Post Office. The headed section then deems references in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records to that post office to be references to the Richard L. Cevoli Post Office. The honor is the act's whole content.
plaw-109-311-2006: Averill Park, New York, is named in Public Law 109-311, approved October 6, 2006. The facility at 2951 New York Highway 43 is designated the Major George Quamo Post Office Building, under a section headed with that name. Designation and references appear as subsections. References in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records to the Averill Park facility are deemed references to the Major George Quamo Post Office Building. The rank Major is part of the honor as enacted.
plaw-109-312-2006:
Famous brands get a clearer shield from copycats in Public Law 109-312, the Trademark Dilution Revision Act of 2006, approved October 6, 2006. It amends the Trademark Act of 1946 on dilution by blurring or tarnishment, the harm done when a famous name is weakened or stained by someone else's use.

The owner of a famous, distinctive mark may win an injunction against a later use likely to dilute it, even without confusion, competition, or proven money injury. A mark counts as famous if the general consuming public widely knows it as a source sign for its owner's goods or services. Courts may weigh all relevant factors in judging that fame, the new text says.
plaw-109-313-2006:
The government's buying office is rebuilt by Public Law 109-313, the General Services Administration Modernization Act, approved October 6, 2006. It creates a Federal Acquisition Service inside the General Services Administration, led by a Commissioner appointed by the Administrator.

The new service takes over work once done by the Federal Supply Service and the Federal Technology Service, plus related jobs the Administrator assigns. The act's purpose also replaces the General Supply Fund and the Information Technology Fund with a single Acquisition Services Fund, tying the new office to its money. Regional executives may be appointed to run its work across the country.
plaw-109-314-2006: Care of the memorial to fallen police officers is changed by Public Law 109-314, approved October 6, 2006. It amends the law that set up the fund for the memorial's upkeep. The Interior Department, through the National Park Service, must make a cooperative agreement with the National Law Enforcement Officers Memorial Fund, Inc., a District of Columbia nonprofit, to run the fund. Under it, the Secretary transfers all money in the National Law Enforcement Officers Memorial Maintenance Fund to the corporation. Later wording adjusts what the fund is for.
plaw-109-315-2006: Babylon, New York, receives its naming act as Public Law 109-315, approved October 10, 2006. The facility at 110 Cooper Street is designated the Jacob Samuel Fletcher Post Office Building, in a headed section split into designation and references subsections. References to the Babylon facility in United States laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records are deemed references to the Jacob Samuel Fletcher Post Office Building. The act contains no findings about Fletcher and makes no other change.
plaw-109-316-2006: Small business programs that were about to lapse are bridged by Public Law 109-316, approved October 10, 2006, in a single section. Any program, authority, or provision under the Small Business Act or the Small Business Investment Act of 1958 stays authorized through February 2, 2007. That covers pilot programs too. It applies to items in force on September 30, 2006 and set to expire before February 2, 2007. The terms are those in effect on September 30, 2006, with no changes made by this act.
plaw-109-317-2006:
A Virgin Islands ranch may one day join the national parks, and Public Law 109-317, approved October 11, 2006, orders the study. Castle Nugent Farms, on the southeast shore of St. Croix, is the largest private parcel in the Virgin Islands and a working cattle ranch for 50 years. 

Congress found it holds the islands' largest and healthiest fringing coral reef, dry forest and pasture, and pre-Columbian and colonial remains. It also holds a 17th century Danish estate house and over four miles of oceanfront. Turtle and night heron nesting grounds lie there. So does the Senepol cattle breed developed on St. Croix.
plaw-109-318-2006: One map swap is the whole of Public Law 109-318, approved October 11, 2006, adjusting the Yuma Crossing National Heritage Area in Arizona. It rewrites the boundary section of the area's 2000 act. The heritage area now comprises the lands generally shown on a map titled Yuma Crossing National Heritage Area Boundary Adjustment, numbered 903-80071 and dated October 16, 2005. No acreage or place list appears in the text; the map itself carries the new line. The act's title adds only the standard phrase for other purposes.
plaw-109-319-2006: Historic Missouri homes get a park study under Public Law 109-319, approved October 11, 2006, called the Ste. Genevieve County study act of 2005. The area studied includes the Bequette-Ribault, St. Gemme-Amoureaux, and Wilhauk homes and related historic assets in the county. Within three years after money is provided, the Secretary of the Interior, working with Missouri, must judge whether naming the area a National Park System unit is suitable and workable. The study must weigh effects on nearby private land, and a report goes to two congressional committees.
plaw-109-320-2006:
Two invasive trees in the West are targeted by Public Law 109-320, the Salt Cedar and Russian Olive Control Demonstration Act, approved October 11, 2006. The Interior Secretary, through the Bureau of Reclamation and the Geological Survey and with the Agriculture and Defense departments, must run an assessment and demonstration program.

The program must measure how far salt cedar and Russian olive have spread in the western United States. It must show strategic ways to manage both trees over the long term and bring back native plants in their place. It must also judge money-making ways to dispose of the plant material left by removal. A formal agreement between Interior and Agriculture runs the work, and the first assessment is due within a year of funding.
plaw-109-321-2006: Colorado water canals pass to their local district under Public Law 109-321, approved October 11, 2006. The Secretary of the Interior must convey all federal interest in named Colorado-Big Thompson Project facilities to the Northern Colorado Water Conservancy District. The facilities lie in Larimer, Boulder, and Weld counties: the St. Vrain Supply Canal, the Boulder Creek Supply Canal running to Boulder Reservoir and also called the Boulder Feeder Canal, and the South Platte Supply Canal. Congress finds the district has finished repaying the project's capital costs under its 1938 contract.
plaw-109-322-2006: Wetlands conservation funding is renewed in one line by Public Law 109-322, approved October 11, 2006, the North American Wetlands Conservation Reauthorization Act of 2006. It amends section 7(c) of the North American Wetlands Conservation Act, the law that pays for protecting waterfowl habitat across the continent. The words fiscal year 2007 are struck, and each of fiscal years 2008 through 2012 is inserted in their place. That keeps money authorized for five more years, through 2012, for the wetlands program.
plaw-109-323-2006: Education waiver power tied to an earlier spending act is extended by Public Law 109-323, approved October 11, 2006. It amends section 105 of title IV of division B of Public Law 109-148, the defense act in this slice that also carried hurricane measures. The Secretary of Education's waiver authority, which covered fiscal 2006, may now also be used, at the Secretary's choice, for fiscal year 2007. A cross-reference is updated so a later date points to the respective succeeding fiscal year instead of naming 2007 outright.
plaw-109-324-2006:
About 171 acres in New Mexico go to a county under Public Law 109-324, the Rio Arriba County Land Conveyance Act, approved October 11, 2006. The Secretary of the Interior must give Rio Arriba County the federal land, with any improvements, for free and subject to existing rights. The land lies on the Sebastian Martin Land Grant near Alcalde, as shown on a September 23, 2004 map. 

If any part stops being used for public purposes, it may revert to the United States. If the county sells land, it must get fair market value and pay the gross proceeds to the Secretary for Bureau of Land Management use in New Mexico.
plaw-109-325-2006: Federal moving-cost experiments run longer under Public Law 109-325, approved October 11, 2006, extending relocation expenses test programs for federal employees. It amends section 5739 of title 5 in two ways. A limit of not more than 24 months on a test program is struck out. The program's overall span grows from seven years to eleven years. The changes count as if they had been part of the Travel and Transportation Reform Act of 1998, so no gap in authority opens between the old and new wording.
plaw-109-326-2006:
Great Lakes fish and wildlife work is renewed by Public Law 109-326, approved October 11, 2006, amending the 1990 act of the same name. Its job is to carry out the Fish and Wildlife Service's recommendations from the Great Lakes Fishery Resources Restoration Study.

Congress found the lakes' fish and wildlife communities are changing in structure and function, and that good management treats the lakes as ecosystems and joins many partners. More action and better coordination were needed, the act says, and key actions lacked funding. The 1990 law lets federal agencies, states, and tribes work as partners by funding restoration, a frame this act builds on.
plaw-109-327-2006: Baltimore honors one of its own members of Congress in Public Law 109-327, approved October 12, 2006. The facility at 6101 Liberty Road is designated the United States Representative Parren J. Mitchell Post Office, spelling out the office in the name. A headed section gives designation and references together. References to the Liberty Road facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records are deemed references to the United States Representative Parren J. Mitchell Post Office.
plaw-109-328-2006: Olathe, Kansas, names its building for a governor in Public Law 109-328, approved October 12, 2006. The facility at 110 North Chestnut Street shall be known as the Governor John Anderson, Jr. Post Office Building. The act then deems any reference in a federal law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record to that facility a reference to the Governor John Anderson, Jr. Post Office Building. Kansas appears several times in this slice's naming run; this is its governor entry.
plaw-109-329-2006: Green River, Wyoming, is the town in Public Law 109-329, approved October 12, 2006, designating the facility at 350 Uinta Drive as the Curt Gowdy Post Office Building. The act's single section is headed with the Gowdy name and contains designation and references subsections. References in United States laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records to the Green River facility are deemed references to the Curt Gowdy Post Office Building. The sample gives no account of Gowdy's career.
plaw-109-330-2006: Mission, Kansas, follows Olathe in this run with Public Law 109-330, approved October 12, 2006, for the facility at 6029 Broadmoor Street. It is designated the Larry Winn, Jr. Post Office Building, under a section headed with that name. References to the Broadmoor Street facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records are deemed references to the Larry Winn, Jr. Post Office Building. The designation and references are subsections of the one section.
plaw-109-331-2006: A courthouse not yet built is named in advance by Public Law 109-331, approved October 12, 2006. The United States courthouse to be constructed in Greenville, South Carolina, identified as building number SC0017ZZ, shall be known as the Carroll A. Campbell, Jr. United States Courthouse. That future tense sets this act apart from the courthouse naming for an existing building beside it in this batch. References to that courthouse in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, or other records are deemed references to it by the Campbell name.
plaw-109-332-2006: Tyler, Texas, has two street numbers in its naming act, Public Law 109-332, approved October 12, 2006. The federal building and United States courthouse at 221 and 211 West Ferguson Street are together designated the William M. Steger Federal Building and United States Courthouse. The double designation matches the double address. References in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records to that building and courthouse are deemed references to them under the Steger name. The act changes the name only.
plaw-109-333-2006: East St. Louis, Illinois, closes this batch in Public Law 109-333, approved October 12, 2006. The facility at 950 Missouri Avenue is designated the Katherine Dunham Post Office Building, in a headed section with designation and references parts. References to the Missouri Avenue facility in United States laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records are deemed references to the Katherine Dunham Post Office Building. As usual, the enrolled text states the honor and leaves Dunham's story to the reader's knowledge.
plaw-109-334-2006: Woodside, New York, in Queens, is the place in Public Law 109-334, approved October 12, 2006. The facility at 39-25 61st Street, a hyphenated Queens address, is designated the Thomas J. Manton Post Office Building. The act's headed section contains designation and references subsections. References to that facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records are deemed references to the Thomas J. Manton Post Office Building. The text states the honor without explaining Manton's career.
plaw-109-335-2006: Akron, Ohio, gets a combined federal naming in Public Law 109-335, approved October 12, 2006. The federal building and United States courthouse at 2 South Main Street are together designated the John F. Seiberling Federal Building and United States Courthouse. References in any federal law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record to that building and courthouse are deemed references to them under the Seiberling name. The act follows the courthouse pattern used in Tyler, Texas, in the prior batch of this slice.
plaw-109-336-2006: West Chester, Pennsylvania, is named in Public Law 109-336, approved October 12, 2006, designating the facility at 101 East Gay Street as the Robert J. Thompson Post Office Building. The single section is headed with the Thompson name and split into designation and references. References to the West Chester facility in United States laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records are deemed references to the Robert J. Thompson Post Office Building. Nothing in the text describes Thompson.
plaw-109-337-2006:
A stretch of river in Colorado becomes a protected area under Public Law 109-337, the Rio Grande Natural Area Act, approved October 12, 2006. The Rio Grande Natural Area is created to conserve, restore, and protect the natural, historic, cultural, scientific, scenic, wildlife, and recreational resources of the area. 

Its boundaries take in the Rio Grande River from the southern edge of the Alamosa National Wildlife Refuge to the New Mexico border, reaching a quarter mile out from either bank. The Secretary must prepare a map and legal description, and a Rio Grande Natural Area Commission is created.
plaw-109-338-2006:
Heritage areas and soda ash share Public Law 109-338, the National Heritage Areas Act of 2006, approved October 12, 2006. Its full purpose line also mentions temporarily lowering the royalty charged for sodium produced, an unrelated item carried in the same bill.

Title I is the soda ash royalty reduction, with a study. Title II establishes National Heritage Areas, beginning with the Northern Rio Grande National Heritage Area, complete with findings, a management entity's duties, the Secretary's duties, private property protections, a sunset, and funding. A second subtitle begins the Atchafalaya National Heritage Area in the contents. Such areas honor regional history and landscape without becoming national parks.
plaw-109-339-2006: Jacksonville, Florida, has its courthouse named by Public Law 109-339, approved October 13, 2006. The United States courthouse at 300 North Hogan Street shall be known as the John Milton Bryan Simpson United States Courthouse, a four-part personal name carried in full. References to that courthouse in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records are deemed references to it under the Simpson name. The bill passed the House in February 2005 and waited until September 2006 for the Senate, by the record in the sample.
plaw-109-340-2006: Ukraine may build a famine memorial in Washington under Public Law 109-340, approved October 13, 2006. The Government of Ukraine is authorized to place a memorial on federal land in the District of Columbia. It honors the victims of the manmade famine in Ukraine in 1932-1933. The text calls it the Ukrainian famine-genocide. The memorial must follow the Commemorative Works Act, with four listed sections of that act waived. The United States government will pay none of the cost of building or maintaining the memorial.
plaw-109-341-2006: Only part of a building is named by Public Law 109-341, approved October 13, 2006, in Alexandria, Virginia. The portion sits at 2100 Jamieson Avenue. It is attached to the main tower and called the A-Wing in the plans. It is occupied by the United States Attorney's office for the Eastern District of Virginia, Alexandria Division. That portion becomes the Justin W. Williams United States Attorney's Building. Money is authorized for signs and a plaque honoring Williams, a detail most naming acts here leave out.
plaw-109-342-2006: A park, not a building, is designated by Public Law 109-342, approved October 13, 2006, in St. Louis, Missouri. The parcel of land on the site of the Thomas F. Eagleton United States Courthouse becomes the Clyde S. Cahill Memorial Park. Section 3 fixes the land: the parcel bounded by South 10th Street, Clark Avenue, South 9th Street, and Walnut Street. References to that parcel in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, or other records are deemed references to the Clyde S. Cahill Memorial Park.
plaw-109-343-2006: McAllen, Texas, is the city in Public Law 109-343, approved October 13, 2006. The federal building at 320 North Main Street shall be known as the Kika de la Garza Federal Building, Kika being the name as enacted, in place of a full first name. References in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records to that McAllen building are deemed references to the Kika de la Garza Federal Building. The act is a plain federal building naming, in two sections.
plaw-109-344-2006:
Darfur is the subject of Public Law 109-344, the Darfur Peace and Accountability Act of 2006, approved October 13, 2006. It imposes sanctions on individuals responsible for genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity, backs protection for civilians and aid work, and supports peace efforts in the Darfur region of Sudan.

The contents add sanctions in support of peace, extra powers to deter and stop genocide in Darfur, and continuation of existing restrictions. Assistance efforts in Sudan and reporting duties follow. Its definitions name the African Union Mission in Sudan. They also name the Comprehensive Peace Agreement signed in Nairobi on January 9, 2005, between Sudan's government and the SPLM/A. That sets the act in the diplomacy of that moment.
plaw-109-345-2006: Beaver, Pennsylvania, honors a man with a memorial building name in Public Law 109-345, approved October 13, 2006. The facility at 777 Corporation Street is designated the Robert Linn Memorial Post Office Building, in a headed section with designation and references parts. References to the Beaver facility in United States laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records are deemed references to the Robert Linn Memorial Post Office Building. The act states no facts about Linn.
plaw-109-346-2006: Clinton, Illinois, should not be confused with the Clinton, Massachusetts, entry earlier in this slice; Public Law 109-346, approved October 13, 2006, is a separate act for a separate town. It designates the facility at 105 North Quincy Street as the Gene Vance Post Office Building. References to that facility in any federal law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record are deemed references to the Gene Vance Post Office Building. The designation is the whole of the law.
plaw-109-347-2006:
Port security is tightened across the board by Public Law 109-347, the Security and Accountability For Every Port Act of 2006, called the SAFE Port Act, approved October 13, 2006. Its aim is better maritime and cargo security through layered defenses.

Title I covers United States seaports. Area security plans must include salvage response, facility security plans face new rules and surprise inspections, and workers need a transportation security card, which felons convicted of certain crimes cannot get. Other sections order long-range vessel tracking, joint operations centers for port security, arrival notices for foreign vessels, and stronger crew identification. Port security grants and training programs follow in the next subtitle.
plaw-109-348-2006: San Juan, Puerto Rico, appears again near the end of this slice in Public Law 109-348, approved October 13, 2006. The Investigations Building of the Food and Drug Administration at 466 Fernandez Juncos Avenue is designated the Andres Toro Building. The references section speaks of the federal building referred to in section 1, a small wording slip, since the act names a specific agency building. References in federal records to it are deemed references to the Andres Toro Building.
plaw-109-349-2006: Morris, Illinois, has its own name inside its honoree's name in Public Law 109-349, approved October 13, 2006. The facility at 202 East Washington Street is designated the Joshua A. Terando Morris Post Office Building, joining the person's surname and the town's name in one title. The headed section gives designation and references as subsections. References to the Morris facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records are deemed references to that full Terando Morris name.
plaw-109-350-2006: Chillicothe, Ohio, closes the October 13, 2006 postal naming group with Public Law 109-350. The facility at 40 South Walnut Street is known and designated as the Larry Cox Post Office, in the plain form. Its headed section pairs designation with references: mentions of the Chillicothe facility in United States laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records are deemed references to the Larry Cox Post Office. The act gives no information about Cox himself.
plaw-109-351-2006:
Banks and the Federal Reserve get rule relief from Public Law 109-351, the Financial Services Regulatory Relief Act of 2006, approved October 13, 2006. Its stated aim is less regulatory burden and better productivity for insured deposit banks and other institutions.

Title I gives broker relief, requiring joint rulemaking on the definition of broker in the Securities Exchange Act. Title II changes monetary policy, letting the Federal Reserve pay interest on reserves and giving its board more freedom in setting reserve requirements. Title III turns to national banks. It covers voting in shareholder elections and simpler dividend math. It repeals an outdated limit on the Comptroller of the Currency. It also gives banks stronger power to invest in community development.
plaw-109-352-2006:
Dallas Love Field's flight limits are loosened by Public Law 109-352, the Wright Amendment Reform Act of 2006, approved October 13, 2006. The Wright Amendment had long fenced in service from Love Field, and this act amends its section of the 1979 air transportation law.

Airlines may now sell and provide through service and ticketing between Love Field and any United States or foreign destination. The route must pass through a point in Texas, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Kansas, Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, or Alabama. The old section itself is repealed eight years after enactment. Nonstop international flights from Love Field remain barred, and the airport cannot become a first entry or last departure point for the country.
plaw-109-353-2006:
North Korea is added to a sanctions frame built for Iran and Syria by Public Law 109-353, the North Korea Nonproliferation Act of 2006, approved October 13, 2006. Its policy statement cites North Korea's drive to make missiles, nuclear weapons, and other mass destruction weapons. It also cites United Nations Security Council Resolution 1695 of July 15, 2006. That resolution told member states to block transfers tied to those programs. 

United States policy, the act says, should sanction people who move such weapons and related goods to or from North Korea just as transfers involving Iran and Syria are sanctioned. Amendments to the Iran and Syria Nonproliferation Act follow.
plaw-109-354-2006: A Georgia barrier island map is swapped by Public Law 109-354, approved October 16, 2006, revising the Jekyll Island unit of the John H. Chafee Coastal Barrier Resources System. The old map subtitled GA-06P, in the official map set named in the Coastal Barrier Resources Act, is replaced by a new map with the unit's full title, dated July 10, 2006. The Secretary must keep the replacement map on file for public inspection. Boundaries change only as the new map draws them.
plaw-109-355-2006: Florida's Grayton Beach unit gets the same map treatment as Georgia's Jekyll Island in Public Law 109-355, approved October 16, 2006. The Coastal Barrier Resources System map for Grayton Beach Unit FL-95P in Walton County is replaced. The new map is titled Grayton Beach Unit FL-95P and Draper Lake Unit FL-96 and dated July 24, 2006. It replaces a map with nearly the same title dated October 24, 1990. The Secretary of the Interior keeps the maps on file for public inspection under the Coastal Barrier Resources Act.
plaw-109-356-2006:
Running the nation's capital is the subject of Public Law 109-356, the 2005 District of Columbia Omnibus Authorization Act, approved October 16, 2006, the last law in this slice. It authorizes improvements in how the District of Columbia government operates.

Title I covers governance. One subtitle gives budget flexibility, more power to use reserve funds, Government Services Administration help getting space for the Public Defender Service, entry into an interstate insurance compact, and metered taxicabs. A courts subtitle modernizes the Register of Wills office. It raises pay caps for nonjudicial court staff and clarifies pay for lawyers serving poor defendants. It also lets District courts hold proceedings outside the District in emergencies.
plaw-109-357-2006:
Public Law 109-357 of the 109th Congress, passed in 2006, is the Byron Nelson Congressional Gold Medal Act. It orders a Congressional gold medal for Byron Nelson, a golfer praised as a player, a teacher, and a commentator.

The findings in the sample praise Nelson's short but bright career. He won 54 events in 13 years, with a record 11 straight wins in 1945. That year he won 18 events in all. He also won five major titles, two of them at the Masters. The sample stops partway through the findings, before the terms for the medal itself.
plaw-109-358-2006:
In Public Law 109-358 of 2006, the 109th Congress passed the Lake Mattamuskeet Lodge Preservation Act. It deals with a lodge and refuge office site in North Carolina. The law hands that land from the federal government to the state.

The act tells the Secretary of the Interior to give the state about 6.25 acres with no payment. The land holds Mattamuskeet Lodge and the Mattamuskeet refuge office. As a term of the deal, the state must fix up and keep up the lodge. The lodge is on the National Register of Historic Places. The state must use the site as a public place for saving the state's natural and cultural resources.
plaw-109-359-2006:
Public Law 109-359 of the 109th Congress, from 2006, is the Long Island Sound Stewardship Act of 2006. It sets up the Long Island Sound Stewardship Initiative. The law aims to guard key sites around Long Island Sound.

The findings call the Sound a national treasure of great cultural and green value. Eight million people live in its watershed, and its health feeds more than five billion dollars a year in local trade. Yet less than a fifth of its shore is open to the public, and about a third of its tidal marshes have been filled. The new program is meant to find, guard, and improve the best upland sites in the Sound area.
plaw-109-360-2006:
The National Fish Hatchery System Volunteer Act of 2006 is Public Law 109-360 of the 109th Congress. It backs volunteer work and local team-ups for federal fish hatcheries. Those sites raise fish and help support wild fish stocks.

The findings say the system runs more than 60 hatcheries plus fish tech and health centers. It aids the rescue of more than 50 species at risk and the return of over 100 native species. Many sites are old, some from the late 1800s, and need costly upkeep. The law seeks more volunteers, gifts, and partners so that public funds can go further.
plaw-109-361-2006:
Public Law 109-361 of 2006 is the Veterans' Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2006, from the 109th Congress. It raises key pay rates for veterans hurt in service. It also raises support pay for the families of some veterans who have died.

On December 1, 2006, the Secretary of Veterans Affairs must raise the set dollar sums for disability pay. The raise also covers extra pay for dependents, the clothing allowance, and support pay for spouses and children left behind. Each sum goes up by the same rate as Social Security benefits. The sample stops before it gives that rate in full.
plaw-109-362-2006:
Northern California land is the subject of Public Law 109-362, the Northern California Coastal Wild Heritage Wilderness Act of 2006. Passed by the 109th Congress, it names new wilderness areas in the north of the state.

The act marks out parts of the Mendocino and Six Rivers national forests as wilderness. It also covers some Bureau of Land Management land in Humboldt, Lake, Mendocino, and Napa counties. It names the Elkhorn Ridge Potential Wilderness Area as well. Parts of the Black Butte River are named a wild or scenic river, and the act also adjusts the King Range area line.
plaw-109-363-2006:
Public Law 109-363 of the 109th Congress, passed in 2006, orders a fish hatchery handover in Pennsylvania. Its first title is the Tylersville Fish Hatchery Conveyance Act. The act holds more than this one transfer, but the sample shows only Title I.

Within 180 days, the Secretary of the Interior must give the state the Tylersville part of the Lamar hatchery at no cost. The site is about 40 acres at 43 Hatchery Lane in Loganton, with its buildings, gear, and water rights. The state fish and boat board is to run it as part of the state fish culture program.
plaw-109-364-2006:
The John Warner National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2007 is Public Law 109-364 of 2006. It is the yearly defense law of the 109th Congress. It funds the armed forces and sets troop levels for fiscal year 2007.

The act allows funds for military work and building by the Defense Department. It also covers defense work by the Energy Department and sets how many troops each force may keep. The sample shows only the first findings, which honor Senator John Warner. They note his near 28 years on the Senate Armed Services Committee and his own past service in the Navy and the Marine Corps.
plaw-109-365-2006:
Older Americans Act Amendments of 2006 is the short title of Public Law 109-365, passed by the 109th Congress in 2006. It updates the Older Americans Act of 1965. It also allows funds for that law for fiscal years 2007 through 2011.

The sample shows the act's table of contents rather than its full rules. The listed parts cover the Administration on Aging, elder abuse prevention, and the work of the Assistant Secretary. They also list pension advice, food and diet teaching, reports, and checks on how funds are used. A later title covers grants for state and town programs on aging.
plaw-109-366-2006:
Passed in 2006, Public Law 109-366 is the Military Commissions Act of 2006 of the 109th Congress. Its stated aim is to allow trial by military commission for breaches of the law of war.

The act first guards the President's power to set up such panels in martial law or held lands. Its contents list then covers the commissions themselves and changes to the military justice code. It also takes up treaty duties, habeas corpus claims, and review of commission verdicts. One part revises the Detainee Treatment Act of 2005 to shield some federal staff. The sample ends as the main commission section begins.
plaw-109-367-2006:
Border control is the aim of Public Law 109-367, the Secure Fence Act of 2006. The 109th Congress passed it in 2006. It seeks firm control of the land and sea borders of the United States.

Within 18 months, the Secretary of Homeland Security must act to gain and keep that control. The act calls for steady watch with staff and tech, such as drones, ground sensors, satellites, radar, and cameras. It also calls for more checkpoints, all-weather roads, and vehicle barriers. Control is defined as stopping all unlawful entries, from people to drugs. The Secretary must report progress to Congress each year.
plaw-109-368-2006: One narrow fix makes up Public Law 109-368, passed by the 109th Congress in 2006. It clears up how food aid services for older Americans are to be run. The act tells the Secretary of Agriculture to fill state and tribal food buying requests for fiscal year 2007 sent in before November 14, 2006. Those requests back the food services incentive program, and the health secretary must repay the farm agency for the cost.
plaw-109-369-2006: Public Law 109-369 of 2006 is a joint resolution of the 109th Congress on stopgap federal funding. It changes the Continuing Appropriations Resolution, 2007, set by Public Law 109-289. The change strikes the end date named in that resolution and puts in December 8, 2006. In plain terms, it keeps the stopgap funding in force a short while longer.
plaw-109-370-2006:
Connecticut rivers are the focus of Public Law 109-370, passed in 2006 by the 109th Congress. Its full name is the Lower Farmington River and Salmon Brook Wild and Scenic River Study Act of 2005. It orders a study, not a final listing.

The act adds a stretch of the lower Farmington River to the study list in the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act. The study stretch runs down to where the river meets the Connecticut River. Salmon Brook, with its main stem and east and west branches, is added too. Within three years of funds being freed up, the Secretary of the Interior must send Congress a report on what the study found.
plaw-109-371-2006: Public Law 109-371 of 2006, the Pactola Reservoir Reallocation Authorization Act of 2005, deals with one dam in South Dakota. Congress found that a 1977 law barred shifting the dam's costs without its consent. The act lets the Secretary of the Interior shift the building costs of Pactola Dam and Reservoir. The shift follows an August 2001 deal with Rapid City and the Rapid Valley district, moving costs from farm watering to city, factory, and fish and wildlife uses.
plaw-109-372-2006:
Idaho land swaps are set up by Public Law 109-372, the Idaho Land Enhancement Act of 2006. The 109th Congress passed the act to allow a trade of federal land inside the state.

The act rests on a deal first signed in April 2005 and changed in March 2006. The parties are the Bureau of Land Management, the Forest Service, the state, and the city of Boise. The sample's terms list about 605 acres of bureau land the state is to gain. They also list about 7,220 acres of national forest land in the trade. The sample stops partway through those land terms.
plaw-109-373-2006:
A loan debt from a 1990 water deal is wiped out by Public Law 109-373 of 2006. Its title is the Fort McDowell Indian Community Water Rights Settlement Revision Act of 2006. It revises one term of the Fort McDowell settlement law.

The act cancels the duty of the Fort McDowell Yavapai Nation to repay a loan made under the 1990 act. Apart from that change, the Nation's rights under the old settlement stay as they were. The act also treats the cancelled debt as meeting terms tied to it in the old law. The sample ends partway through that effect section.
plaw-109-374-2006:
Crimes against animal firms are the target of Public Law 109-374, the Animal Enterprise Terrorism Act of 2006. The 109th Congress said it gives the Justice Department the power it needs to catch, charge, and convict people who commit such acts.

The act rewrites section 43 of title 18 of the federal code. It bars travel or use of mail and trade links to harm or block an animal firm. Covered acts include harm to firm property, or to property of people tied to the firm. Threats, vandal acts, trespass, and pestering meant to make a person fear death or grave harm are also covered, as are plots and attempts.
plaw-109-375-2006:
California forest land changes hands under Public Law 109-375, the Sierra National Forest Land Exchange Act of 2006. The 109th Congress passed it to set the terms of one swap inside that forest.

The trade pairs 160 acres of federal land with about 80 acres of private land. The Sequoia Council of the Boy Scouts of America is the named group in the act's terms. If the private owner offers the land within one year, plus a cash payment of 50,000 dollars, the Secretary of Agriculture must hand over the federal parcel. The sample ends inside the swap terms.
plaw-109-376-2006: School land in El Paso County, Texas, is freed of a federal claim by Public Law 109-376 of 2006. The act tells the Secretary of State to release the back-claim of the United States in three tracts of the San Elizario Grant. The Clint school district gets the land clear, on one term. Any money from selling the land must go to public school uses.
plaw-109-377-2006:
Exchanging land in Colorado is the job of Public Law 109-377, the Pitkin County Land Exchange Act of 2006. The stated aim is to allow, direct, and speed a swap among three parties.

Those parties are the United States, Pitkin County, and the Aspen Valley Land Trust, a nonprofit group. The federal side, as the sample lists it, holds about 5.5 acres of national forest land in the county. It also holds 12 more forest parcels that add up to about 5.92 acres. The sample stops while still listing the federal land in the trade.
plaw-109-378-2006:
New study work for the Trail of Tears National Historic Trail is ordered by Public Law 109-378 of 2006. It updates the National Trails System Act. The study asks if more routes and sites tied to the Cherokee removal should join the trail.

Within six months, the Secretary of the Interior must finish the study and send it to Congress. The routes named are the Benge and Bell routes. Also named are water route sites in four states and the roads from the forts where Cherokee people were held to the depots they left from. Linked campgrounds are part of the study too. The act grants no new funds, but it lets the Secretary take gifts for the trail.
plaw-109-379-2006:
Settling a tribal claim is the core of Public Law 109-379, the Pueblo of Isleta Settlement and Natural Resources Restoration Act of 2006. The 109th Congress passed it to close the case of Pueblo of Isleta v. United States.

Congress found that the case was pending in the Court of Federal Claims under the Isleta Jurisdictional Act. The Pueblo and the United States had reached a deal that needed this law to take effect. The act aims to drain wet farm land and send water back to the Rio Grande River. It also aims to heal forest land, to cut fire and soil loss, and to end all claims under the old act.
plaw-109-380-2006: Frannie, Wyoming, gains a small town lot for free under Public Law 109-380 of 2006. The Secretary of the Interior must hand the town all federal rights in about 37,500 square feet once held back by the Commissioner of Reclamation. The United States keeps any oil and gas rights in the land. The act also cancels a 1990 special use permit and two old orders, from 1913 and 1920, as they touch that lot.
plaw-109-381-2006: One Delaware bridge gains a senator's name under Public Law 109-381 of 2006. The State Route 1 Bridge over the Chesapeake and Delaware Canal is named the Senator William V. Roth, Jr. Bridge. Any mention of the bridge in a federal law, rule, map, paper, or record is to be read as a mention of the bridge by that new name.
plaw-109-382-2006:
Wild land in two states is set aside by Public Law 109-382, the New England Wilderness Act of 2006. The 109th Congress passed it to add land to the national wilderness system and to name a national recreation area.

The sample shows the act's table of contents. Its first title covers New Hampshire, with new wilderness areas, maps, and rules for running them. Its second title covers Vermont in the same way. That title also sets up the Moosalamoo National Recreation Area, again with a map and rules. The sample ends with that contents list, before the act's own text.
plaw-109-383-2006:
Stopgap federal funding is stretched again by Public Law 109-383, a joint resolution of the 109th Congress from 2006. It further amends the Continuing Appropriations Resolution, 2007, first set by Public Law 109-289.

The main change moves the stopgap end date to February 15, 2007. Other changes add work under a chemical weapons cleanup building account and add payment dates in early 2007. One change renames a purchase line to cover partnership purchases and space station support. A further change lets some funds flow at the current rate for offices already cleared. The sample ends as new sections are added.
plaw-109-384-2006: Renaming a water plant in Byron, California, is all that Public Law 109-384 of 2006 does. The Bureau of Reclamation plant at 19550 Kelso Road, long known as the Tracy Pumping Plant, is to be known as the C.W. `Bill' Jones Pumping Plant. Any mention of the plant in a federal law, map, rule, paper, or record is to use the new name.
plaw-109-385-2006:
Mining and leasing are barred on a large New Mexico forest unit by Public Law 109-385 of 2006. Its title is the Valle Vidal Protection Act of 2005. The land is the Valle Vidal Unit of the Carson National Forest.

The unit holds 101,794 acres, named as Management Area 21 in the forest plan. The act pulls it out of entry and sale under the public land laws. It also pulls it out of the mining laws and the mineral and geothermal leasing laws. Rights already held stay valid. If such rights are given up or bought by the United States, the land is barred at once.
plaw-109-386-2006:
Farm water debts are eased by Public Law 109-386 of 2006, passed by the 109th Congress. It lets the Secretary of the Interior revise repayment deals with four irrigation districts in the Pick-Sloan Missouri Basin Program.

For the Bostwick district in Nebraska, the act evens out the yearly total owed for building and water supply charges. It also adds ten years to the dates for deposits into two reserve funds. The Kansas Bostwick district, No. 2, gets the same fix in the sample. The sample then starts the same terms for the Frenchman-Cambridge district, with the Webster district also named in the act's heading.
plaw-109-387-2006:
Two Wisconsin towns gain forest land for work sites under Public Law 109-387 of 2006. At a town's request, the Secretary of Agriculture must hand over national forest land in Forest County.

Laona is to get about 176 acres from the Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest. The town is to pay 300,000 dollars, the judged fair market value, and use the land as an industrial park site. Wabeno is to get about 173 acres on like terms, also for an industrial park. The sample gives Laona's full legal land lines and stops inside Wabeno's part. Each transfer starts only when the town asks for it.
plaw-109-388-2006:
Virginia takes over two federal fish hatcheries under Public Law 109-388 of 2006. Its title is the Paint Bank and Wytheville National Fish Hatcheries Conveyance Act. The 109th Congress directed the handover to the state.

Within 180 days, the Secretary of the Interior must give the state both hatcheries at no cost. The gift covers the land, buildings, gear, easements, leases, and water rights. The state fish and game office is to run them in the state fish culture program. If the land is used for any other end, it goes back to the United States.
plaw-109-389-2006: An old girls' school in Smyth County, Virginia, is handed to a church group by Public Law 109-389 of 2006. The Secretary of Agriculture must give the Evangelical Lutheran Coalition for Mission in Appalachia up to six acres at no cost. The site holds the former Konnarock Lutheran Girls School in the Mount Rogers National Recreation Area. The group takes the land as it stands and pays for the survey.
plaw-109-390-2006:
Bank contract rules are tightened by Public Law 109-390, the Financial Netting Improvements Act of 2006. The 109th Congress passed it to improve the netting process for financial contracts.

Netting lets firms offset what they owe each other under linked deals. The sample shows detailed changes to the Federal Deposit Insurance Act. They rework the term securities contract as used when a bank fails and a receiver steps in. The changes cover repurchase deals, guarantees made by new contracts, and how settlements count. The sample ends inside that list of wording changes, so the act's later parts stay unseen here.
plaw-109-391-2006:
Forest lines move in two states under Public Law 109-391, the Ouachita National Forest Boundary Adjustment Act of 2006. The 109th Congress redrew the edges of that forest in Oklahoma and Arkansas.

The new lines follow five maps, all dated May 15, 2001. They cover growth areas named Broken Bow, Southern Tiak, Northern Ouachita, Southern Ouachita, and Eastern Ouachita. The maps stay on file at the Forest Service chief's office for public viewing. The Secretary of Agriculture may make small fixes to them. Federal land gained inside the new lines is to be run as Weeks Act land.
plaw-109-392-2006: Lake Pontchartrain cleanup work gains more time under Public Law 109-392 of 2006. The act amends the Federal Water Pollution Control Act. In the basin program part, it strikes the year 2005 and puts in 2011, which renews the program. It also makes one small fix, renumbering a wet weather pilot projects part from section 121 to section 122.
plaw-109-393-2006: More time to build a power dam is granted by Public Law 109-393 of 2006. It covers the Arrowrock Hydroelectric Project, federal project number 4656. If the license is in force, the energy commission must, on the holder's request, add three years to start building. If the license has ended, the commission must bring it back and still add three years.
plaw-109-394-2006:
Keeping Native tongues alive is the aim of Public Law 109-394, the Esther Martinez Native American Languages Preservation Act of 2006. It amends the Native American Programs Act of 1974 to back immersion programs.

The act grows a program for the survival of Native American languages. It adds backing for language nests, site programs that teach and care for at least ten children under age seven. In a nest, the Native tongue is the main speech, for at least 500 hours a year per child. Parents get classes in the tongue too. The sample also begins terms for language survival schools for older pupils, then stops.
plaw-109-395-2006:
A gold medal for a farm scientist is set up by Public Law 109-395 of 2006. Its title is the Congressional Tribute to Dr. Norman E. Borlaug Act of 2006. The 109th Congress voted the medal for Dr. Borlaug himself.

The findings trace his path from an Iowa farm to the University of Minnesota, where he earned two degrees. They note his later post at Texas A&M University. After World War II he spent 20 years in poor rural Mexico. There he bred wheat that fought disease and gave far bigger yields. Congress credits that green revolution with saving huge numbers from hunger in Mexico, India, and Pakistan. The sample ends as his method spreads on.
plaw-109-396-2006:
Land deals in the capital are eased by Public Law 109-396, the Federal and District of Columbia Government Real Property Act of 2006. It covers sale, purchase, handover, and swaps of land in the District of Columbia.

The aim stated is to help such land be used, built up, and rebuilt. Title I covers swaps between the General Services Administration and the District. When the District hands the federal side the land named in the act, it gains U.S. Reservation 13 and the Old Naval Hospital. Reservation 13 is about 66 acres bounded by Independence Avenue Southeast, 19th Street Southeast, and G Street Southeast. The sample ends inside that land list.
plaw-109-397-2006: Harlem honors a music great in Public Law 109-397 of 2006, a naming act of the 109th Congress. The post office at 167 East 124th Street in New York, New York, is named the Tito Puente Post Office Building. Any mention of that site in a federal law, map, rule, paper, or record is to use the new name.
plaw-109-398-2006: Dallas gains a named post office under Public Law 109-398 of 2006. The site at 8135 Forest Lane is named the Dr. Robert E. Price Post Office Building. From then on, any mention of that site in a federal law, map, rule, paper, or record is to use Dr. Price's name. The bill passed the House in December 2005 and the Senate in December 2006, and was signed on December 18, 2006.
plaw-109-399-2006: In Lincoln, California, the post office at 200 Gateway Drive takes a new name under Public Law 109-399 of 2006. Congress named it the Beverly J. Wilson Post Office Building. Federal laws, maps, rules, papers, and records that mention the site are to use that name from then on. The bill passed the House on September 28, 2006, and the Senate on December 6, and was signed on December 18, 2006.
plaw-109-400-2006: Cleveland, Texas, is home to the post office renamed by Public Law 109-400 of 2006. The site at 1213 East Houston Street is named the Lance Corporal Robert A. Martinez Post Office Building. Any federal law, map, rule, paper, or record that names the site is to use that name. The bill passed the House on September 28, 2006, and the Senate on December 6, and was signed on December 18, 2006.
plaw-109-401-2006:
Atomic energy ties with India are the subject of Public Law 109-401 of 2006. Title I is the Henry J. Hyde United States-India Peaceful Atomic Energy Cooperation Act of 2006. The act frees a planned pact with India from some terms of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954.

The sample shows the sense of Congress that opens Title I. It calls stopping the spread of nuclear arms a key aim of United States foreign policy. It calls the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty the keystone of that policy and a clear success. It warns that states that never joined the treaty sit outside its rules. It urges that such states act with care with any nuclear tech they build.
plaw-109-402-2006: Pensacola's post office at 101 Palafox Place is renamed by Public Law 109-402 of 2006. Congress named it the Vincent J. Whibbs, Sr. Post Office Building. In any federal law, map, rule, paper, or record, the site is to be known by that name. The bill passed the House on September 28, 2006, and the Senate on December 6, and was signed on December 18, 2006.
plaw-109-403-2006: Tucson honors a noted lawmaker in Public Law 109-403 of 2006. The post office at 1501 South Cherrybell Avenue is named the Morris K. `Mo' Udall Post Office Building. Federal laws, maps, rules, and records that mention the site are to use the Udall name. The bill passed the House on September 25, 2006, and the Senate on December 6, and was signed on December 18, 2006.
plaw-109-404-2006: Flushing, in New York, gains the name set by Public Law 109-404 of 2006. Its post office at 29-50 Union Street is named the Dr. Leonard Price Stavisky Post Office. Note that the act says Post Office, not Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in federal records is to use that exact name.
plaw-109-405-2006: Westchester, Illinois, has the post office named by Public Law 109-405 of 2006. The site at 10240 Roosevelt Road is named the John J. Sinde Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, paper, or record is to use that name. The bill passed the House on September 28, 2006, and the Senate on December 6, and was signed on December 18.
plaw-109-406-2006: Maywood, Illinois, gains a named post office under Public Law 109-406 of 2006. Its site at 415 South 5th Avenue is named the Wallace W. Sykes Post Office Building. Federal laws, maps, rules, papers, and records that mention the site are to use that name. The bill passed both chambers in the fall of 2006 and was signed on December 18, 2006.
plaw-109-407-2006: Woodville, Texas, is the town in Public Law 109-407 of 2006, a post office naming act. The site at 307 West Wheat Street is named the Chuck Fortenberry Post Office Building. Any federal record that mentions the site is to use that name. The act was signed on December 18, 2006, after passage by the House in September and the Senate in December.
plaw-109-408-2006: Two fallen officers share the honor in Public Law 109-408 of 2006. The post office at 200 Lawyers Road, NW, in Vienna, Virginia, is named the Captain Christopher P. Petty and Major William F. Hecker, III Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record is to use that joint name. The act was signed on December 18, 2006.
plaw-109-409-2006: Farmington, Minnesota, has the post office named by Public Law 109-409 of 2006. The site at 216 Oak Street is named the Hamilton H. Judson Post Office, with no Building in the name. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, paper, or record is to use that name. The act was signed on December 18, 2006.
plaw-109-410-2006:
Water sharing in Montana is allowed by Public Law 109-410 of 2006. It lets two tribes lease water rights for a set time to a rural water group.

The Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes of the Fort Peck Indian Reservation may lease rights held under the Fort Peck-Montana Compact. The buyer is the Dry Prairie Rural Water Association, and the Secretary must approve the deal. A lease may run no more than 100 years and may be approved with no pay to the tribes. The act bars any sale that gives the water away for good.
plaw-109-411-2006: Tulsa, Oklahoma, has the post office named by Public Law 109-411 of 2006. The site at 6110 East 51st Place is named the Dewey F. Bartlett Post Office, with no Building in the name. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, paper, or record is to use that name. The act was signed on December 18, 2006.
plaw-109-412-2006: Great Falls, Montana, honors a Medal of Honor holder in Public Law 109-412 of 2006. The Armed Forces Readiness Center there is named the Captain William Wylie Galt Great Falls Armed Forces Readiness Center. The act's title notes that Galt held the Congressional Medal of Honor. Any federal record that mentions the center is to use his name. The act was signed on December 18, 2006.
plaw-109-413-2006: Thomaston, Georgia, honors a soldier in Public Law 109-413 of 2006. The post office at 103 East Thompson Street is named the Sergeant First Class Robert Lee `Bobby' Hollar, Jr. Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, paper, or record is to use that name. The act was signed on December 18, 2006.
plaw-109-414-2006: Farmington, Missouri, has the veterans clinic named by Public Law 109-414 of 2006. The site is the Robert Silvey Department of Veterans Affairs Outpatient Clinic. Any mention of the clinic in a federal law, map, rule, paper, or record is to use that name. The bill passed the Senate in November 2006 and the House in December, and was signed on December 18.
plaw-109-415-2006:
HIV and AIDS care grants are renewed by Public Law 109-415, the Ryan White HIV/AIDS Treatment Modernization Act of 2006. It revises and extends title XXVI of the Public Health Service Act, the part that funds life-saving care.

The sample shows the act's contents. Title I gives emergency relief grants to hard-hit areas, by formula and by added need. It sets rules on how fast grant funds must be spent. Title II covers care grants, the AIDS Drug Assistance Program, and aid for new hot spots. It also lists an early diagnosis grant program. The sample ends inside that contents list.
plaw-109-416-2006:
Autism research gets a push from Public Law 109-416, the Combating Autism Act of 2006. It amends the Public Health Service Act to fight autism by research, screening, action, and teaching.

The sample shows changes on centers of excellence for autism work. The head of the National Institutes of Health is told to grow and join up the agency's autism spectrum work. The fields named range from genetics and brain growth to food, drugs, and poisons. The work is to probe cause, with a look at factors in the world around us. It is also to probe finding cases early, stopping them, and treating them.
plaw-109-417-2006:
Readiness for health crises is the theme of Public Law 109-417, the Pandemic and All-Hazards Preparedness Act of 2006. It amends the Public Health Service Act on public health security and response to all hazards.

The sample shows the act's contents. One title sets up a new Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response and a National Health Security Strategy. A second covers state and local readiness, tech for tracking a crisis, staff growth, and vaccine tracking. It also covers a science board on biosecurity. A third title takes up the disaster medical system and surge capacity in hospitals. The sample ends there.
plaw-109-418-2006:
Chesapeake Bay water routes form a new trail under Public Law 109-418 of 2006. Its title is the Captain John Smith Chesapeake National Historic Trail Designation Act. It adds the trail to the National Trails System Act.

The trail runs about 3,000 miles along the bay and the streams that feed it. It crosses Virginia, Maryland, and Delaware, plus the District of Columbia. It traces the trips Captain John Smith made in 1607 to 1609 to chart the bay's lands and waters. A map from May 2006 is kept on file at the National Park Service. The Secretary of the Interior runs the trail, with help from bay groups.
plaw-109-419-2006:
A Concord farm with war roots is studied in Public Law 109-419 of 2006. The farm is the Colonel James Barrett Farm in Massachusetts, about six acres with a house and outbuildings. It is on the National Register of Historic Places.

The act tells the Secretary of the Interior to run a boundary study within two years of funds being freed. The study weighs the farm's weight in the Revolutionary War. It also weighs how well the farm could join Minute Man National Historical Park. Points to check include public use, running costs, and private property issues. The study must also judge if other plans could guard the farm as well.
plaw-109-420-2006:
Worry over skilled plane and space workers drives Public Law 109-420 of 2006. It sets up an Interagency Aerospace Revitalization Task Force. The group's job is a national plan to recruit, train, and grow that workforce.

Congress found that the aerospace field makes nearly 15 percent of the nation's output and backs about 11 million jobs. It also found that field jobs hit a 50-year low in 2004. More than a quarter of factory staff in the field could retire by 2008. United States pupils rank near the bottom in math and science tests. The task force is to build a federal plan, starting with better work across agencies.
plaw-109-421-2006: Trust land for a Paiute tribe is set by Public Law 109-421 of 2006. About 240 acres, with any buildings on them, are held in trust by the United States for the Utu Utu Gwaitu Paiute Tribe of the Benton Paiute Reservation. The land lies in section 11 of a named township near the Mount Diablo line. One firm term bars class II and class III gaming on the land.
plaw-109-422-2006:
Underage drinking is the target of Public Law 109-422, the Sober Truth on Preventing Underage Drinking Act, or STOP Act. The 109th Congress passed it in 2006 to back programs against drinking by the young.

The act rewrites a part of the Public Health Service Act. It sets terms for the alcohol trade, school-based prevention in grades K through 12, and youth, meaning people under 21. It cites a 2003 report called Reducing Underage Drinking: A Collective Responsibility. Congress states that a broad, joined effort is key. That effort spans prevention, care, law enforcement, and research, with federal aid for state work.
plaw-109-423-2006:
Nurse visas for needy areas gain three more years under Public Law 109-423 of 2006. Its title is the Nursing Relief for Disadvantaged Areas Reauthorization Act of 2005. It extends changes first made by a 1999 act of like name.

Those changes ease entry rules for nurses from abroad who work in areas short of health staff. Under the new act, the changes apply to petitions filed in a set span. That span ends three years after this act became law. The act also frees steps to carry it out from the usual rule-making law. The sample ends inside that freedom clause.
plaw-109-424-2006:
Wave warnings get a boost from Public Law 109-424, the Tsunami Warning and Education Act of 2006. It backs the tsunami program of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, run by the National Weather Service.

The stated aims are to improve spotting, forecasting, warning, and damage control for tsunamis. The Pacific warning system is to be updated for wider cover, fewer false alarms, and sharper forecasts. Cover is to grow to the Atlantic Ocean, the Caribbean Sea, and the Gulf of Mexico. The act also backs mapping, modeling, and research. It backs teaching so that people at risk know what to do when a wave nears.
plaw-109-425-2006: Travel time off for Justice Department lawyers is the sole point of Public Law 109-425 of 2006. Lawyers hired by the department, plus assistant United States attorneys, may earn make-up time off for travel. The right comes under section 5550b of title 5 of the federal code. It holds in spite of an older funding law clause. It applies to travel on or after the day the act became law.
plaw-109-426-2006: Free official mail in the search for lost children is made lasting by Public Law 109-426 of 2006. The whole act is one line. It strikes section 5 of Public Law 99-87, the clause that set an end date for the mail right. With that clause gone, the use of penalty and franked mail to find and recover missing children has no set end.
plaw-109-427-2006: A bust of Sojourner Truth is headed for the Capitol under Public Law 109-427 of 2006. Congress found that Truth was a towering figure in the women's suffrage movement. It also found that the Portrait Monument in the rotunda, given in 1920 for the Nineteenth Amendment, shows her peers but not Truth herself. Within two years, the Joint Committee on the Library must accept a donated bust of her. It must then place the bust in a fit lasting spot in the Capitol.
plaw-109-428-2006:
Fine wool labels are pinned to fiber size by Public Law 109-428 of 2006. Its long title is the Wool Suit Fabric Labeling Fairness and International Standards Conforming Act. It amends the Wool Products Labeling Act of 1939.

The act ties each Super grade to the mean width of the wool fiber, in microns. Super 80's needs a mean of 19.75 microns or finer. Each step up the scale cuts the limit: 19.25 for 90's, 18.75 for 100's, and so on down. The sample runs through Super 150's at 16.25 microns, then stops. The point is fair labels that match world standards and guard buyers.
plaw-109-429-2006:
War of 1812 battle sites in Michigan are studied under Public Law 109-429, the River Raisin National Battlefield Study Act of 2006. It tells the Secretary of the Interior to run a special resource study.

The sites sit in Monroe County and tie to the Battles of the River Raisin, fought on January 18 and 22, 1813, and what came after. The study must weigh the sites' national weight. It must also weigh how well they could join the National Park System. The Secretary is to ask federal, state, and local bodies, plus groups with an interest. A report is due within three years of the first funds.
plaw-109-430-2006:
Drought tracking gets a national home in Public Law 109-430, the National Integrated Drought Information System Act of 2006. It sets up that system inside the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

The system is run by the Under Secretary, through the National Weather Service and other weather and climate programs. The act first defines drought as a lack of rain that drains surface and ground water. Such a lack may hit farms, towns, property, or the land itself with heavy costs. The system's core job is an early warning service. It is to gather key drought signals and give sound, timely forecasts and ratings of how bad a drought is.
plaw-109-431-2006:
Power-hungry data centers are put under the lens by Public Law 109-431 of 2006. Its stated aim is to study and boost the use of energy-saving computer servers in the United States.

Within 180 days, the head of the Environmental Protection Agency must send Congress a study, done through the Energy Star program. It is to track the fast growth and power use of data centers run by the government and by firms. It is to weigh shifts to low-power chips and servers and the savings they could bring. It is also to weigh gains for the power grid and any hit to speed or trust in the gear.
plaw-109-432-2006:
Tax breaks and health care share one large act in Public Law 109-432, the Tax Relief and Health Care Act of 2006. It amends the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to extend tax rules that were set to lapse.

The sample shows the start of the act's contents, in Division A. The reliefs kept alive include a deduction for college tuition costs. They also include the new markets tax credit, a choice to deduct state and local sales taxes, and the research credit. Job credits, combat pay rules, and teacher cost write-offs are listed too. So are brownfield cleanup write-offs and credits for hiring on Indian reservations. The sample ends inside that list.
plaw-109-433-2006: Tank leak cleanup funds gain wider use under Public Law 109-433 of 2006. The act amends section 9508 of the tax code, which guards the Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund. It widens the list of sections for which fund money may be spent. The list now runs to added parts of sections 9003 through 9013. The act makes one matching fix in the Solid Waste Disposal Act, and it takes effect at once.
plaw-109-434-2006: Permit speed money for the Army gains two more years under Public Law 109-434 of 2006. The whole act changes one date in section 214(c) of the Water Resources Development Act of 2000. The end date moves from December 31, 2006, to December 31, 2008. That extends the Army Secretary's power to take and spend funds from non-federal public bodies to speed permit work.
plaw-109-435-2006:
Deep reform of the mail system is the work of Public Law 109-435, the Postal Accountability and Enhancement Act of 2006. Its stated aim is to reform the postal laws of the United States.

The sample shows the first part of the act's contents. Early titles set terms for postal services and a modern system for setting rates. Rates are split between products the post office leads and those it fights rivals for. Later titles in view set modern service standards and a postal service plan. They also set fair play rules, with a fund for rival products and a deemed tax on their income.
plaw-109-436-2006:
Michigan's sea past is surveyed under Public Law 109-436, the Michigan Lighthouse and Maritime Heritage Act of 2006. It tells the Secretary of the Interior to run a special resource study of maritime sites in the state.

The Secretary is to work with the state, its historic preservation officer, and other public and private groups. The study's aim is to find sound ways to guard key maritime sites for the long term. It is also to find how the public can best learn about and visit them. The study must review past site lists and studies. It must then suggest the care plans that would guard the sites best.
plaw-109-437-2006:
Fake claims to war medals are the target of Public Law 109-437, the Stolen Valor Act of 2005. It amends title 18 of the federal code to guard the name and meaning of the Medal of Honor and other awards.

Congress found that false claims about the Medal of Honor, the service crosses, and the Purple Heart harm what those awards stand for. It also found that police had too little power to charge such fakes. The act widens the crime in section 704 to cover buying, shipping, trading, and ads for medals and awards. It then starts a new crime for false claims of having won them. The sample ends there.
plaw-109-438-2006:
Trade finance gains new life in Public Law 109-438, the Export-Import Bank Reauthorization Act of 2006. It renews the Export-Import Bank of the United States, the federal bank that backs sales abroad.

The sample shows the act's contents. Early parts extend the bank's powers and keep an Africa advice group. They cover loans for mild defense goods bound for civil use and name touchy trade fields. Later parts push small firm exports, bar cheats, and seek more openness. They set caps on loans, guarantees, and insurance as a whole. Still later parts cover tied aid, notice to loan seekers, and green energy sales.
plaw-109-439-2006: Charity gifts in bankruptcy are cleared up by Public Law 109-439 of 2006. Its title is the Religious Liberty and Charitable Donation Clarification Act of 2006.
