Qi Wang and co-authors test a teaching model that blends AI, case-based learning, and a flipped classroom for reproductive medicine residents, in a 2026 randomized controlled trial. Lecture teaching often fails to build clinical decision-making during residency rotations, a problem as infertility care grows more complex. The trial ran at the First Hospital of Jilin University.

Fifty obstetrics and gynecology residents were randomized to the blended model or to traditional lectures. The blended group worked through cases with virtual patients before class on one platform, reviewed cases on another, and then debated them in class. After the course, the blended group scored higher on theory tests, on observed clinical evaluations, and on structured clinical exams. They also reported stronger motivation, better clinical thinking, and more self-guided learning than the lecture group. The authors recommend the model as an effective, transferable way to train reproductive medicine doctors.
pmc-13218606:
Louise-Helene Gagnon, Humara Edell, and Patricia E. Lee review the diagnosis and management of urinary incontinence in women in a 2026 article. Incontinence is common and undertreated, because patients stay silent: many assume leaking is normal with aging or feel embarrassed to raise it. Earlier work suggests a majority of women never seek care, and it costs Canada an estimated 2.6 billion dollars a year.

The first step is classifying the problem, because treatment follows the type. Stress incontinence leaks urine when abdominal pressure rises, as with coughing or exercise, while urge incontinence follows a need to urinate, usually with frequency and night-time trips. First-line care is conservative: behavioural therapy, pelvic floor and bladder training, noninvasive options, and attention to contributing conditions. Surgery is the second-line answer for stress incontinence, and medication for urge incontinence. Matching the plan to the type is what makes treatment work.
pmc-13219706:
Amir Hossein Alipour, Fatemeh Hoda Fallah, and Bahman Abedi Kiasari build blood tests for two widespread polyomaviruses in a 2026 study. BK and JC viruses infect most people in childhood, then persist, becoming dangerous when immunity is suppressed, as in transplant patients. Reliable antibody tests are the backbone of tracking who carries them.

The team produced the viruses' VP1 shell proteins in insect cells and used them to build ELISA assays, then ran sixty-seven serum samples. Antibodies to BK virus appeared in 77.6 percent of samples and to JC virus in 34.3 percent, with both rising with age, as expected for infections acquired. Competition experiments showed the two tests did not confuse one virus's antibodies for the other's, confirming specificity. Antigens made in the insect-cell system gave stronger signals than alternatives. The authors offer the assays for population surveys and for watching at-risk patients such as transplant recipients.
pmc-13222006:
Ni Luh Lany Christina and co-authors review how endometriosis affects ovarian reserve, in a 2026 systematic review of studies published between 2015 and 2024. Endometriosis causes chronic pelvic pain and infertility, and cysts on the ovaries can erode the egg supply. Ten studies met the quality and reporting standards the team applied.

Women with endometriosis showed lower hormone markers and fewer visible follicles than healthy comparison groups. Chronic inflammation and oxidative stress were identified as damaging routes. Surgery to remove cysts can ease symptoms and may aid fertility, yet it can also remove healthy tissue and deepen reserve loss. Early diagnosis and personalized planning are the authors' main prescriptions.
pmc-13227206:
Rogério Aires and colleagues check a 2026 mouse study of whether cyclophosphamide, a drug widely used to suppress the immune system in experiments, quietly disturbs the brain. If it did, countless neuroimmune studies could be confounded. Male mice received weekly injections for three or four weeks, then underwent behaviour batteries, brain tissue checks, and gene-expression measurement.

Immune suppression clearly took hold in the body, with slower weight gain and altered white-cell counts. Behaviour, though, barely moved, showing only mild, passing changes in strength and sickness-like signs. Brain tissue showed no structural damage and no activation of star-shaped support cells. One gene, Lgals3, rose significantly in the brain, a molecular footnote in an otherwise reassuring picture of central resilience.
pmc-13227806:
Abdulelah K Alqawlaq and colleagues report a 2026 Saudi case of a teenager with an ultra-rare skeletal disorder who went from wheelchair use to walking with support after staged joint surgery. Whole-genome sequencing confirmed spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia with joint laxity type 3, caused by a fault in the EXOC6B gene. The disorder loosens joints, invites repeated dislocations, and had severely damaged both hips and knees since early childhood.

Surgeons replaced both hips first, then both knees, tailoring the plan to her anatomy. Pain fell markedly and mobility returned step by step until she could walk with assistance. The team presents the case as the first surgically managed report of this condition in Saudi Arabia, arguing rare-disease patients deserve individualised operative planning.
pmc-13229406:
Kuang Ma and colleagues present MultiVTP in 2026, a computer method for finding human proteins that viruses target. A single host protein can serve several viruses, so the task is framed as multilabel prediction. The work uses only information inside host proteins themselves.

MultiVTP samples small graphs around each query protein and combines several kinds of protein features. A graph transformer then looks for patterns shared across viruses and patterns tied to one virus. Tests against other models showed stronger accuracy, even when training data were limited. Applied across the human proteome, the method points to new candidate targets for single viruses and for several viruses at once.
pmc-13230506:
Simon Hefner and colleagues test in 2026 whether photos of fingernails and eyelids can estimate hemoglobin without a blood draw. Their HeMonitor study enrolled three hundred sixty-seven patients with blood cancers plus healthy donors for comparison. Machine learning models learned to predict lab hemoglobin values from the images alone.

The best model landed close to lab values, with spread near one unit on the reported scale. A second exploratory layer combined each estimate with patient reports of overall health and fatigue. Lower estimates generally matched worse quality of life, which fits the known burden of anemia. Agreement with clinician judgment looked encouraging in borderline ranges. Home monitoring built this way still needs testing in planned follow-up studies.
pmc-13233006:
Charles Amoatey Odonkor and colleagues published a 2026 pilot study testing whether shoe-mounted sensors can measure walking as accurately as laboratory cameras. Twenty people took part, half with knee osteoarthritis and half healthy. Each person walked at a self-chosen pace, a fast pace, and an endurance pace while sensors and a motion capture system recorded more than 5,000 strides.

Sensor estimates of walking speed matched the camera system almost exactly, and stride length and cadence also agreed closely. Everyone finished the protocol with minimal problems. Participants who reported more physical activity tended to walk faster with longer strides, though the small sample makes that pattern tentative. The authors see the sensors as a practical way to track walking outside the lab.
pmc-13233806:
Miguel Castro and colleagues published a 2026 environmental study of peatland restoration in Kalimantan, Indonesia. Drained tropical peat burns readily, and Indonesia's peat fires rank among the country's largest greenhouse gas sources. After catastrophic fires in 2015, the government and partners blocked drainage canals to rewet peatlands. The team used statistical counterfactual methods to estimate what would have burned without the rewetting between 2017 and 2022.

Effects varied by place, and canal blocks whose rewetted zones overlapped performed best at preventing fire. If every block worked at that level, rewetting could avoid up to 6.4 percent of the burnt area and deliver economic returns above one hundred percent within a decade at the best sites. The authors argue restoration pays, provided blocks are placed to overlap.
pmc-13234106:
Zhixiang Jiang and colleagues published a 2026 materials study on parking helpful bacteria on biochar, charcoal made from heated plant waste. Anchored microbes survive harsh conditions better, a boon for cleaning salty or polluted soils. The team made biochars from several feedstocks at two temperatures and measured how well each loaded the soil bacterium Bacillus subtilis.

Biochars cooked at seven hundred degrees carried far more bacteria than those made at four hundred, by roughly fourteen to sixty percent. Loading changed the char surface, adding carbon and nitrogen, enriching chemical groups, and flipping it from water-repelling to water-loving. Modeling pointed to chemical, single-layer attachment driven by charge pull, hydrogen bonds, and water-shy forces together. Bacteria settled in two stages, sticking and filling pores first, then locking in with their own glue-like coatings. Anchored bacteria also tolerated salt far better.
pmc-13235406:
Ariyawan Tantipongpiradet and colleagues tested in 2026 whether an olive-derived compound can protect rats against chronic stress. Hydroxytyrosol, produced through biotechnology, was given daily in an oral jelly before and during a period of unpredictable restraint stress. Rats of both sexes underwent tests of anxiety, mood, memory, and social behaviour. Brain tissue from the hippocampus was also sequenced cell by cell.

Stress alone produced anxiety-like behaviour, reduced pleasure response, memory problems, and social withdrawal in the animals. Treatment prevented those behavioural changes across the tests reported. Stress-related drops in dopamine and serotonin were also prevented, while a stress hormone rise was blunted. Thousands of gene changes across neurons and support cells were largely normalized by treatment. The authors identify hydroxytyrosol as a dietary candidate for building stress resilience.
pmc-13235706:
Perin and colleagues estimate what killed newborns and young children worldwide between 2000 and 2024. Their secondary analysis covers 195 countries. It uses a Bayesian statistical model to split deaths by cause, drawing on journal studies, health surveys, and World Health Organization mortality records, among many other sources.

Cause splits matter because the big killers of the first month differ from those of ages one to four. Fresh estimates show where past gains came from and where deaths still cluster. Governments and aid groups use such numbers to aim vaccines, newborn care, and nutrition money. The authors update an earlier round of estimates with data through the pandemic years.
pmc-13235906:
Reginato and Brandl build a new tool for naming the small, hidden fishes of coral reefs. Reefs hold more than a third of all marine species, yet many reef fishes are tiny, shy, and easy to confuse. Specialists who can tell them apart are few, so much reef life goes unrecorded in surveys.

Their tool joins deep learning with the branching structure of biological classification and very detailed images. Teaching the model the family tree, not just the final name, helps it sort look-alike species. Better identification from photos could widen reef monitoring sharply, letting cameras and computers do work that now waits on a handful of experts.
pmc-13236106:
Taro Higuchi, Hiro Nakao, and Yoshitsugu Fukuda described in 2026 a bone infection in a four-month-old girl that looked like a paralysed leg. She had stopped extending her left leg for six days and resisted during nappy changes. Early hip imaging at a community clinic had shown nothing abnormal. She had no fever, redness, swelling, or loss of appetite on presentation.

Examination in infants localizes pain poorly, so the authors stress imaging the whole affected limb early. Prompt recognition matters because acute bone infection can settle into chronic disease and form enclosed abscesses. Such abscesses near the growth plate can disturb later bone growth, requiring long follow-up. Serious disease can hide behind quiet presentations without fever or general symptoms in this age group. A systematic workup for limb disuse in infants forms the article's central practical message.
pmc-13236506:
Javier Cifuentes-Quin and co-authors compared in 2026 side effects of two shortened radiotherapy schedules for prostate cancer in Colombia. More than two hundred men treated at one oncology centre between 2018 and 2025 entered the comparison. One schedule spread dose over moderately fewer sessions, while the other compressed treatment into very few sessions. Toxicity was graded with standard criteria for both early and later effects.

Early side effects occurred in about a quarter of the moderately compressed group, notably above the ultra-compressed group. Later side effects also appeared far more often under the moderate schedule in the records. Erectile dysfunction was the single most common late problem recorded in follow-up. Adjusted analysis confirmed lower odds of early toxicity with the ultra-compressed schedule independently. The authors argue the shorter course suits middle-income settings by improving efficiency and access without worse safety.
pmc-13239306:
Samuel Gonçalves Encarnação and colleagues pooled twenty-three observational studies in 2026 on device-measured activity, sitting time, and frailty in older adults. Wearable accelerometers supplied the movement data, avoiding the rosy bias of self-report. Fourteen studies fed the activity meta-analysis and eleven the sedentary-time one.

Spontaneous physical activity correlated moderately and inversely with frailty: more movement, less frailty. Sedentary time correlated positively, with most analyzed studies agreeing. Both pools varied a lot between studies, and removing single studies shifted the numbers noticeably, so the authors keep the claims at association level. Even so, the direction is consistent enough to back programs that get older adults moving and sitting less. Frailty prevention, they argue, is partly a daily-steps problem.
pmc-13239706: A 2026 correction notice in the journal Food Science and Nutrition amends the funding statement of a study by Noreen and co-authors on bioactive compounds from jujube fruit. The notice is a correction only, with no new results or changed conclusions. It adds two omitted funding sources, a Hallym University research fund award from 2023 and a Korean National Research Foundation programme grant, and the authors apologise for the omission.
pmc-13240406:
Abdisalam Ahmed Sandeyl and colleagues describe lungs wrecked by earlier tuberculosis in a 2026 Ugandan case report. A 60-year-old man with six years of poorly completed tuberculosis treatment arrived with three weeks of worsening cough, foul yellow sputum sometimes streaked with blood, breathlessness, and chest pain.

Scans showed extensive damage, with widened distorted airways, large air blisters, and scarring worst in the left lung. Sputum grew two bacteria, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Streptococcus pneumoniae, confirming an infective flare on top of the structural damage. Intravenous antibiotics, later matched to the culture results, plus supportive care eased his symptoms. The case underlines the cost of incomplete tuberculosis treatment.
pmc-13240906:
Nguyen at Vietnam's National Economics University weighed land use efficiency and urban form across three Indochina capitals. Hanoi, Vientiane, and Phnom Penh were tracked from 2017 to 2024. The assessment paired the UN land-consumption indicator with spatial clustering statistics. A shape index gauged how compact each capital's footprint stayed.

Land expansion outran population growth in all three cities. Phnom Penh showed the most compact, strongly grouped growth despite the fastest land uptake. Hanoi sprawled with weaker clustering, while Vientiane expanded in loose, fragmented patches. Nguyen urges tighter spatial planning before these trajectories harden.
pmc-13241206:
Singh and colleagues at Royal Darwin Hospital charted chronic melioidosis across Australia's Northern Territory over thirty-four years. Cases with symptoms lasting two months or more came to one hundred twenty-six. That was under a tenth of all melioidosis recorded since 1989. Chronic cases were set head-to-head with acute presentations.

Pneumonia and skin infections dominated, and scans were often first read as cancer or tuberculosis. Chronic patients carried fewer classic risk factors like diabetes. Their blood tests turned positive far less often, and death was much rarer. Antibody tests, notably, flagged eighty-seven percent of chronic cases at diagnosis.
pmc-13241506:
Galectins, a family of proteins that bind sugar chains on other molecules, take center stage in a review by Popatia and colleagues at the University of Ottawa. The authors map how these proteins steer signaling inside and outside cells. Sixteen mammalian galectins fall into three structural types, each with its own binding habits. Their influence reaches growth, blood vessel formation, and immune control.

Across diseases, the review links galectins to cancer spread, heart and vessel damage, brain degeneration, metabolic problems, and autoimmunity. Some family members push in opposite directions depending on tissue, which complicates drug design. Trials already test blockers ranging from modified carbohydrates and pectins to antibodies. New tools such as single-cell glyco-RNA sequencing and CRISPR glycoengineering may sharpen future galectin drugs.
pmc-13241606:
Phimha and colleagues at Khon Kaen University measured what a denture visit really costs elderly Thai patients and their caretakers. The team surveyed three hundred forty-six patient-caretaker pairs at three tertiary hospitals. Data came from structured questionnaires collected over six months. Costs were split into direct payments and lost income.

Each visit drained about one hundred forty-eight purchasing-power-adjusted dollars from the household. Patients carried the largest share through medical payments and their own lost earnings. Caretakers absorbed well over a third of the burden, almost entirely as forgone wages. Visits averaged more than six hours, and the authors urge policies that cut both household costs and clinic time.
pmc-13241706:
Draidi's team in Doha chased a bleeding source that hid from every camera and scan. Their patient, 69, kept returning with black stools and severe anemia needing transfusions. His blood pressure swung wildly between spells. Standard upper and lower scope exams found nothing at all. CT vessel scans also failed to find the elusive leak.

A swallowed camera capsule hinted at far small-bowel bleeding without pinpointing it. Sepsis tangled the transfusion-dependent course. Keyhole surgery finally exposed two jejunal pouches with engorged vessels. Cutting out that bowel segment stopped the bleeding for good.
pmc-13242106:
Güner's team at Hacettepe fix a naming slip in their 2023 study of swallowing problems and frailty in Alzheimer's disease. The Methods named the thinking test the Mini-Mental State Examination. The team in fact used the test's standard form. Rights and trademark claims forced the fix. The study first appeared in BMC Geriatrics.

Every mention now reads Standardized Mini-Mental State Examination, shortened to SMMSE. The mark rests with the test's creator and its licensed seller. The authors state plainly that the data, results, and takeaways stand untouched. The journal amended the article in full.
pmc-13242206:
Hesti Witasari Jos Erry and a large team publish a 2026 systematic review of stem cell exosomes from 3D spheroid cultures for tooth pulp regeneration. Tiny vesicles released by stem cells carry healing signals without using live cells. Growing the parent cells as spheres may strengthen those signals compared with flat dish culture.

Ten early lab studies met the review standards. Vesicles from sphere cultures encouraged blood vessel growth, tooth-forming cell development, and calmer immune responses. Several studies reported stronger repair markers than vesicles from flat cultures. Few studies, however, tested tooth pulp outcomes directly; others offered indirect evidence from different tissues. The authors call the approach promising but preliminary, and they ask for standardized studies before clinical use.
pmc-13242506:
Mahmoud Abdel-Nasser and colleagues studied how to protect a badly decayed old manuscript without harsh chemicals. Their paper appeared in Scientific Reports in 2026. The eleventh-century manuscript, paper pages and leather binding alike, suffered stains, acidity, weakened fibers, and missing pieces. Imaging and chemical tests documented the damage, and the team cultured the fungi living on it, finding thirteen strains, led by Aspergillus species that secrete fiber-eating enzymes.

Their proposed remedy pairs an extract from bacterial probiotics with nanoparticles made by green methods. The goal is a treatment that suppresses the manuscript's own fungi while sparing the artifact, the conservator, and the environment. Traditional synthetic fungicides can endanger all three. The study first proves how much of the decay is biological, driven by enzymes the fungi release. It then argues this gentler mix deserves a place in museum practice.
pmc-13242806:
Yanchi Wang and co-authors publish a 2026 questionnaire study of nursing students at one Chinese university, linking childhood trauma to early psychotic-like symptoms. Such prodromal symptoms can precede psychosis and cause real distress. The study tested whether depression and anxiety carry part of the trauma effect.

About a quarter of the students reported prodromal symptoms. Overall, trauma scores and distress scores both rose alongside symptom scores. Pathway analysis found significant mediation only for physical abuse and sexual abuse. For each, depression and anxiety together carried about half of the association with symptoms. The authors note the one-time design cannot prove cause. They suggest support for affected students should target mood and anxiety symptoms directly.
pmc-13242906:
Deepika Beereddy and co-authors describe a severe immune complication of cancer immunotherapy that resisted standard treatment. Their case report appeared in Cureus in 2026. A seventy-seven-year-old woman with advanced endometrial cancer developed weakness, drooping eyelids, double vision, and breathing trouble twenty-four days after one combined dose of chemotherapy and pembrolizumab. Tests showed inflammation of heart muscle, skeletal muscle, and the nerve-muscle junction, plus an overactive thyroid.

This overlap syndrome can be fatal, and her case proved stubborn. Pulse steroids and plasma exchange helped too little, so rituximab was added, and continuing heart inflammation later forced two further immune drugs, abatacept and ruxolitinib. Under the escalated regimen her symptoms and blood markers finally improved, and she went home on a tapering plan. The authors urge doctors who spot one part of the triad to screen for the others.
pmc-13243106:
Ying Lei and colleagues wrote this 2026 review on Crohn's disease, a long-term gut illness that often leads to disability. Watching the disease closely matters, but common checks can be invasive, slow to show change, or unable to see through the full bowel wall.

The review centres on blood fats and on creeping fat, a layer of belly fat that wraps around the inflamed bowel in this disease. During active illness, patients show a typical pattern of disturbed blood fats tied to body-wide inflammation. Creeping fat itself feeds inflammation and scarring, and scans can use it to predict surgery risk and return of disease after an operation.
pmc-13243406:
Søren Esben Rytter Heilskov and colleagues revisit an old idea about acts that seem to make no sense in a 2026 essay on criminal insanity. Courts lean on delusions, stated in words, when judging whether psychosis drove a crime. Yet some disturbed acts are never explained by the person who did them.

The essay returns to psychiatrist Klaus Conrad and his notion of senseless actions in early schizophrenia. A historical case from Karl Wilmanns shows how such acts can mark the slide into open psychosis. The authors argue that these acts reflect a broad break in how a person finds meaning in the world. Judging them fairly needs the person's life story as context, they conclude.
pmc-13244506:
Muhammed Hassan Nasr and co-authors ran a placebo-controlled trial of high-dose vitamin D in men with type 2 diabetes. Their study appeared in the Journal of Pharmaceutical Policy and Practice in 2026. Sixty men at Taibah University in Saudi Arabia took either fifty thousand units of vitamin D3 weekly or a dummy pill for twenty-four weeks. Blood tests tracked vitamin levels, insulin resistance, fasting sugar, and glucose control.

The supplement did its first job well: vitamin D levels climbed in the treated group and deficiency was corrected, while the placebo group barely moved. But the hoped-for metabolic payoff never came. Insulin resistance, fasting glucose, and glycated hemoglobin all failed to improve beyond placebo. Weight and lipids likewise showed no shift. The authors conclude vitamin D should be prescribed to fix deficiency, not marketed as a glucose treatment. Their negative result matters because hopes were high.
pmc-13246506:
Nguyen and colleagues measured what marine plastic costs small-scale fishers in Viet Nam, in this 2026 Communications Earth and Environment study. Working in the Mekong and Red River deltas, the team interviewed nearly two hundred nearshore fishers, ran follow-up verification interviews, and audited the debris hauled up in hundreds of fishing nets.

Plastic cost each vessel roughly thirty-four hundred dollars a year, about an eighth of vessel revenue and a quarter of the owner's income, through lost time, damaged gear, and reduced catches. Fishers also reported injuries, and even deaths, from entanglement incidents at sea. The burden fell hardest on lower-income Mekong fishers. Paying fishers to collect plastic at priority spots, the authors suggest, could cut pollution and support livelihoods together.
pmc-13246706:
Dana Baron Shahaf and colleagues test a one-channel brain wave marker during heart surgery in 2026 work. Thinking often dips after surgery in older patients, sometimes for good. A live marker of brain trouble during the operation could open a window to act.

The team studied EEG and test data from 100 adults having cardiac surgery. Their Brain Reactivity Index tracked with thinking change in patients aged 65 and over. The link showed within the first half hour of anesthesia. It held strongest for patients whose starting scores sat in a middle band. Younger patients showed no such link. The marker may flag risk while care can still adjust.
pmc-13246806:
Jander, Bergner, Schönwald, and co-authors examined whether a newer Parkinson's infusion therapy also eases non-motor symptoms, in this 2026 Journal of Neurology study. Foslevodopa/foscarbidopa delivers Parkinson's medication continuously under the skin and is approved for motor swings in advanced disease, but its effects on sleep, pain, mood, and gut problems were poorly documented. The team followed twenty-one day-clinic patients for nine weeks.

Standard non-motor scores improved by roughly a third, a change past the threshold patients can feel, with the largest gains in sleep disturbance, pain, and constipation. Questionnaire scores for gut symptoms, sleep quality, and depression also improved early on. Four patients developed psychotic symptoms, a known risk. The authors call the results encouraging but exploratory, needing controlled trials.
pmc-13247306:
Liu and co-authors tested a plant extract against hair graying in this 2026 Dermatology Research and Practice study. Graying is driven largely by oxidative stress killing or disabling the melanocytes that pigment hair, and no effective treatment exists. The team tested Gynostemma pentaphyllum extract, from a vine used in Asian herbal medicine, on pigment cells and mice stressed with hydrogen peroxide.

In cell culture the extract kept melanocytes alive, cut their death rate and internal reactive oxygen, and raised melanin production and the activity of two protective enzymes. In mice it visibly protected hair follicles from peroxide damage. The authors link the effect partly to the Wnt/beta-catenin signaling pathway and propose the extract as a candidate anti-graying treatment, pending human testing.
pmc-13248106:
Okura and co-authors report a genetic kidney-tubule disorder hiding until old age, in this 2026 Case Reports in Endocrinology article. Bartter syndrome type 3, a defect in salt handling in the kidney's loop of Henle, normally declares itself in childhood. Their patient was a sixty-six-year-old woman whose only clue was severe, stubborn low blood potassium found without symptoms, alongside the syndrome's typical alkaline blood and overactive hormone signals.

Ordinary potassium replacement, even at high doses, failed to fix her levels. Careful diuretic challenge tests separated Bartter physiology from its mimic, Gitelman syndrome, and gene sequencing confirmed a homozygous stop variant in the CLCNKB gene. A low-dose combination of an ACE inhibitor and spironolactone then normalized her potassium safely. The authors urge keeping Bartter syndrome in mind for unexplained low potassium at any age.
pmc-13248306:
Hao and a large team searched eye scans for warning signs of abnormal blood vessel growth, in a 2026 study. Their patients had chronic central serous chorioretinopathy, a fluid disorder under the retina that sometimes develops a harmful vessel membrane. Using widefield dye imaging, they compared eyes with and without that complication.

The study covered two hundred ninety-three eyes from two hundred twelve patients, and about a third had the vessel growth. A dominant drainage vein in one corner, vessel links near the macula, and pale scattered spots each stood out in the affected group. The authors propose these features as markers that flag eyes needing closer watching.
pmc-13248906:
Belongia and a large Vaccine Safety Datalink team checked whether COVID-19 vaccines ever made the disease worse, reported in 2026. Enhanced disease after vaccination was a theoretical worry when the shots were authorized. The team estimated vaccine protection against hospitalization and severe illness across variant waves from 2021 to 2023, watching for any negative protection.

Two original doses protected against hospitalization at over ninety percent during the pre-Delta and Delta periods. Protection dipped under Omicron but stayed clearly positive, and booster or bivalent doses restored much of it. At no point, for any dose or variant, did the numbers suggest enhanced disease. The authors close a long-standing safety question with real-world data.
pmc-13249606:
Srivastava and an Indian team profiled immune signals in spinal fluid from patients with autoimmune encephalitis, in a 2026 study. In this condition the immune system attacks the brain, and antibody tests are slow or sometimes come back negative. The researchers measured six signaling proteins in fluid from forty-three patients and thirty-four comparison patients.

Every measured signal ran higher in the encephalitis group. Two attractant proteins, CXCL10 and CXCL13, stood out and rose together with a third, interleukin-6. Patients without detectable antibodies showed the same pattern as those with them. The authors propose the panel as a supporting test that can speed recognition, while stressing it cannot diagnose the condition alone.
pmc-13249706:
Huizenga and colleagues asked teenagers directly how they cope with mental health struggles, in a 2026 pair of Dutch studies. An online tool let adolescents describe, in their own words, what they do about attention problems, behavior problems, or emotional problems, and rate how much each tactic helps. The first study ran during the pandemic with two hundred eighteen participants.

Fifty-one distinct strategies surfaced, some familiar from coping research and others invented by teenagers themselves, and tactics differed by symptom type. The strategies used most were also rated most helpful. A second study after the pandemic, with one hundred eighteen fresh participants, reproduced the picture closely. Helpfulness did not depend on whether a tactic aimed at solving the problem or avoiding it.
pmc-13250506:

pmc-13251306:

pmc-13251506:

pmc-13251706:

pmc-13252706:
JunYoung Seo and co-authors simplify patient leaflets with a chatbot in this 2026 study. Digital therapeutics are software treatments with real evidence behind them, but their explanation sheets are often too hard to read, which holds back uptake.

pmc-13252806:
Adanze Cynthia and colleagues map health care access for Sub-Saharan African migrants in Europe in this 2026 scoping review. This growing population faces heavy barriers to care, and the review gathers what is known as these communities age.

pmc-13252906:
Loai Albinsaad and colleagues describe a one-sided thyroid in this 2026 case report. A 34-year-old Saudi man came in with swelling on the right side of his neck that pressed on his throat, causing trouble swallowing and breathing.

pmc-13253706:

pmc-13254206:

pmc-13254506:

pmc-13254906:

pmc-13255206:
Somayeh Momenyan and co-authors trace PTSD paths after road crashes in a 2026 cohort study. They followed 1,042 survivors recruited from Canadian emergency departments between 2018 and 2020. pmc-13255706:

pmc-13256206:

pmc-13257306:

pmc-13257406:

pmc-13257506:

pmc-13258906:

pmc-13259206:

pmc-13260106:

pmc-13260206:

pmc-13261806:

pmc-13263506:

pmc-13264306:

pmc-13264406:

pmc-13265006:

pmc-13265206:

pmc-13265706:

pmc-13265906:

pmc-13268706:

pmc-13269206:

pmc-13269606:

pmc-13269806:

pmc-13270106:

pmc-13271106:

pmc-13271306:

pmc-13271906:

pmc-13272506:

pmc-13272806:

pmc-13273606:

pmc-13273906:

pmc-13274206:

pmc-13275506:

pmc-13275806:

pmc-13276306:

pmc-13276506:
Ahmad Rashidi and co-authors publish a 2026 dataset on crustal strain in the Kopeh Dagh Belt of northeastern Iran. The dataset pairs satellite positioning measurements with earthquake records for tectonic analysis. It is meant for reuse in modelling how this mountain belt deforms.

Positioning data come from sixteen stations, expressed in a Eurasia-fixed frame, with stated uncertainties. Earthquake records span 1969 to 2024 and include location, magnitude, depth, and fault-plane details. The region was split into twenty triangular subnetworks so strain could be computed for each. Derived values cover rotation, main stress directions, and stress regime, all supplied in machine-readable tables.
pmc-13276606:
Emily Gutzwiller and Katie Huff present a 2026 journal article comparing two intravenous fat blends for sick newborns. Babies whose intestines fail need nutrition by vein, which can damage the liver. Fish oil emulsion is one remedy, but its dose cap limits calories; mixed oil blends allow more fat.

The team reviewed charts of forty-six newborns with this liver complication. Twenty-two got the mixed oil and twenty-four got fish oil alone. Daily weight gain was similar between groups, with no clear difference. Fish oil babies nonetheless improved their weight scores over time more than mixed oil babies. They achieved that on fewer total calories and far less fat, balanced by more carbohydrate calories. The authors say the trade-offs need study for longer-term outcomes before either blend can be declared better for growth.
pmc-13276706:
Arun Poudel and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on building artificial capillaries, the body's tiniest blood vessels, on a chip with exact control. Lab models usually let vessel cells self-assemble in gel, which yields random tube sizes and patchy flow. Systematic study needs reproducibility that self-assembly cannot give.

Their method carves microchannels with an ultrafast laser, casts them in collagen inside a multi-chamber chip, then lines them with vessel cells. Tube widths can be set from eight to forty micrometers, with shapes from straight and curved to tapered and branched. The lined channels formed strong barriers, and flow measures matched high-end computer simulations closely. Branches or blockages can even be edited in later. A shared chamber design lets partner cells grow alongside. The authors envision shipping ready chips worldwide for microvessel research.
pmc-13276806:
Timothy E O'Toole leads a 2026 randomized clinical trial of carnosine, a compound found in muscle and brain, as a daily supplement. Adults were assigned by chance to carnosine capsules or a placebo, meaning a dummy capsule, for about twelve weeks. The trial enrolled 299 people and tested strength and endurance.

Grip strength, calf raises, a two-minute step test, and walking speed were measured before and during the trial. Carnosine helped calf raises in people under forty and step counts in men over forty. Other measures showed no clear gain. The authors read the benefit as narrow, mainly for short repeated effort in some groups.
pmc-13277106:
Thinh Toan Vu leads a 2026 survey of family caregivers for lung cancer patients in northern Vietnam. Caregiving can bring low mood and a poorer quality of life, and the team tested whether resilience, the ability to bounce back, sits between the two. A total of 213 adult caregivers at a provincial hospital took part in 2023 and 2024.

Caregivers rated life quality at about half of the top score, with leisure, mood, and money areas rated worst. Depressive symptoms were tied to lower life quality, while resilience was tied to higher quality. Part of the link from low mood ran through lower resilience. Programs should screen for depression and build resilience together, the authors say.
pmc-13277406:
Alexander McKenzie leads a 2026 study of an enzyme from a fungus, Daldinia childiae, that can add oxygen to other molecules. Such enzymes, called unspecific peroxygenases, are valued as green catalysts for making chemicals with precision. The team produced the enzyme in two host systems and mapped its three-dimensional structure.

The structure showed a differently shaped active tunnel from a well-known relative enzyme. That difference changed which products the enzyme made. For example, it turned menthol into one specific alcohol product, while its relative gave a different one exclusively. Small structural changes can redirect these catalysts, the work shows, which matters for designing enzymes for drug and chemical making.
pmc-13278406:
Bashiru Garba leads a 2026 survey of health workers in Mogadishu, Somalia, on drug resistance in germs. Drug resistance means antibiotics lose their power to cure infections. Weak labs, uneven prescribing, and easy access to antibiotics can speed it in fragile health systems. The team surveyed 426 staff at seven hospitals on attitudes, knowledge, and awareness of careful antibiotic use.

Scores were fairly high in all three areas, and the three rose together. Yet many held wrong beliefs, such as using antibiotics for all infections or stopping once they felt better. A master's degree predicted stronger attitudes. Mid-career years, oddly, predicted lower knowledge and awareness. Training must target firm wrong beliefs, the authors say.
pmc-13278906:
Robert Bielitzki and colleagues test whether cuff pressure must be measured on both legs for blood flow restriction exercise, in a 2026 trial. Trainers set cuff pressure as a share of the pressure that fully blocks artery flow. Bilateral exercise inflates both legs at once, yet that pressure is usually measured one leg at a time.

Twenty-five young healthy volunteers were measured in lying, seated, and standing positions under both setups. Bilateral inflation gave a slightly higher blocking pressure in every position, by a few millimetres of mercury on average. Standing raised the pressure most, regardless of setup. A few individuals showed large gaps between methods, so the authors advise awareness even though the average effect is trivial.
pmc-13279006:
Xingchen Li and colleagues offer a 2026 review of how to move sick newborns safely inside a hospital. Their term is intrahospital transport, meaning trips between units for scans or care. They searched many databases for guides, reviews and evidence briefs up to late August 2025.

Ten sources yielded thirty five short advice points grouped in seven themes. Themes cover team make up, checks before travel, prep of staff and babies, drugs and gear, watch during travel, and hand over at the end. Most advice rests on guides and expert views, not strong trials. The authors urge care in use and call for larger, stronger studies.
pmc-13279206:
Masa Al Fakih and colleagues published a 2026 interview study of why Syrian refugees in Mount Lebanon, Lebanon, hesitated to take COVID-19 vaccines. Lebanon hosts around 1.5 million Syrian refugees within a strained health system, and uptake in these communities lagged despite their heightened exposure risk. The researchers interviewed people to understand the reasons in their own terms rather than assuming simple refusal.

Doubts grew from limited knowledge about the vaccines, low trust, and poor access to reliable health facts, the study found. The fact that shots were not required, together with social and cultural pressures, also pushed people toward delay. False claims filled the gaps left by official messages. The authors recommend responsive teaching programs designed with refugee communities in mind, arguing that fighting false claims requires trusted messengers and accessible facts, not merely vaccine supply.
pmc-13279306:
Pan Sun and colleagues published a 2026 study measuring the risk that funeral workers pick up Staphylococcus aureus from surfaces they touch. In 2024 the team swabbed 85 high-touch surfaces, including cosmetics, tools, faucets, door handles, and countertops, across four funeral parlors in Anhui, China. They fed the counts into a quantitative microbial risk model of the surface-to-hand-to-mouth route, running 10,000 simulations to rank where exposure concentrates.

The bacterium appeared on about 16 percent of surfaces, and roughly a third of the isolates were the drug-resistant MRSA form. Faucets carried the highest concentrations, and the modeled daily intake from touching faucets ran more than twice that from makeup tools. Transfer efficiency from hand to mouth and faucet contamination drove most of the uncertainty. The authors argue that cleaning high-touch fixtures and strict hand hygiene deserve priority in funeral hygiene rules, which are rarely studied this way.
pmc-13279506:
Gong-Fu Lin and colleagues published a 2026 cross-sectional study of death literacy in patients with advanced lung cancer. Death literacy means knowing how to deal with dying and death care. The team surveyed 103 patients with stage IIIB or later non-small cell lung cancer at a medical center in northern Taiwan. They asked how much patients knew and which life-sustaining treatments they would want.

Cardiopulmonary resuscitation was the least desired option, while antibiotic treatment was the most accepted. Patients scoring higher on death literacy, including its practical, experiential, and factual knowledge parts, were modestly less willing to receive intensive treatments such as dialysis, intubation, transfusion, and feeding tubes. Those in the highest literacy group were clearly less inclined toward aggressive care than the lowest group. The authors suggest that helping patients understand end-of-life matters supports earlier talks about treatment preferences. They call for larger studies.
pmc-13279606:
Jeffrey Araneda and colleagues published a 2026 computational study designing a candidate vaccine against bacterial kidney disease in farmed salmon. The bacterium lives inside host cells, no effective vaccine exists, and Chilean aquaculture leans on antibiotics instead. Working entirely in silico, the team compared three bacterial genomes and screened proteins tied to virulence, iron uptake, and secretion. They used immunoinformatics tools to predict which fragments the salmon immune system would recognize.

From 154 candidate fragments, filtering for antigenicity, safety, and distance from host proteins left 60 epitopes drawn from 15 proteins. Twelve regions were stitched into one chimeric protein of 439 amino acids using linkers. Computer docking against salmon immune receptors gave favorable scores, and a 100-nanosecond molecular dynamics run suggested the construct holds its shape. Surface analysis showed the most exposed regions came from four source proteins. The authors present the design as a rational starting point needing wet-lab tests in fish.
pmc-13280206:
Wei Qiang Chng and colleagues give a 2026 narrative review of skin diseases and fatty liver links. Two chronic skin illnesses, hidradenitis suppurativa and psoriasis, show high rates of metabolic fatty liver disease, called MASLD. Rates run as high as fifty seven percent in affected people, even after checks for obesity and blood pressure. The review traces the shared immunological links, meaning immune paths common to skin and liver disease.

Chronic body wide swelling and immune dysregulation form the bridge in their account. Skin and liver share cytokine paths, immune signal proteins that drive swelling in both sites. The authors urge skin doctors to watch for liver disease in these patients. Drug options that may help both sides hold GLP-1 receptor agonists, a gut hormone drug class, and biologics, lab made immune drugs. Proof on drug safety and worth for the pair still needs work.
pmc-13280806:
Tousif Iqbal Nathani and colleagues studied betel nut chewing and tooth root infection in a 2026 report. Betel nut is chewed daily by many people in Asia and is known to harm the mouth. The team worked at two dental schools in India from 2021 to 2023. They enrolled two hundred twenty-two adults. About half chewed at least one packet a day for a year or more. The rest had never chewed and did not use tobacco.

X-rays showed more infected tooth roots in the chewers than in the others. Risk rose with each added packet per day, by about eleven percent. It also rose a few percent with each added year of chewing. Tooth decay rates did not differ between the groups. The authors say the habit itself, not decay, tracks with root infection.
pmc-13281606:
Chenchen Ma and colleagues summed up new drug news for a fast blood cancer in a 2026 brief review. The cancer is acute myeloid leukemia, which crowds out healthy blood cells. A drug class that blocks a protein called menin helps two gene-defined forms. The review pulls fresh results shared at a large 2025 blood meeting. Four drugs of the class are in trials. Two have won approval for patients whose disease came back.

Trials now test the drugs earlier in care and in pairs with other drugs. Some patients get them as upkeep after main treatment. Open questions crowd the field. Which pairs work best, in what order, and for which gene forms, all need answers. The authors say the class has moved fast from idea to clinic. Careful trial design, they argue, will decide how wide its use should grow.
pmc-13281806:
Xingdao He and colleagues built a brain implant that changes stiffness with heat in a 2026 study. The folded surface of large brains hides much of their signal from flat devices. A stiff device can be placed with ease but grates on soft tissue. A soft one hugs tissue but is hard to place. Their system uses a liquid metal alloy designed with smart software help. The alloy melts near body heat.

Cool, the device stays firm for careful placement. Warm, in the body, it softens a thousandfold and molds to folds. It can slip into deep grooves without tearing tissue while still covering a wide span of surface. Tests in rodents and pigs showed clean signal pickup. The authors say the switchable build solves a long trade-off in brain gear. It may widen what doctors can read from the living brain.
pmc-13282006:
Eduardo Moreira Nader and co-authors report a 2026 study on teaching obstetrics, the care of pregnancy and birth, with a video students can look around inside. Their topic was premature rupture of membranes, when the waters break early. Fifth-year medical students watched a ten-minute case that ran from history taking to writing the prescription.

Sixty students took part and rated the video highly on a five-point scale. All of them said they grasped when to admit the patient, and nearly all grasped why antibiotics were given. Most said the video raised their drive to learn and their interest in obstetrics. Phone and computer viewers rated it much the same. The team calls the format a low-cost, scalable way to rehearse hard cases safely.
pmc-13282406:
Wataru Yamori and co-authors report a 2026 plant study that edited a key photosynthesis gene in the chloroplast to boost plant growth. Rubisco is the enzyme that captures carbon dioxide, but it works slowly, limiting crop yields. Editing its large subunit, coded in the chloroplast genome, is technically hard. The team used a targeted base editor in the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana to create a range of edited plants.

Two single-letter changes raised Rubisco's catalytic speed without lowering its amount. Photosynthesis and growth improved at both today's carbon dioxide levels and higher projected levels. Structural imaging showed the distant changes reshaped the enzyme's active loops, explaining the speed gain. The authors highlight chloroplast editing as a route to better crops without foreign DNA insertion, which matters for public acceptance. Raising photosynthesis could also draw down atmospheric carbon. Field crops, not just lab plants, are the next proving ground.
pmc-13283206:
Caroline Hesselager and co-authors wrote a 2026 research letter on blood stem cell clones in high-grade B-cell lymphoma. The clone state, called CHIP, grows with age and raises inflammation. Past work tied CHIP to worse outcomes in this lymphoma type.

The letter sets out a large population-based study of lymphoma patients. It asks how CHIP links to heart disease, autoimmune disease, and second cancers. CHIP clones carry faults in genes that control gene activity and DNA repair. Such faults give stem cells an edge in growth and survival over time. Inflammation from clones may help lymphomas form and shape their course. Single-cell tests add deeper views of clone behavior.
pmc-13283406:
Ramadan screening in Saudi Arabia's Aseer region found most hypertension previously undiagnosed, Faisal Saeed Al-Qahtani's team reports in 2026. Screening during Ramadan aimed to find undiagnosed cases and link people to care. National trend data place the local results in context.

A total of 657 adults were screened in March 2025 for the local study. Over half had undiagnosed high blood pressure by study measures. About one in six had a prior diagnosis before the screening visit. Older age, male sex, higher body mass, and diabetes predicted known disease. Male sex and higher body mass also predicted hidden disease. Trends from 1990 to 2019 feed projections to 2027.
pmc-13283606:
Seizure alarms deserve a place in complete epilepsy care, three American epilepsy groups state jointly through Caitlin Grzeskowiak's team in 2026. About 3.4 million people in the United States live with epilepsy. A third still have poorly controlled seizures despite modern drug care.

Devices include wearables, home systems, and implants that sense motion, skin, sound, or brain signals. Alerts can speed help, cut injury risk, and track seizure patterns over time. Early proof suggests fewer emergency visits may follow device use for some patients. Cost and insurance payment remain major barriers to wider access. Three epilepsy groups back careful use within full epilepsy care plans.
pmc-13283906:
Seyed Morteza Pourfaraji and co-authors pooled studies in 2026 on whether HER2 overproduction marks worse outlook in stomach cancer. HER2 is a growth signal receptor that some tumours make in excess. The team searched databases for survival data by HER2 status and combined hazard ratios with a random-effects model, covering both removable and advanced cancers.

Thirty-nine studies with 19,903 patients qualified, and about sixteen percent of tumours overproduced HER2. Those patients died sooner overall and progressed sooner than HER2-normal patients. The survival gap held in both removable and advanced groups, while the progression gap reached clarity only in removable disease. The authors back standardised HER2 testing and its use inside multi-marker panels to sharpen prognosis and guide personal treatment choices.
pmc-13284006:
Faster recovery after complex shunt surgery in children with portal hypertension is reported by Samir Hasan and colleagues in 2026. Enhanced recovery pathways cut surgical stress through standard steps around operations. Such pathways were scarce for this childrens condition before this study.

Over 18 years, 103 children had shunt surgery at the reporting center. Groups split into 51 treated before the pathway and 52 treated after it. Feeding and walking started earlier under the new pathway in both measures. Drain use collapsed, intensive care stays shortened, and hospital stays nearly halved. Readmission rates within 30 days stayed similar between eras. Safety held while recovery sped up.
pmc-13284206:
Two-drug induction chemo bought time and sometimes surgery for advanced pancreas cancer in a 2026 phase 2 trial by Zhe Cao and colleagues. Locally advanced disease carries poor outlook and few treatment choices. Nab-paclitaxel plus S-1 served as first treatment across four China centers.

Sixty untreated patients enrolled between April 2019 and March 2023. Nearly half completed the full induction course of up to eight cycles. About a fifth later had tumor removal surgery after shrinking. Six-month freedom from progression cleared seventy percent in the trial. Serious side effects hit over half, mainly low white cell counts. No treatment deaths occurred.
pmc-13285606:
Who leads CAR T cell work in breast cancer, and where is the field heading? Yuechen Xu and co-authors chart the scene in a 2026 bibliometric study. The cell therapy won fame in blood cancers and now probes solid tumors. The team pulled 894 papers from a core database and mapped links with visual tools.

The United States led output, with London and Dresden as hub schools and two journals at the core. Hot terms in recent years include in vivo work, the tumor neighborhood, and targeted therapy. Fresh burst terms point to escape routes and immune control inside tumors. The authors offer the map to help labs spot gaps and partners in a fast field.
pmc-13285906:
Yiming Chen and colleagues answer critics of their acupuncture trial design in a 2026 response letter. A comment had raised three worries: whether needle sensation can be held steady, whether sham treatment truly blinds patients, and whether lost blinding could sway brain signals. The letter takes each point in turn and sets out planned fixes.

Fixed needle points, depths, and a set current strength kept treatment alike for all, the authors note, though felt sensation still varies by person. They plan to log each patient's sense of the current and of the classic needle feeling for later checks. Sham needles do press the skin, they grant, so no blind is perfect in such trials. A blinding index and expectancy scores will enter their models to weigh any mental effects.
pmc-13286406:
Zi-yang Chen and colleagues review records of cataract patients whose dry eye was treated around surgery with a traditional herbal decoction plus artificial tears. The 2026 study covers 72 patients treated in 2023, half receiving the combined approach and half receiving drops alone. Dry eye is common before cataract surgery and often worsens afterward, spoiling comfort and vision quality.

The combined group improved more on tear film stability, tear production, and gland secretion measures. Symptom scores fell further, especially the feeling of grit in the eye. Measures of optical distortion in the cornea also improved more. Overall effectiveness rated higher with the decoction added, and no safety problems were reported in either group.
pmc-13286606:
Jacqueline Sachett and a large team review scorpion stings as a neglected Amazonian health threat in a 2026 evidence synthesis. Tityus scorpions cause nearly all serious cases in the region, and notifications in Amazonas state climbed from under 150 in 2007 to peaks above 800 in recent years. Manaus and Apuí supply most reports, with spread along the Solimões and Upper Negro rivers into Indigenous and riverine communities.

Children stung by one local species can crash with circulatory collapse and breathing distress. Other species trigger body-wide muscle spasms likened to electric shocks, which the available antivenom apparently fails to reverse. Remote settlements face the worst care delays, and the region posts Brazil's highest sting death rates despite fewer cases. The authors call for joined-up networks linking venom science, clinics, and community health.
pmc-13286706:
Maya Eid and co-authors ask whether cocaine's aversive after-effects run in families in a 2026 rat study. The drug's delayed crash, arriving minutes after the high fades, teaches some rats to avoid it, and that avoidance varies wildly between individuals. Offspring of high- and low-avoider rats were tested on a runway task, and seven inbred strains were compared for the same trait.

Pups inherited their parents' leaning, running warily or eagerly in step with the line they came from. Strain differences in avoidance were also marked, again pointing to heritable influence, genetic or otherwise. Control tasks cleared away simpler explanations like general activity, motivation, or shock toughness. Resistance to punishment for food seeking also varied by strain, but independently, suggesting the two addiction-relevant traits answer to separate inherited factors.
pmc-13286806:
Heeyon Kim and a large team examine how IVF outcomes shifted across the COVID-19 pandemic years and whether air quality played a role. The 2026 study reviews egg collection cycles at one Seoul center from 2018 to 2024. Pollution is known to harm egg and embryo development, and the pandemic abruptly changed city air and daily life.

The share of mature eggs ran lower during and after the pandemic than before it. Fertilization rates rose slightly in the later period, while pregnancy rates showed no clear change. Long-term exposure to ozone, carbon monoxide, and nitrogen dioxide interacted with the pandemic period for egg maturity. Several exposures also interacted for pregnancy. Clinics, the authors suggest, should weigh recent and year-long air exposure when judging results.
pmc-13286906:
Jingran Gao and colleagues review organoids that mimic the interface between mother and fetus, a frontier in pregnancy research. Published in 2026, the review explains that these miniature tissues grow from stem cells or tissue progenitors and copy features of the placenta and womb lining. Older flat cell cultures and animal models capture that meeting place poorly.

Researchers use the models to simulate implantation, study communication between mother and fetus, and reproduce problems such as repeated miscarriage and preeclampsia. Drug screening and studies of infections passing from mother to child are also under way. Missing cell types, limited maturity, and shaky standardization hold the field back. Adding immune and blood vessel systems is a stated next direction.
pmc-13287106:
Ulrich Schmid, Stephan Felber, and Hugo Rincon Galeana settle when networked computers can eventually agree in a 2026 theoretical paper. In stabilizing consensus, processes may flip their decisions freely but must finally settle on one shared value, a relaxation of the classic problem where answers lock forever. Some faulty networks forbid the classic version yet allow this one, and results until now came piecemeal.

Working in point-set topology over infinite executions, the authors prove a complete characterization covering nearly any model with mild process and message faults. Semi-open decision sets and semi-continuous maps, tools dating to 1963, turn out to be exactly the right lens, since they let a connected space map onto a split one. Weak and strong validity versions prove equivalent, and every known solvability result in the area gets a unified topological explanation.
pmc-13288206:
Clair Davison and co-authors review what the Attention Training Technique changes in the brain, in a 2026 synthesis. The technique is a short listening exercise from metacognitive therapy for emotional disorders. Patients practice shifting attention among sounds to loosen rigid threat focus. The review gathered studies that measured thinking tasks or brain activity after the training. Searches covered five databases for work from 1990 to late 2025.

Twenty studies with 1,230 participants met the rules for inclusion. Only four used clinical samples, while most tested healthy volunteers or students. Across fourteen thinking tasks, effects ranged from small to large, and the emotional dot-probe task showed the most steady gains. Brain measures from three methods pointed the same way, toward stronger control networks and quieter self-focused activity. The authors note uneven study quality and call for better protocol reporting.
pmc-13288606:
Joanna L Harris and co-authors assemble the first species-level picture of manta and devil rays around the Mascarene islands in a 2026 synthesis. Combining diver reports and citizen-science sightings from 2014 to 2026 for Reunion, Mauritius, and Rodrigues, they logged 107 sightings across 75 separate events.

Thurston's devil rays and oceanic mantas dominated the records, reef mantas and sicklefin devil rays appeared rarely, and many animals stayed unidentified, while Rodrigues produced no records at all. Sightings clustered off Reunion's west and southwest coasts, peaked from late spring into early summer, and included rare courtship and one manta seen again almost four years later. With all mobulids now under strict trade protection, the baseline should guide monitoring.
pmc-13288706:
Florian Bernhardt and a large team study end-of-life care access in Germany in 2026. The work deals with Muslim migrants and their children. Talks ran from August 2021 to December 2022. Six centers in North Rhine-Westphalia took part. The set held 53 adults from 14 nations.

Four groups fed the talks. They were patients in such care and patients outside it. Kin and boundary staff also joined. The core idea was same same but different. Formal equality still felt blocked day to day. Six forces fed delays in a loop. They spanned othering, poor facts, and family roles. Stigma, language, and death views counted too. Native-language help was named as a lever.
pmc-13289006:
Gonzalo Romero-Martinez and colleagues study daily habits and mood in Colombia. Their 2026 survey covers students at one public university. It holds 1,125 students in all. Most were women, at 56.7 percent. Surveys tapped exercise, sitting, and sleep.

Only 15.5 percent met all three daily guides. Meeting more guides linked to lower mood symptoms. Students who met all three had far lower odds of worry. Their odds of low mood were also lower. Enough exercise and sleep each helped alone. Long sitting linked to worse symptoms. The design cannot prove cause and effect.
pmc-13289906:
Emmanuel O Osayi and colleagues present a 2026 surveillance cohort on mother-to-child HIV transmission outcomes in Plateau State, Nigeria. Most child HIV comes from perinatal spread, and how fast illness appears shapes outlook. Records covered HIV-exposed infants with confirmed positive tests who started therapy between October 2018 and September 2022 at fifteen facilities across three districts.

A total of 57 infants entered, with a near even sex split and a mean starting age of 0.7 years for therapy. Follow-up ran from six months to five years after starting drugs. By the end, 70 percent had favorable outcomes, and most of those suppressed the virus fully as reported. The rest died, transferred, stopped, or interrupted care.
pmc-13290106:
A phone-based questionnaire system that writes patient answers straight into the medical record is described by Eunjoung Choi and colleagues in 2026. Their platform, Miri-Alimi, sends previsit questionnaires through a social networking service and transfers structured replies into the electronic record automatically.

In a cardiology clinic study run from August to November 2024, 751 outpatients received the questionnaire link before their visits. The response rate was 38.5%, with first-visit patients answering more often than heart failure follow-up patients, and responders were younger on average. Among follow-up patients, record completeness on breathlessness, swelling, and medication adherence was far higher for responders. Satisfaction among patients and providers ran high, supporting wider use of messaging-based data collection.
pmc-13290706:
A missing immune protein produced a family puzzle and a treatment dilemma in a 2026 report by Mattia Moratti and colleagues on GIMAP5 deficiency. The first Italian pediatric case anchors the study, set beside a review of twenty published patients with this rare disorder of immunity, lymphoproliferation, and progressive liver disease.

The 11-year-old boy carried two faulty copies of the gene, made no detectable protein, and suffered autoimmune cytopenias, severe viral infections, and early liver abnormalities. His T cells looked exhausted and his memory B-cell pool was unusually expanded. His twin carried one faulty copy, made less protein, and showed only a localized vascular anomaly without immune defects. Sirolimus, an mTOR inhibitor, brought the boy's cytopenias into lasting remission. The authors argue such precision treatment can stabilize patients while families weigh a stem cell transplant.
pmc-13291106:
Erhan Hüseyin Cömert leads a 2026 study of pregnancy odds after ICSI treatment. The work centers on the day of embryo transfer. Records from 2020 to 2025 were screened. Three hundred transfers, one per couple, were kept.

Only 37 pregnancies occurred in the set. The main model thus used just four factors. Woman’s age and AMH level were two of them. Sperm source and embryo stage made up the rest. Checks for optimism and calibration were built in. The team calls the work exploratory by design. It should frame counseling talks, not drive choices. A sac on ultrasound defined pregnancy here.
pmc-13291206:
Tiny packets shed by nerve support cells carry stage-linked cargo. Manju Sharma leads a 2026 lab study of these packets from Schwann cells. Such cells switch from wrapping nerves to repair mode after injury. Their shed packets pass signals between cells.

Rat Schwann cells were grown at three life stages. Packet contents were mapped for proteins and small RNA strands. Repair-stage packets held a distinct RNA mix. Adding them to young cells switched on a repair gene. Tweaking one small RNA changed cell growth and movement. Some long RNA strands may sponge up small RNAs in turn. The work maps how packets may steer nerve repair.
pmc-13291306:
Aimed radiation to the prostate may help spread cancer last longer. Christian Trapp leads a 2026 review of patient records. Such cancer is often treated with body-wide drugs alone. Adding prostate radiation is called primary directed therapy.

Records covered 24 men treated from 2011 to 2023. Most had few spread spots and modern scan staging. Nearly all also got hormone blocking drugs. Most had aimed radiation to spread spots too. Half the men stayed free of progress for years. Survival passed the follow-up span for the group. Side effects were tracked as a safety check. Small numbers call for larger trials to confirm.
pmc-13292206:
Markel G Ibarluzea and a large team model a fat-lengthening enzyme to guide drug design, in a 2026 computational study. ELOVL6 stretches sixteen-carbon fatty acids into eighteen-carbon ones in liver and fat tissue. The enzyme is tied to metabolic and brain diseases, making it an attractive drug target. No crystal structure exists, which blocks the usual design route. The team combined predicted structures, molecular dynamics, and free energy calculations instead.

Simulations traced the most favorable path a fatty acid takes into the enzyme's tunnel. They also captured shape changes that come with ligand binding. Known inhibitors were tested in silico and preferred the active site, matching measured binding strengths. Comparing cousin enzymes pinpointed residues likely to grant selectivity for ELOVL6 over its relatives. The authors offer their framework as a starting scaffold for inhibitor programs. Experimental structures can later refine the model.
pmc-13292306:
Or Segal, Hadas Hevron, and Noam Weinbach compare a 2026 study of teenagers living through the same war from different homes. Two hundred Israeli adolescents aged 14 to 18 were assessed four to eight months after the Israel-Hamas war began. Half had been internally displaced from high-risk areas, and half had stayed put, with similar backgrounds otherwise.

Displaced teens reported heavier emotional distress, driven mainly by stress and depression rather than anxiety alone. They also struggled more with regulating emotions and tolerated uncertainty less well. Those two difficulties statistically carried much of the link between displacement and distress. The authors, calling theirs the first such comparison during active war, urge targeted support for displaced adolescents that builds emotion skills and steadiness under uncertainty.
pmc-13292506:
Caren Kamau and co-authors listen to a 2026 qualitative study of mothers and health workers in Kajiado County, Kenya, on what shapes mental health around pregnancy and birth. Perinatal depression may affect up to 30 percent of Kenyan women. Focus groups at five facilities, two urban and three rural, gathered 51 mothers and 39 health workers in March 2025.

Three themes emerged. First, mothers lacked control over money and decisions while carrying most household burdens, with early marriage and female genital mutilation leaving girls unready for motherhood. Second, distance, cost, and low expectations thinned care, and women feared traumatic births and caesarean sections. Third, communities often read mental illness as irrationality or spirit possession, delaying help, with stigma also shadowing caesareans and HIV. The authors tie maternal wellbeing tightly to gender norms.
pmc-13292606: A 2026 notice retracts a 2019 International Journal of Molecular Sciences article by Jin-Woo Jeong and co-authors on fermented oyster extract and bone cells. An editorial investigation confirmed inappropriate image editing and duplication with figures from an earlier paper by a similar group. The authors cooperated, but their explanations and materials could not resolve the problems. The editorial board lost confidence in the findings and retracted the article under MDPI policy, with the editor-in-chief's approval. The authors were informed and stated their disagreement with the decision.
pmc-13294106:
Ana Karen Villa-Merlan and colleagues dissect what makes the scorpion venom peptide Uy234 kill bacteria in a 2026 study. Native peptide from Urodacus yaschenkoi was tested against Staphylococcus aureus and a drug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii isolate. Two altered versions removed single features: one swapped proline at position 9, the other lost the capped tail end.

Only the native peptide stopped growth and killed both pathogens. Fluorescent viability tests showed membrane damage in staph cells only with the native form. Microscopy and artificial membrane work showed thinning, spreading, and dose-dependent leaking. Simulations backed the bench results. Both altered features are essential, a useful rule for peptide drug design.
pmc-13294206:
Huixin Zhang and coauthors study motoric cognitive risk syndrome in brain small vessel disease for a 2026 cross-sectional analysis. The syndrome pairs slow walking with memory complaints and predicts poor outcomes, yet its drivers inside vessel disease were murky. Registry patients aged 55 and older without likely dementia gave clinic data, activity reports, and brain imaging markers, totaling 225 people.

Prevalence was 16.4%, with mean age 65.4 years and 54.2% men. The syndrome tied to lower average systolic pressure and higher total vessel disease burden. Memory complaints alone tied to white matter damage near the cortex, while slow gait tied to lipid problems and worse daily function. Inactivity links stayed imprecise from sparse data.
pmc-13294306:
Maria Shilova and burns colleagues survey laser practice for thick burn scars in a 2026 questionnaire study. Laser care is spreading fast, but protocols vary widely. A team-built survey, translated into Spanish, Chinese, and German, reached burns clinicians worldwide between December 2021 and June 2023, drawing 43 responses.

Nearly everyone used carbon dioxide fractional lasers, a third used pulsed dye lasers, and about half mixed lasers in one session. Most treated both fresh and mature scars, set power by scar thickness judged mostly by eye, and paired steroids or other add-ons. Anesthesia, pain relief, and dressings differed sharply. Shared mapping can seed common standards and trials.
pmc-13294806: A 2026 correction by Guanmin Zhang, Qiuju Hu, and Haiyang Zou repairs the reference list of their article on the endocannabinoid system, exercise, and depression. Several sources had been pasted into the main text as full references and left out of the reference list itself. The notice adds those missing entries, covering work on stress, fear conditioning, brain-derived neurotrophic factor, and exercise effects, and reformats the in-text citations to match. No findings or arguments in the article are touched by the change.
pmc-13295006:
Changhong Jiang and colleagues review nanomedicine for kidney injury after blood flow returns in a 2026 article. Restored flow can itself damage kidneys through oxidative stress, inflammation, cell death, and poor microcirculation. Current diagnosis and treatment lack precision, leaving room for targeted nanoscale tools.

Carriers surveyed include mineral and polymer particles, enzyme-like nanomaterials, cell vesicles, camouflaged particles, and injectable gels. Such systems promise earlier detection, delivery straight to injured tissue, and longer drug action with less body-wide toxicity. The authors stress that safety, body handling, and movement into clinics remain open problems needing urgent work before routine use.
pmc-13295106:
Barbara Strasser and colleagues review how food and drink choices change the sense of effort during endurance exercise in a 2026 article. How hard exercise feels helps decide how long people can keep going, in sport and in daily life alike. Anything that softens that feeling may therefore lift performance.

Proven aids such as caffeine, beta-alanine, and carbohydrate mouth rinsing are examined alongside less settled options like certain amino acids and probiotics. Routes include slower fatigue build-up, better motor signal flow, and changed brain network activity tied to effort. The authors call for work on best doses and mixtures for each sport and person.
pmc-13295806:
Junli Feng and colleagues map where a plant pathogen could live worldwide in a 2026 study. Phytopythium litorale may threaten plant health and wild ecosystems as climates shift. Records numbering 150 from around the globe and 36 environmental factors fed a habitat model.

Suitable ground now covers a vast area across North America, Europe, Asia, and Oceania. Coldest-season temperature, seasonal temperature swing, and cold-season rain controlled the pattern most strongly. Future climates expand the suitable zone and push it toward higher latitudes, with the centre moving far northeast. The maps give officials a head start for watching borders and forests.
pmc-13296706:
In a 2026 review, Yaliang Huang and co-authors cover light- and electricity-based sensors for amyloid-beta oligomers, a toxic clump tied to Alzheimer's disease. Standard tests are costly and slow, while these sensors promise sensitivity in small, portable devices.

The review covers direct and sandwich-style designs and the catchers they use, from antibodies and aptamers to printed plastic moulds. Nanomaterials and signal boosting tricks that sharpen accuracy and stability get special focus. Remaining hurdles and next steps are laid out, aiming to guide sensor design for early Alzheimer's diagnosis and related precision medicine work.
pmc-13296806:
Junmei Chen and colleagues reconstruct, in 2026, how climate shrank the range of dawn redwood, a famous relict tree now confined to a small corner of China. Using 755 fossil records with deep-time niche modelling, they trace where the genus could live across past eras.

The tree spread widely across mid-to-high latitudes in the earlier era, then retreated toward lower latitudes as the world dried and cooled. Yearly rainfall was the key driver across both eras. Ice ages of the recent period then crushed its range. The authors say the story guides conservation of relict plants under future warming.
pmc-13297506:
Claudia Moriello and colleagues test whether tomato extracts can shield human red blood cells from mercury harm, in a 2026 laboratory study. Mercury drives oxidative stress, an overload of reactive oxygen that damages cells, and red cells are exposed around the clock with few repair tools. Extracts came from two tomato types, Piccadilly and Piennolo, and cells were stressed with mercury chloride.

One extract held more protective plant compounds, yet both shielded cells about equally well. Treated cells made fewer reactive oxygen species, kept their fat layers and sulfur groups intact, and held onto their internal antioxidant store. A danger signal that normally flips to the cell surface stayed hidden, keeping the blood less prone to clotting. Diet-derived compounds may thus guard blood cells directly.
pmc-13297606:
Faizaan Fazal Khan and Goo-Rak Kwon ask whether carrying more copies of a risk gene variant speeds the slide from mild memory trouble to Alzheimer's dementia, in a 2026 study. The variant, APOE ε4, is often treated as a simple yes-or-no factor. Records from a large imaging initiative covered 1,115 people with mild impairment, grouped by whether they held zero, one, or two copies.

Just over a third worsened to dementia during follow-up. Typical time without worsening fell sharply with each added copy. It ran from over eighteen years with no copy to under three and a half years with two copies. The no-copy figure rests on late follow-up, though. Each copy raised the hazard even after brain size and test scores were counted. Larger memory-centre volume, by contrast, protected.
pmc-13298206:
