They grew slow, had gut wall flaws, and low-grade body fire. Gut germs grew up late and off pace, and their waste stuff fell short. Heart traces showed a long beat gap, a sly sign. The team calls the ill a whole-body one from the first weeks, not a brain ill alone.
pmc-13377706:
Jungang Chen and others show that blocking HA signals restores rapamycin sensitivity in primary effusion cancer in a 2026 study. This Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus-driven cancer, arising in body cavities of immunocompromised patients including those with HIV, progresses rapidly with median survival of months despite chemo, partly due to multidrug defence.

Hyaluronan signals switching on drove rapamycin defence in cancer cells. Small HA oligosaccharides targeting that signals boosted rapamycin effect against cancer growth in vivo. The work provides a framework for HA-aimed trials as adjuncts that could cut chemo toxicity, improve treatment, and prolong survival for a disease with few strong options.
pmc-13379406:
Akinobu Taniguchi and colleagues study sirolimus-linked lipid problems in neonates and infants in a 2026 paper. Sirolimus is increasingly used for complex vascular and lymphatic anomalies in very young children, yet dyslipidemia timing and severity in this group were poorly known, though well known in adults. A single-centre cohort at Nagoya University Hospital was combined with global VigiBase pharmacovigilance data.

The cohort included ten patients, median age 44.5 days, with lipids checked before and after treatment. After starting sirolimus, all ten developed high triglycerides and nine in ten developed broader lipid abnormalities in the sample shown. Age-stratified reporting odds and time-to-onset were estimated from VigiBase, adjusted for sex, region, and other drugs. The work urges lipid monitoring from the start of sirolimus therapy in infants.
pmc-13380306:
Solomon Olusegun Nwhator argues in a 2026 perspective that gum disease may be quietly distorting results in sleep apnea trials. Such trials often use inflammation markers in the blood as stand-ins for treatment effect, assuming the signal comes from the airway. Gum disease, though, is a common hidden source of the same signal.

The author notes that gum disease is more common in people with sleep apnea and raises one key marker in the blood substantially. Treating the gums lowers that marker about as much as early airway therapy does. Yet published trials have not reported gum health. The piece proposes a simple model that splits the measured signal into parts, so trials can adjust for the mouth.
pmc-13380506:
Veerasit Kaewbundit, Damrongvudhi Onwimol, and Papis Wongchaisuwat present a 2026 method for judging rice seed vigour from photographs. Vigour means a seed can sprout quickly and evenly and produce strong seedlings. Standard checks are slow, labour-heavy, and destroy the seed, so a camera-based method could help growers and seed producers.

Their approach photographs seedlings at several growth stages and combines the images. Some models use hand-measured features of shape and colour, while others learn features directly with deep learning networks. Comparing single-stage with multi-stage models shows whether tracking growth over time improves accuracy. The method also highlights which features drive each judgement, making the results easier to explain.
pmc-13380806:
Yasar Caliskan and a very large international team report a 2026 study of genetic testing practices for people being assessed as living kidney donors. Testing is used more often in this setting, but hard data on how centres actually use it were lacking. The study drew on an international registry built for this purpose.

Centres recorded de-identified details for donor candidates who had genetic testing, a family history of genetic kidney disease, or a related recipient whose disease cause was unknown. Data were collected between June 2023 and November 2025. The registry shows how widely testing is used and what it finds. Such evidence can help centres set consistent policy for donors and families.
pmc-13382306:
M S Arias and a large team report a 2026 farm study using a fungus to control gut parasites in free-range laying hens. Parasite eggs and cysts survive in soil, so outdoor hens face constant reinfection. The fungus used feeds on parasite stages and is harmless to the birds.

On two small farms, fungal spores were sprayed in shelters and pens before hens arrived, then at intervals afterwards, while one plot received only water. Droppings were checked for three parasite types. Counts fell sharply in the sprayed plots, by well over half and in some cases completely. The approach also tracked bird productivity, welfare, and health, offering a chemical-free control option.
pmc-13383506:
Naji Al-Bawah's team measured sitting time among university students across Yemen, in a 2026 national study across many centers. Sitting behavior independently risks physical and mental ill health, and Yemeni students face long sitting hours from academic demands. The team surveyed 8312 students aged 18 to 30 from 28 universities in 10 cities with the Arabic sitting questionnaire.

Mean daily sitting time reached 326.3 minutes, and 28.6 percent reported long sitting of 7 hours or more daily. Television led sitting pastimes, followed by study work and phone use. Private university enrollment, science and engineering study, smoking, and lack of campus exercise sites all raised odds of long sitting, pointing to concrete campus fixes.
pmc-13383906:
Yuqing Pang and colleagues study how the ErZhi formula acts on muscle in bone-and-muscle loss using rat models in 2026 work. The formula is known to help osteosarcopenia, a combined loss of bone and muscle, but its muscle effects were little reported. Rats received the formula or a standard drug for twelve weeks after a model was set up.

Treated rats kept larger muscle fibers and showed less fiber scarring than untreated model rats. Energy hubs in muscle cells worked better, with higher membrane potential and far lower harmful oxygen species. Chemical profiling found 35 changed compounds and pointed to energy and lipid pathways as central to the benefit.
pmc-13384206:
Jaime Guerrero and co-authors measure how a key growth receptor pairs up on living cell surfaces in 2026 work. VEGFR2 must join in pairs to switch on, but single-molecule imaging sees only a small labeled share of receptors. The team joined that imaging with a random-motion math model to infer rates for the full receptor pool.

A shortened receptor stayed mostly single, while the full-length receptor paired and split again often. The main gap between them lay in how fast pairs form, not how fast they break apart. Knowing those rates should sharpen models of how blood vessel growth signals pass into cells.
pmc-13385206:
Fatemeh Fotouhi and co-authors reanalyse protein-cutting data from dying muscle cells and find that some cuts by caspases, the enzymes that dismantle cells during apoptosis, are being hidden. Their 2026 study builds on an N-terminomics dataset, a method that reads the new ends created when proteins are cut, from mouse myoblasts that were either differentiating or dying.

The team proposes that after a caspase cut, a second enzyme trims two amino acids from the new end. Because identification relies on that end's sequence, the trimming disguises the original caspase site. Several hidden substrates appeared only in dying cells, not in differentiating cells that also had active caspase-3, suggesting the hidden cuts may specifically mark apoptosis. The authors argue that accounting for this sequential cutting can reveal missed caspase substrates in existing datasets and sharpen understanding of cell fate decisions.
pmc-13385906:
Meng Xia's team mapped why kinin receptor blockers favor one subtype over another, in a 2026 structural study. Kinin receptors B1R and B2R regulate vasodilation, swelling, and pain, and their blockers show promise in angioedema, pancreatitis, and asthma. The team solved three cryo-EM structures: B1R with peptide blocker R715, B1R with small-molecule blocker ELN441958, and B2R with Win64338.

Together with functional assays and docking, the structures reveal distinct binding modes. Three non-conserved residues at the bottom of the ligand pocket confer subtype selectivity. Both receptors share an antagonism mechanism in which blocker binding restricts movement of a toggle-switch tryptophan residue, locking the receptor in an inactive form.
pmc-13386006:
Guo and colleagues analyzed in 2026 what clinicians change in notes drafted by ambient AI, systems that listen to visits and write the record. Such tools are spreading fast, but the editing step that turns a draft into a signed note was little studied. Eight coders examined drafts from 200 real encounters, building an eleven-code scheme spanning clinical content, word choice, and style, then synthesized patterns from the edits.

Factual content drew the most edits: orders such as tests and procedures led, followed by symptoms, drug prescriptions, and diagnosis wording, while word choice and style edits were far rarer. Five edit types covered most work: fixing factual mismatches, adding specialty detail, stating how certain a diagnosis is, turning patient phrasing into clinical terms, and tightening or reordering text. The authors urge builders to support specialty tuning and personal styles, and trainers to teach steady review habits.
pmc-13386506:
Rezaie Dorostkar and colleagues genotype two Candida species from human and animal patients, in 2026 mycology research. Candida krusei and Candida parapsilosis infect both people and livestock, and tracking their strains reveals whether clinics and farms share populations. The team collected 30 human samples from Imam Khomeini Hospital and 30 from farms, 15 of each species per source. They typed them with two DNA fingerprinting methods and screened for virulence and drug-resistance genes by multiplex PCR.

Resistance pump genes appeared at different frequencies across four groups. In human C. krusei samples, the CDR1 gene appeared in two-thirds of isolates, CDR2 in one-third, and MDR1 in none. Animal C. krusei carried all three more evenly, while human C. parapsilosis showed CDR1 in 80 percent of its isolates. Fingerprint trees grouped the strains for epidemiological comparison. Rezaie Dorostkar argues combined typing and resistance profiling is needed to follow yeasts between hospitals and farms.
pmc-13386606:
Zhaoquan Jiang's team traced how daily living ability shapes self-care in rural empty-nest elders in China, in a 2026 survey study. The team surveyed 1025 rural empty-nest older adults in Chaoyang, Liaoning, between February 2022 and March 2023, measuring daily living, social alienation, psychological resilience, and self-care ability.

Daily living scores correlated positively with social alienation and negatively with resilience and self-care. Social alienation correlated strongly and negatively with both resilience and self-care, while resilience correlated positively with self-care. Chain mediation analyses tested whether alienation and resilience carry the daily-living effect stepwise, pointing to social connection as a care lever.
pmc-13389806:
Abbas and colleagues used Monte Carlo modeling in 2026 to check radiation dose accuracy for pancreatic cancer treatment when a metal bile duct stent is present. Patients often carry these self-expanding stents for blocked bile flow, and their dense alloy bends CT scan readings, which can throw off the dose plans made by standard software. The team rechecked two treated patients whose plans used focused high-dose radiation in five sessions.

A new outlining method that splits the hollow stent core from its metal wall shrank the modeled stent size and fixed much of the scan error. Standard simulation overstated tumor dose by about 15 percent. The planning software understated dose beside the stent by up to about 12 percent and understated dose to the nearby duodenum, the first stretch of small bowel, by a similar margin. The authors say stent-aware modeling should be routine in such plans.
pmc-13390406:
Valentina Lumia leads the 2026 development of a fast DNA test for a lethal fig tree fungus that can be detected while still inside the wood. The fungus Ceratocystis ficicola causes bark canker, wood staining, and wilt, and has newly appeared in Greece and Italy.

Fig is an important Mediterranean crop, and the fungus sits on a European quarantine list, yet isolating it has been hard and reliable tests were lacking. The team built and validated a real-time PCR assay aimed at in-wood detection. Plant health inspectors and fig growers gain a tool for earlier and more certain detection, which supports quarantine action before an outbreak spreads through orchards.
pmc-13392606:
Shardul D Kulkarni and co-workers tested what happens to stray copying in the genome when parts of the CCR4-NOT complex, a machine that trims and destroys RNA messages, are removed. Cells normally copy many stretches outside genes, including jumping elements called retrotransposons, but destroy the products fast to protect orderly gene use. The team depleted two subunits of the complex, one of them CNOT4.

Fresh RNA profiling showed copying switching on widely across gene and non-gene regions, while few genes switched off. Among the quieter genes were KRAB zinc-finger genes, whose products hold jumping elements down, and those elements duly became active, including full-length copies sitting outside genes. Active sites clustered near binding spots for the zinc-finger proteins. The complex also shortens the life of jumping-element RNA directly, giving cells two layers of control.
pmc-13393506:
Nagasaki and team present a 2026 multi-site test of ultrasound formulas that estimate fetal weight before birth, a number guiding many delivery decisions. Using a prospective Japanese cohort, they compared the population-specific Shinozuka formula with the widely used global Hadlock-3 formula in 310 pregnancies scanned within seven days of delivery. A separate look covered 40 small-for-gestational-age fetuses.

Shinozuka estimates landed much closer to birth weight: 83.9 percent fell within 10 percent of the true weight, against 61.6 percent for Hadlock-3. Its median absolute percentage error was also lower, and it underestimated weight less than the global formula did. The advantage held when scans were restricted to three days before delivery and in the small-baby subgroup. The authors argue that maternity units should validate and choose weight formulas fitted to their own population rather than trusting one global standard.
pmc-13394506:
Heng Yang and colleagues present, in 2026, a new mouse model for bronchiectasis, a lasting lung disease. Airways widen and fill with mucus, and a germ named Pseudomonas often settles in for good. No solid animal model existed, so the team packed live germs into agar beads. They dosed mouse airways again and again with the beads plus an enzyme named papain.

Scans showed widened airways that reached the lung edges, much as in patients. Tissue held clusters of immune cells and thick mucus, and lung tests worsened. Germ-filled beads alone did less harm. The authors offer the model for studies of cause and for trials of new drugs.
pmc-13395506:
Alec Lachniet and co-authors compare, in 2026, robot, computer-guided, and hand-done knee replacements at one centre. Records covered 4,273 patients who had a first knee replacement from 2020 to 2023. Most operations, near nine in ten, used manual tools. Patient surveys ran before surgery and up to a year after.

No method won on patient scores or complication counts. Robot cases cost about fifteen hundred dollars more per patient on average. Use of guidance rose over the years while robot use fell. Robot and guided groups skewed younger and healthier. The authors, none tied to makers, say surgeon comfort still rules. Fancy tools must prove worth beyond precision claims.
pmc-13395906:
Felipe Franco da Graça and co-authors scan, in 2026, spinal cords of adults with spinal muscular atrophy over a year. The illness, from faulty SMN1 genes, wastes movement nerve cells, and firm progress markers are scarce. Twenty-six adults and 27 controls had neck cord scans. Gray matter size, total cord size, and water-flow measures were tracked alongside strength tests.

Gray matter size ran lower in patients and tracked well with strength and nerve scores. Total cord size was lower too but tied weakly to function. Water-flow reads flagged harm in sense paths, past the known motor damage. No scan measure shifted over the follow-up year. The authors back gray matter size as a marker pick.
pmc-13396606:
Diana T. Samuels and co-authors report outcomes for a drug pairing used as salvage therapy when leukemia or a related marrow disorder returns after a stem cell transplant. Their 2026 study covers acute myeloid leukemia and myelodysplastic syndromes that relapsed after allogeneic transplantation, a point where options run short.

The pairing joins a hypomethylating agent, a drug that loosens chemical silencing on genes, with venetoclax, which frees cancer cells to die. Two headline findings lead the report. The combination was well tolerated in this fragile group. It also worked in patients whose earlier treatment already included venetoclax-based therapy, a group often assumed to be out of reach for the drug.
pmc-13396906:
Mingzhu Li and co-authors traced how two partner proteins in liver cells keep bile acids in balance, in a 2026 mouse study. CBP and p300 are editors that loosen DNA packaging; when bile acid handling fails, liver diseases follow, yet this pair's role in that system was unclear.

Mice lacking both proteins only in the liver were profiled for their chemicals and gene activity. Gene-tagging and binding tests showed the pair switch on a factor called KLF10 by acetylating its gene region, and KLF10 in turn supports the pump that exports bile salts from liver cells. A cholestasis model, where bile flow is blocked, confirmed the chain in living disease.
pmc-13397006:
Tabea Margareta Grace Pakull and co-authors checked whether open-weight language models can draft plain-language versions of molecular tumor board reports that patients can actually use. Their 2026 study starts from a daily problem: these boards issue expert recommendations in dense technical German that patients rarely understand.

Writing lay versions by hand is hard to sustain in busy cancer centers. Closed commercial models are often barred by strict data protection rules, so the authors tested openly available models under real deployment limits. Clinicians then judged the drafts for quality and usability, asking whether machine help could make a patient's own treatment plan readable without a doctor rewriting every line.
pmc-13397706:
Sung-Jin Cha and fellow authors set out a trial plan comparing weaker and stronger iodine dye for heart artery scans. Their 2026 protocol covers 258 adults aged 40 or over with known or suspected coronary disease who need computed tomography imaging. Less dye could spare kidneys and cut cost, but only if the pictures stay clear enough to trust.

Half the group will get dye at 270 mg of iodine per mL and half at 350 mg per mL under matched scan settings. The main check is whether vessel brightness holds up with the weaker mix during angiography scans. pmc-13398606:

pmc-13426506:
Hyewon Jeon and colleagues review stimuli-responsive, cell-mimicking vesicles for drug delivery in a 2026 pharmaceutical article. Vesicles can carry both water-loving and fat-loving drugs together, enabling combination therapy, yet ordinary carriers accumulate poorly at targets and spread nonspecifically. Adding responses to cues such as pH, enzymes, or light allows controlled release at the right place and time with less body-wide toxicity.

Newer designs go further, acting as artificial cells that can synthesize compounds on site, react to signals, and communicate with living cells. The review argues vesicle engineering is moving from passive transport toward programmable therapeutic platforms.
pmc-13428106:
Apiliogullari and colleagues tested in 2026 whether blood markers can quickly identify intracerebral hemorrhage, bleeding inside the brain, where fast diagnosis shapes treatment and survival. Scans confirm the diagnosis but take time and access. The team measured four brain proteins in blood, plus several hormone signals, in patients and healthy volunteers.

Samples came from 71 patients with scan-confirmed bleeding and 30 healthy controls, repeated over two weeks. All four brain markers separated patients from controls at every time point. One marker, GFAP, a protein from support cells, was far higher in patients on day one, by orders of magnitude. Two hormone signals also ran higher in patients, and marker levels did not differ by age group. The authors present the panel as promising but caution that telling one stroke type from another still needs study.
pmc-13428706:
Mthembu and colleagues use modeling to test whether ring shaped peptides can jam a chaperone the malaria parasite needs to survive stress. Plasmodium falciparum, the deadliest malaria parasite, leans on Grp78, a folding helper in its protein workshop, when drugs batter it. Two peptide families, gramicidin S and the tyrocidines, already kill the parasite. Their 2026 study docks these rings onto the chaperone's structure and runs simulations to see where they stick and what they change.

The peptides settled on a patch of the chaperone's substrate binding part, spanning its arch and pocket. Human versions use other spots. Long simulations kept them bound. The fit looked like a conformational lock: the chaperone loses the flexing its work cycle needs. The rings also favored the parasite's workshop chaperone over its cytosolic cousin and over human counterparts. All results are predictions, the authors stress, awaiting wet lab proof.
pmc-13429006:
Marcello Arca and a large team trace, in a 2026 study, how fat particles move through the blood of people born without a key regulator protein. ANGPTL3 normally slows the breakdown of triglyceride-rich particles, and people lacking it enjoy lifelong low blood fats and less heart disease. The team studied three people with no working copy of the gene, four with one copy, and ten matched controls. Tracer methods followed fat transport after meals across particle types.

Production of the particles ran at normal speed in everyone. In those with complete deficiency, breakdown ran astonishingly fast, clearing particles in minutes instead of hours. Their LDL particles, the cholesterol carriers tied to heart risk, came out oddly composed yet were cleared faster too. Half-deficiency gave a milder speed-up. Drug developers mimicking this state gain a detailed picture of what to expect and watch for.
pmc-13429106:
Daniel J. Davis and co-authors ask, in a 2026 study, whether stiffer shoe soles can repay some of the energy older walkers lose. Aging shifts walking work from the ankle toward the hip, and slopes make the deficit worse. Nineteen volunteers around age 70 walked under several slope conditions wearing shoes fitted with carbon fiber insoles of rising stiffness. Joint motions, forces, and breathing costs were measured throughout.

Stiffer soles cut energy lost at the front of the foot but raised losses at the heel, leaving whole-foot results mixed. Peak ankle effort rose about 10 percent in the stiffest shoes. Knee and hip mechanics barely changed, and overall energy cost showed no consistent saving. The authors float a different hope: stronger ankle demand might train calf muscles over time. Footwear designers get precise limits on what a flat stiff insole can do.
pmc-13430206:
Franz Felix Konen leads a large German team testing, in a 2026 study, whether updated multiple sclerosis rules can be applied with ordinary hospital tools. The 2024 revision of the McDonald criteria lets doctors diagnose MS earlier by counting the optic nerve as a fifth site and by accepting certain spinal fluid markers. The study enrolled 215 adults after a first suspected demyelinating event or with silent MRI lesions, worked up the standard way between 2020 and 2025.

Under the new rules about 94 percent met the diagnosis at the first assessment, against about 84 percent under the older rules. Optic nerve evidence supplied most of the extra diagnoses, and reclassifying silent-lesion cases supplied most of the rest. An electrical eye test caught optic nerve involvement in about 89 percent of cases. Newer MRI markers were not even needed for the gain shown.
pmc-13431006:
Shilling and colleagues further tested in 2026 a questionnaire that measures how cancer and its treatment disrupt patients' everyday roles, such as caregiving and money duties. The scale was first built for advanced cancer, but its makers meant it for all cancers and stages. This study checked it in people treated with curative intent, three years after diagnosis.

The data came from 1,077 survivors of breast, gynecological, and blood cancers in a long-running British cohort. The sixteen-item scale held together well, and its subscales were mostly sound. Scores lined up with related measures of work, social life, and quality of life in the pattern predicted. A statistical model confirmed the scale's three-part structure, though its parts overlapped more than expected. The authors conclude the scale is fit for wider use in survivorship research.
pmc-13431306:
Li and colleagues tracked gut microbes in Hu sheep lambs in 2026 through diarrhea and antibiotic treatment, using gene sequencing of feces. They compared lambs in early diarrhea, lambs in late recovery after a four-drug treatment mix, and healthy lambs, rebuilding hundreds of microbial genomes from the sequence data.

They assembled 482 high-quality genomes, most from the three phyla typical of ruminant guts. In early diarrhea, usually friendly bacteria carried more virulence genes. By late recovery the diarrhea had eased, yet resistance genes against two drug classes had grown, a leftover risk from the combined antibiotics. Two potential disease-causing genera also surged during diarrhea and carried hundreds of virulence genes each. The authors say antibiotic clearing of sensitive microbes, more than diarrhea itself, drove the deepest community change.
pmc-13432906:
Rashid Iqbal and colleagues sprayed quinoa leaves with two natural compounds to shield the crop from tellurium, a toxic element leaking into farm soils. Serotonin, a plant signal chemical, and allantoin, a protective nitrogen compound, were tested together under controlled plots.

Tellurium stress alone slashed growth and yield and raised cell damage markers in the plants. Sprayed together, the two compounds lifted grain yield by about 90 percent over stressed plants that got no spray. They also cut tellurium reaching the grain by about two thirds, keeping the harvested food safer. Soil microbe life and nutrient levels recovered as well, so Iqbal backs the spray pair for poisoned fields.
pmc-13434306:
Nathan F Bellis and coauthors detail in 2026 how a virus that infects gut bacteria throws its own copy enzyme into the host cell. The enzyme is huge, with about 3,500 building units in one chain. Two helper proteins leave with it to form a short lived entry machine.

Images of full and emptied virus shells show one helper forming a pore in the outer wall. The second helper builds a tunnel through the gap beyond the wall. A hub in the tail senses contact with the host and times the release. The loose chain form may let the huge enzyme thread a narrow channel.
pmc-13434606: Untalan, Pagote, and Tejero write to refine a Canadian ultra-processed food screener built on the NOVA classification. They flag self-reported intake as prone to recall bias. They urge adding food-environment indicators, such as source and affordability. They also suggest pairing NOVA categories with standard examples or nutrient markers. That would fix inconsistent boundaries. They close by recommending the screener be embedded in existing public health systems for policy impact.
pmc-13437206:
Sung Ho Hwang, writing in 2026, asks why heart artery CT scans expose patients in poorer countries to far more radiation than in rich ones. A world study of 19,302 patients in 101 countries found doses about twice as high in low-income settings, and the median African dose ran over five times the Western European level.

Newer scanners cut dose by over a fifth, yet doses stayed far higher in poor countries even after machine type was weighed. How well teams tune their settings and run the scan matters just as much. Low tube voltage, scans timed to the heartbeat, and smarter image rebuilding can each trim exposure. New deep learning rebuilding alone has cut dose by forty to sixty percent without blurring detail in cited studies. The piece argues training, careful patient setup, and shared know-how must travel with the hardware if dose gaps are to close.
pmc-13437506:
Andrea Gonsek and colleagues recorded brain activity in stick insects to learn how a night-active animal sorts smell from touch and sound. In darkness, the stick insect leans on its long antennae, feeling obstacles up close and catching scent and air movement from afar. Their 2026 study set up long-term recordings from many neurons at once in the antennal lobe, the brain's first smell station.

Hexanal, the smell of freshly cut leaves and a food cue for this leaf eater, lit a distinct pattern across the network. Mechanical stimulation, likely standing in for airborne vibration such as sound, also drove cells in the same region. A large share of neurons answered both kinds of input, showing the lobe is no pure smell center. The team frames the work as a first step toward using the stick insect to model how near-range touch and far-range scent merge.
pmc-13437906:
Surender and colleagues screened the whole genome in 2026 to find genes that sway how glioma, a brain tumor, responds to CDK4/6 blockers, drugs that halt cell division machinery. These drugs have disappointed in glioblastoma, so partners that sensitize or protect tumors are prized. Using CRISPR gene cutting and gene activation across five human glioma cell lines, the team hunted for modifiers, then checked the hits in cultures and in animals.

Losing a gene called AMBRA1 or boosting CCNE1 made cells resist the blockers. Breaking CHEK1 or FAM122A turned lethal only when the blockers were present, a pattern called synthetic lethality. Cells lacking AMBRA1 became extra sensitive to checkpoint kinase blockade, exposing a tailored weakness. Pairing a CHK1 blocker with a CDK4/6 blocker killed glioma cells in synergy in dishes, in patient-derived cultures, and in animals. The authors propose the pairing for glioblastoma trials.
pmc-13438106:
Soliman and colleagues design a fresh family of compounds that both attack bacteria and shield antibiotics from bacterial defense enzymes. Beta lactamase enzymes break penicillin type drugs, a core driver of drug resistance. Their 2026 study builds a series of dihydropyrimidinones, ring shaped molecules. It tests them against two Gram positive and one Gram negative bacterial species, then against resistant strains and the purified defense enzyme.

Most compounds showed moderate bacteria killing next to the standard drug amoxicillin. Against resistant strains the compounds acted as boosters, restoring partner drug action by blocking the defense enzyme. Three leads, coded 3d, 3i, and 7b, blocked the purified enzyme at lower doses than clavulanic acid, the standard blocker used in clinics. The team names those three as hits worth refining into selective, stronger blockers for resistant infections.
pmc-13439706:
Dai and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the human evidence for transmission ratio distortion, the bending of Mendel's rule that each parent passes either gene copy with equal odds. Distortion is well proven in other species, where selfish elements hijack reproduction, but human claims were scattered. The team gathered reports from the nineteen seventies through 2025 that met set criteria.

Ninety-six studies covering forty-two variants, genes, or regions qualified. Taken together they offered only preliminary and often conflicting evidence, and the methods shared repeated biases such as small samples and selective reporting. True biological proof of a mechanism was rare or impossible in most reports. The authors conclude that human distortion remains unproven at any locus, but urge fresh attention now that very large family-based genome datasets can test the claims properly.
pmc-13441506:
Carlo Covello and colleagues burn away a chest lymph node metastasis through the food pipe wall, reporting a 2026 case of ultrasound-guided radiofrequency ablation. Their patient, a 58-year-old man with past clear cell kidney cancer, showed a growing posterior mediastinal node on combined PET and CT imaging, measuring thirty by seventeen millimetres. Chest surgery was attempted first and abandoned because the node could not be reached safely.

A linear ultrasound scope passed down the oesophagus placed a fine ablation needle into the node's centre under live imaging. Radiofrequency energy ran at thirty watts across five cycles starting centrally, with bubbling in the tissue marking effective heating. Peripheral zones were then completed in a final phase. The authors present scope-guided ablation as a minimally invasive option for selected chest nodes that surgery cannot reach, a use so far documented in few patients.
pmc-13441706:
Sara Costa and colleagues test how little facial information people need to read an emotion, building displays from just five moving dots, in a 2026 study. Reading expressions uses both face structure and muscle motion, yet separating the two is hard. Their Clepsydra model places dots on the two eyebrows, the two mouth corners, and the nose, replaying genuine expressions as pure motion. Ninety-one participants judged the six basic emotions in dot form and in full-face form.

Five emotions were read above chance from dots alone: happiness, surprise, anger, disgust, and sadness. Fear stayed at chance, and it was most often mistaken for surprise, which shares its upper-face muscle actions. Anger and disgust were also swapped for each other in patterned ways. The authors offer the five-dot model as a clean tool for isolating motion's share in expression reading.
pmc-13442706:
Çelik and co-authors farmed Mediterranean mussels at 1 meter and 10 meters depth for a full year. They wanted to see how depth and season shape the mussels' fatty acid makeup. They also tracked the nutritional quality of their lipids. They identified 37 fatty acids in the harvest. Standard lipid health indices were computed across seasons at both depths.

Polyunsaturated fats dominated at both depths. They made up 48.63 percent of lipids at 1 meter and 48.88 percent at 10 meters overall. The valuable long-chain omega-3 fats EPA and DHA followed narrower, steadier seasonal patterns in the deeper mussels than near the surface. At the shallow depth, atherogenicity and thrombogenicity indices spiked sharply in autumn, to about 0.79 and 0.30. Deep-water values drifted only gradually through the year. The authors conclude season drives composition most, but depth stabilizes quality. Depth management could standardize farmed mussel products, they suggest.
pmc-13443106:
Ke-ran Li and colleagues identify a growth factor, MYDGF, that drives new vessel growth in the retina in a 2026 study. Wayward vessel growth threatens sight in diabetic eye disease and in early-life eye states. Single-cell gene reads and patient checks showed MYDGF runs high in retina lining cells during the diabetic growth phase.

Dish tests showed the factor speeds lining cell growth, motion, and sprouting. Mice bred to lack the factor in lining cells grew fewer vessels, both in normal youth growth and in disease-like growth. The factor works through a chain of G proteins and a Gab1 link to the Akt-mTOR path. Cutting chain parts muted the vessel push. The authors name the chain as a drug aim for eye vessel disease.
pmc-13443206:
Paul Fruton and colleagues watch supercritical carbon dioxide split into layers under uneven heat in a 2026 study. Past the critical point, the fluid is taught as one smooth phase with no sharp gas-liquid edge. A steady heat slope, set to keep the fluid stable, broke that calm picture in their cell.

Shadow views showed crisp layers parted by thin zones where traits jump fast. Marks grew sharpest near Widom lines, where fluid responses peak in the supercritical range. Flicker spectra rang with gravity wave tones at many pitches, proof of true layering. One run could sweep many states at once in their setup. The authors say far-from-calm supercritical fluids can hold structure that calm views miss.
pmc-13443306:
Nuraly Akimbekov and colleagues join coal cleaning and mine soil repair through microbe sulfur work in a 2026 review. Microbes that move sulfur can strip it from coal before burning, yet the same cycles run in spoil heaps and sour mine water. The review ties those worlds into one frame.

Pyrite burn-up, organic sulfur shifts, sulfate cuts, and metal trapping each get weighed for gains and risks. The same microbe acts can clean waste and heal soil, or can sour land and free metals. Outcomes turn on air reach, water links, buffer strength, and carbon supply. The authors urge field-tested, risk-led plans over lone microbe hunts. Their frame treats coal yards and mine soils as one linked system.
pmc-13444506:
Sabreena Moosa and colleagues report a lung aneurysm fed by an odd artery fistula in a 2026 case paper. A bronchial artery had joined a pulmonary artery, a rare link, and a pouch swelled where pressures clash. Plain CT without contrast could not pin the cause of the chance-found pouch.

Cone beam CT, spun during the vessel session, mapped the inflow bronchial artery and the outflow pulmonary path in fine detail. That map steered the fix: plugs in the inflow bronchial artery to starve the pouch. Born or gained, such links are scarce in print, and pouch pairs are scarcer. The authors credit cone beam views for both the call and the plan. Rupture of such pouches can kill, so the stakes run high.
pmc-13444706: Tachkov and colleagues' 2026 article on a European network on antibody treatment in chronic inflammatory diseases received a correction to its reference list in Clinical and Translational Science. Two changes align the in text citations with the list. One reference, a study of cancer drug payment decisions, has been removed. Another, the Petrova statement on education in therapeutic drug monitoring, has been moved to follow the Holford and Petric entry. The notice prints the corrected entries and closes with an apology; no findings or claims of the article change.
pmc-13446306:
Li Huang and colleagues build a six-question screen for sarcopenia, the age-linked loss of muscle bulk and strength, for older adults in Chinese communities, in a 2026 study. Long test batteries slow case finding in busy clinics. The team drew a first item pool from past papers, then pruned it with expert rounds and classic test theory.

Older adults in three community settings in Chengdu and Hangzhou took the screen, judged against Asian and European gold rules for the condition. At the lowest cut score tried, the screen caught near nine in ten Asian-rule cases and near all European-rule cases. Accuracy held in a good band across both rule sets. The authors pitch the short form for fast first-pass checks in the community.
pmc-13447206:
Cheng Zeng and co-authors test a combined body measure as a heart risk marker in type 2 diabetes in a 2026 analysis. The index joins waist size, height and blood fat levels to capture belly obesity and metabolic strain in one number. Whether it predicts major heart events and death beyond standard factors was the question.

Data came from a large diabetes trial and its follow-up, covering more than ten thousand people with the index recorded at the start. Over roughly nine years, close to one in five had a major heart event and a similar share died. Higher index values linked to higher risk for both outcomes after standard factors were taken into account. Adding the index also improved how well standard models sorted future risk.
pmc-13447906:
Yashayaeva and colleagues check a new imaging system for planning head and neck radiotherapy in this 2026 prospective trial. During treatment, patients lose weight and tumors shrink, so plans must be recalculated on fresh images. The HyperSight cone-beam CT, fitted to a treatment machine, promises image quality near standard CT plus tools to suppress artifacts from dental metal. The team scanned 25 patients on three systems and compared dose calculations.

The advanced iterative reconstruction gave the highest agreement with reference scans in slices free of metal artifacts. In slices containing dental metal, the artifact-reduction reconstruction held up best as artifact severity grew, while the conventional cone-beam system consistently scored lowest. Overall three-dimensional pass rates at the standard tolerance exceeded 99 percent for the best HyperSight mode, supporting its use in adaptive planning.
pmc-13448206:
M García-Briega leads a team building a three-dimensional culture platform that mimics the bone marrow home of multiple myeloma in 2026 work. Myeloma cells survive treatment partly because neighbouring marrow cells and matrix shelter them, an effect flat lab cultures miss. A model that rebuilds that shelter could predict drug resistance more honestly before animal or patient testing.

Cone-shaped agarose wells gather the abnormal plasma cells together, while magnetic alginate microbeads stand in for matrix, layered with collagen and other natural coatings. Pellets of marrow support cells were added to recreate direct and indirect contact. Three myeloma cell lines grew and resisted drugs inside the platform as expected. Patient marrow cells from two Spanish hospitals survived up to fourteen days, letting researchers watch the abnormal fraction over time.
pmc-13448306:
Fernandes and colleagues present in 2026, as abstract TLSB-07, a retrospective study of which breast cancer patients receiving chemotherapy before surgery go on to develop brain metastases, and how quickly. Risk factors and timing in this treatment setting were poorly defined.

Combining two Sunnybrook cohorts gave 586 patients who had received the pre-surgery chemotherapy; about twenty-six percent developed brain metastases over a median follow-up of thirty-eight months. The median time from diagnosis to brain spread was just under thirty months. It was shortest in triple negative disease at eighteen months and longest in hormone-sensitive, HER2-negative disease at about forty-nine months. Failing to achieve a complete response to chemotherapy carried the largest hazard, followed by inflammatory breast cancer and residual cancer in the lymph nodes. The authors argue brain screening for the highest-risk patients deserves study.
pmc-13448906:
Simon Vanhentenrijk and colleagues review in 2026 what is known about autoantibodies that actively disturb heart muscle function rather than merely marking disease. The review explains how B cells, helped by certain T cells, mature into plasma cells that pour out these antibodies. Imbalances in that output can disturb normal heart physiology, promote scarring of the muscle, and worsen outcomes.

Older schemes sorted such antibodies into heart-specific and non-heart-specific groups, but the authors show why that split breaks down. Many targets, including beta-1 adrenergic receptors, M2 muscarinic receptors, and ion channels, appear in many tissues, and cross-reaction is itself a functional trait. They therefore organize the findings by molecular target and by what each antibody does. The survey covers activation of complement, toxin neutralization, and recruitment of killer cells, giving clinicians a more useful map of this growing field.
pmc-13449506:
Du and team compared three years versus one year of BCG bladder therapy. BCG is the immune treatment instilled after surgery for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer. The comparison covered 140 Chinese patients treated at one center from 2017 to 2024. China's guideline recommends one year, based on local strain differences. Evidence for the longer course used elsewhere is missing.

Seventy-two patients received the three-year regimen and 68 the one-year regimen under routine clinical allocation at the center. Recurrence-free survival favored the longer course, with a hazard ratio of 0.31 in the survival analysis comparing the groups. Adjusted modeling confirmed the three-year schedule as an independent protective factor, at a hazard ratio of 0.282 in the model. The benefit held in high-risk subgroups tested. Only 27 recurrences occurred. Completion rates differed sharply, at 25 versus 51.5 percent. The authors label the findings hypothesis-generating, pending prospective trials.
pmc-13449806:
Matheus Santos França and colleagues write in 2026 about children and teenagers with Behçet disease who lack the genetic marker most associated with it, HLA-B51. The disease is an inflammatory disorder first described in 1937. It clusters along the old Silk Road and strikes hardest in the Middle and Far East, where the marker is common and tied to severe cases. Childhood disease is harder to pin down because symptoms arrive piecemeal, so classification criteria exist alongside judgment.

Pediatric data from Latin America are scarce, so the team analyzed 32 patients at a Brazilian tertiary rheumatology center, a multiethnic setting where 15.5 percent of healthy people carry the marker. Median age at diagnosis was four and a half years, half the patients were female, and most declared white ethnicity. Their letter investigates what HLA patterns, including B51-negative status, mean for how these children's disease presents and should be treated.
pmc-13449906:
Wang and co-authors catalogue the imaging of a rare tumour that grows inside veins. Their 2026 retrospective series reviews nineteen cases of intravenous leiomyomatosis. In that condition a benign uterine growth extends worm-like through pelvic veins and can reach the heart. One endometrial stromal sarcoma initially mistaken for it is included. Complete removal depends on mapping the tumour's full extent beforehand.

Nearly half had no symptoms, and about 58 percent were initially missed or misdiagnosed. Only three cases showed the textbook worm-like extension on imaging. MRI proved best at revealing the characteristic contours and vein filling defects. CT in its venous phase most clearly defined how far intravascular tumour reached. Both uterine and ovarian veins were involved most often. The single sarcoma stood out through much higher metabolic activity on PET-CT and a raised tumour marker. The authors recommend combining ultrasound with cross-sectional imaging.
pmc-13451606:
Özçıbık Işık and a multicenter Turkish team asked whether lung cancer spread to multiple N2 lymph node stations worsens survival versus a single station. The N2 nodes are the middle chest nodes. They were recently split into N2a and N2b in the ninth staging edition. Their series covered 149 resected patients staged before surgery across seven clinics, from 2002 to 2023.

Ninety-eight patients had single-station and 51 multiple-station involvement. Mean ages were 61.3 and 59.6 years in the two groups respectively. Overall survival did not differ significantly between single and multiple station groups in the Kaplan-Meier comparison reported. What did predict survival was adenocarcinoma histology, overall stage, and receiving treatment before surgery. All were significant in the cohort analysis. Regression confirmed tumor pathology type and preoperative therapy as independent prognostic factors. Station count alone should not drive decisions, they suggest.
pmc-13451806:
Wafira Wilson and co-authors ask in 2026 whether the heart rhythm at arrest shapes who gains from a heart-lung machine rescue. The rescue, ECPR, pumps blood for patients whose hearts will not restart with standard care. Registry data from Australia and New Zealand covered 249 adults treated between 2019 and 2022.

Overall, a sixth of patients lived six months with good daily function. Those whose first rhythm could take a shock did better, at about a fifth, even though the other group had more witnessed arrests and shorter low-flow times. Survivors from the non-shock group stayed longer in intensive care and hospital. The authors say rhythm should weigh in rescue choices, pending larger work.
pmc-13451906:
Juan Sebastian Theran Leon writes in 2026 a letter that questions a study using heart-signal marks and a learning model to sort cardiology patients. The letter grants the study team credit for clear methods, plain accounts of missing follow-up, and candor about weak rule-in power. Its core worry is what the model was truly asked to predict.

The stated aim was to spot who needs top-level care, yet the model was trained on death and later heart events in people already sent to such care. That makes the task forecast, not triage, the letter argues. It also notes that no check was shown for how close the model's risk scores sit to real rates, and it urges a plain statement of intended use.
pmc-13452006:
Dou and Zhu take stock of dance based programs for mental health by reviewing the reviews themselves. Their 2026 umbrella review gathered 90 review articles from five databases and graded the strong designs, such as systematic reviews, with a standard quality tool. Weaker review types were used to map how the field defines dance work and what it chooses to measure.

The field splits three ways, the authors find. Labels and delivery vary from formal dance movement therapy to vague group dance. Therapy reviews stress symptom relief, while others stress well being, energy, and social bonds. Most studies rely on generic mood scales rather than measures tuned to movement. On quality weighted evidence, dance programs show promise for well being, connection, and some symptoms, but low review quality and mixed groups keep confidence limited.
pmc-13452206:
Ruiming Du and co-authors build in 2026 a vision model that splits 3D scans of bare apple trees into single branches. Branch-level maps feed both breeding scores and pruning robots, yet common methods first round point clouds into blocks, which loses fine shape. Their model instead pours raw point traits into sparse block codes on the fly.

Tests showed clear gains over base models on most split scores. Those gains carried into farm tasks, with truer branch counts and pruning maps. The authors add a caution: scores tuned to plant work, not generic vision scores, should judge such tools, since a small vision gain can hide a big farm gain, or the reverse.
pmc-13452306:
Willem Geuskens and co-authors study in 2026 who gets back to work after a shoulder joint swap, and what helps. Their cohort held 103 patients under 63 with at least two years of follow-up, who filled work and shoulder forms. Two thirds made it back to work, at a mean of sixteen weeks.

Over half of those back went to their old job full time. Higher schooling, lighter physical work, sick leave under a year before surgery, and backing at work all tied to return. Age, sex, weight, swap kind, and problems after surgery did not. Returners also scored their shoulders better, a loop the authors say clinics can plan around.
pmc-13452406:
Michael J Wesley, William J McGarrigle, and Mark T Fillmore test whether rapid brain stimulation can be paired safely with a dose of alcohol in the lab. Their 2026 pilot study used short magnetic pulses aimed at the front left of the brain, a spot tied to self control. Ten healthy young adults took part in the blinded trial, which used a sham treatment for comparison.

Each person did a go and no go task sober, then again near peak blood alcohol after real or sham stimulation. Everyone finished both rounds with no serious side effects and no one quit over the stimulation. Alcohol alone raised the number of failed stops on the task. Early hints pointed to even more failed stops after real stimulation, but the group was far too small to settle that question.
pmc-13452506:
Stoess, Hannibal, and Greb show that a silicon atom's coordination number can act as a switchboard for molecules carrying two light-responsive units, a route toward multistate information storage beyond simple on-off photochromism. Their two silicon-based diarylethene Lewis acids close their rings one at a time under light, with coupling between the units changing as silicon binds four or five partners.

Adding a donor molecule let the team select single ring closure only, activate switching by wavelength, or shut photoreactivity off entirely, depending on which base was bound to the silicon center. Without donors, each closure step strengthened the molecule's Lewis acidity, culminating in the first photoswitchable Lewis superacid reported. Reversible silicon-nitrogen and silicon-oxygen bond swapping also let them reach switching-state distributions that pure photochemistry cannot exceed statistically. The authors establish valency control as a design rule for multiphotochromic systems.
pmc-13453306:
Bongiolatti and colleagues study separate lung cancers in both lungs, and ask which patients surgery on both sides helps. These cases are hard to tell from spread of one cancer, and operating twice demands a reason. Their 2026 study reviews forty five patients who had lesions removed between 2017 and 2024. It tracks survival and recurrence over a median of three years, and tests features as predictors.

Five year survival reached three quarters, which the authors call adequate. One feature dominated the outlook: spread through air spaces, tumor cells floating in the air sacs beyond the mass. It appeared in a fifth of patients. Every survival curve split on it. Patients with the feature saw survival and disease free survival collapse to zero, against strong rates without it. Adjusted risk ran several times higher. Checking for this spread, they conclude, should shape follow up after bilateral surgery.
pmc-13453506:
Benjamin W Sheffer, Verena M Schreiber, and Rachel M Thompson recount a three week traveling fellowship for children's bone surgeons across Europe in spring 2026. Every two years, the Pediatric Orthopaedic Society of North America sends three members to European centers, hosted by their European counterpart society. Their 2026 account moves through sites in the Netherlands and Belgium and ends in Sevilla, Spain.

The fellows watched new surgical methods, compared how each country's system backs patient care, and traded research ideas with host teams. Stays included a lake house near Amsterdam and a welcome dinner cooked by the European society's president. The trip closed with the European society's annual meeting. The authors frame the tour as time to think big with peers, build cross border ties, and urge the next group of members to apply.
pmc-13454206:
Heather Pathak and eight co-authors chart how Powassan virus, a tick borne virus, invades the mouse brain and what damage follows. The virus kills 10 to 30 percent of human neurological cases and leaves lasting harm in about half of survivors. Their 2026 study infects standard lab mice by four routes, from vein to skin, and tracks virus, barrier, and immune response over time.

Every route led to severe brain disease, with the virus spreading from the body into the brain in clear phases. Brain invasion came with heavy tissue change and a leakier blood brain barrier. Gene and protein reads showed interferon signaling, inflammation, and cell death programs switched on, with support cells activated and neurons dying. In survivors, viral RNA and mild inflammation lingered past the acute phase. The authors offer the full map for drug and vaccine work.
pmc-13455106:
Yuri A. Mastrikov and seven colleagues compute, in a 2026 theory study, how swapping one atom for another changes the electronics of a layered iron oxide. The material family matters for fuel cells and catalysts. Lanthanum was substituted for strontium across the full range, and the results were set against a sister material that instead loses oxygen.

Both routes raise the iron oxidation state by the same average amount. Yet the electron behavior differs sharply. The lanthanum version keeps its electrons more spread out and mobile. The oxygen-loss version distorts its lattice more, because each missing oxygen carries a double positive charge and breaks iron-oxygen bonds. A single-charge stand-in ion disturbs the structure less. The authors draw a general lesson: the kind of charged defect, not just its amount, sets a material's electronic character.
pmc-13455506:
Scott D. Wrigley, Sarah A. Johnson, Christopher L. Gentile, and Tiffany L. Weir pool, in a 2026 re-analysis, gut data from three earlier clinical studies to ask what changes first as heart and metabolic risk creeps up. People with such disease often show poorer gut diversity, but cause and effect stay tangled. The combined data compared healthy volunteers with people showing early risk signs.

Simple diversity scores did not differ across risk levels. A stricter consensus method told a subtler story: as risk rose, a roster of health-linked microbes thinned out, including Akkermansia, Bacteroides, and Bifidobacterium. Community maps also changed shape. In higher-risk guts, microbe networks grew looser and more fragmented, with fewer partnerships. The authors propose that losing key microbes and their web of ties may help push early risk toward disease.
pmc-13457006:
Huixin Yu and seven colleagues report, in a 2026 case, a melanoma that began in the food pipe and reached the brain within months. Melanoma starting in the esophagus is rare, hard to cure, and quick to return even after removal. Their patient was a 47-year-old man who arrived with trouble swallowing.

Camera examination found several cauliflower-like growths in the mid-esophagus, and biopsy proved melanoma that had already reached nearby lymph nodes. Surgeons removed the esophagus. Follow-up treatment paired an immune drug with a targeted pill. Five months later, brain scans showed multiple spread spots. Doctors removed one cerebellar tumor, zapped the rest with focused radiation, and gave a chemotherapy pill. His decline was still swift, with body-wide progression, and he died ten months after diagnosis. The authors present the case as a measure of this cancer's aggression.
pmc-13457706: Small-molecule TRPV6 inhibitors — discovered as potential anti-cancer agents by structure-based virtual screening. Lixuan Wang, Xin Deng, Ruoyang Hu, and others screen the structures. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is drug discovery. It virtually screens TRPV6 into drugs. Drug discovery.
pmc-13459506:
Yike Su and co-authors built two genetic transformation systems for peach, a fruit tree whose genes have been hard to study because no efficient method existed for inserting DNA. Their 2026 work used a soil bacterium, Agrobacterium rhizogenes, on stem pieces of the Hanlumi cultivar. Tuning the bacterial strain and dose produced transgenic callus tissue and hairy roots with stable marker expression. A second, faster system delivered genes temporarily into stem and fruit callus, letting the team test flavor genes within weeks.

Both systems were put to work on the pathway making C6 aldehydes, the green, fresh smelling compounds behind peach aroma. Boosting the genes PpLOX1 or PpHPL1 significantly raised hexanal and E-2-hexenal levels in the callus. Silencing PpLOX6 or PpHPL1 markedly lowered them instead. The paired results confirm all three genes as key controls of peach flavor chemistry and give breeders working tools.
pmc-13459606:
Shuyan Qin, Nana Zhao, Lei Shen, Yanan Zhang, and Shengfang Ge survey in 2026 how language-processing tools that also read images could change eye care. Ophthalmology generates both narrative clinical text and detailed pictures, and combining the two promises better diagnosis and smoother workflows. Their review covers transformer models for text, for images, and for linking the two kinds of information together.

Uses fall into three groups: merging text and images for fuller analysis, stronger screening and prediction systems, and clearer communication with patients. Obstacles include privacy, specialized vocabulary, opaque model reasoning, uneven data formats, and regulatory proof. The authors point to few-shot learning, real-time systems, and privacy-preserving training across sites as promising directions needing joint effort from clinicians and developers.
pmc-13461106:
Georgios Karamitros and colleagues used in 2026 artificial intelligence tools to audit racial representation across plastic surgery publishing over twelve years. Web scraping gathered authorship data from twenty-four journals between 2010 and 2022, covering more than sixteen thousand publications, and a name-classification program trained on census data inferred each author's race. Patterns in first and senior authorship, mentoring pairings, and output per author were compared.

White researchers dominated throughout, holding about two thirds of first authorships and nearly three quarters of senior slots by 2022. Black authorship fell over the period while Asian representation grew on both ends of the byline. White authors also published more papers per person than Asian, Black, or Hispanic colleagues. Black senior authors mentored across racial lines most often, and the authors urge earlier pipeline support.
pmc-13461506:
Vardhan and colleagues built in 2026 an explainable decision support system that classifies flatfoot, a foot deformity where the inner arch drops or vanishes, from foot images. They compared classic machine learning fed with hand-crafted texture features against deep learning networks, testing many of each. Careful subject-wise validation kept the same person out of both training and test sets.

Vardhan found the classic random forest reached only about seven in ten correct. A deep network, ResNet101V2, averaged about 93 percent accuracy, with its best single run near 98 percent. A hybrid that fed deep features into a decision tree did better still, at 97 percent accuracy with perfect specificity in their test. Explanation maps showed the models looked at the arch and heel for flat feet, matching clinical logic. The authors back the hybrid for screening use.
pmc-13461606:
Liu and colleagues present a 2026 case report and review tackling a diagnostic puzzle between two look-alike blood cancers. Chronic myeloid leukemia in megakaryocytic blast crisis and a rare acute leukemia both carry the Philadelphia chromosome and produce the same platelet forming blasts. The first is very rare, under three percent of chronic myeloid cases.

Their patient fitted chronic myeloid leukemia in blast phase best and got a targeted kinase inhibitor plus chemotherapy induction and consolidation. Liu reports complete remission and then deep molecular remission held for thirty-five months, even though stem cell transplantation was declined for cost reasons. The review draws out signs that tell the two apart, such as prior disease history and spleen and blood patterns. A diagnostic and treatment framework is offered.
pmc-13461706:
Xiaoli Yang and co-authors present a 2026 computer method for turning brain waves into sentences. Reading language from scalp recordings is hard: the signals are weak and noisy. Rather than recovering a sentence word for word, the team argues the signal holds only core meaning points. Their system, named Brain-CLIPLM, works in two stages matched to that limited scale.

First, a learning step aligns brain patterns with a set of keywords and pulls out meaning anchors. Next, a large language model uses those anchors, guided by reasoning prompts and similar stored examples, to rebuild a sentence. On a Zurich test set, the system placed the sentence in its top five guesses two thirds of the time. Control tests showed the anchors added sentence detail beyond what the language model alone could guess. The authors frame brain-to-text work as meaning recovery first, wording second.
pmc-13461806:
Gao and colleagues pooled in 2026 the evidence on the prognostic nutritional index for liver cancer patients having part of the liver removed. The index blends a blood protein level with a white cell count to reflect nutrition and immune state. The team searched four databases to April 2026 for studies linking the index, measured before surgery, to survival after curative liver resection.

Gao included 16 studies and found patients with a higher index lived longer on every measure. Their overall death risk was less than half that of low-index patients, and disease-free and recurrence-free survival also improved. Dropping any single study did not flip the result. Signs of publication bias appeared for overall survival, but the link stayed significant after correction. Cut-off choice varied between studies and may explain some spread, the authors note, so the index suits risk checks beside standard tools.
pmc-13461906:
Giordano and co-authors analysed a 2026 cross-sectional dataset on verbal fluency, the ability to list words quickly by a starting sound, across adult ages. Fluency fades with age, but the shape of that decline and what modifies it were debated. Data came from the Look Up 8+ study of community dwelling adults.

Among 3,615 adults aged thirty to eighty, the median fluency score was ten words in thirty seconds. Giordano found performance peaked around ages forty-five to fifty and then fell progressively lower with advancing age. More education linked strongly to higher scores, as did healthy diet, physical activity, and normal blood sugar. Greater central body fat linked to lower fluency and steepened the age decline, while slower chair stand performance also tracked poorer scores.
pmc-13462006:
Fangfang Shen and co-authors used explainable machine learning on seven randomized trials to find which lung cancer patients actually benefit from immunotherapy given around surgery. Benefit varies widely, and straight line statistics miss curved relationships. In their 2026 analysis, multilevel meta regression was fused with a gradient boosting model interpreted by SHAP values, which rank each factor's contribution. The trials covered neoadjuvant and perioperative immune checkpoint treatment in resectable non small cell lung cancer.

Benefit on event free survival grew with PD-L1 expression overall. It peaked where at least half the tumor stained positive, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.44 in that subgroup. The machine learning view complicated the story: differences between trials drove most heterogeneity. The PD-L1 relationship bent into a U shape, with both very low and very high expression predicting benefit in some histologies. Squamous tumors stood out.
pmc-13463506:
Yuwen Shi leads a team that tracked porcine rotavirus A in Guangxi Province, in southern China, from 2022 to 2025. The virus causes gut illness in pigs and spreads through dung. The group tested pig gut tissue and fecal swabs, then read the genes of the strains they found.

About seventeen in each hundred tests came back positive, with the G9P[13]I5 type most common. The VP4 gene varied more than the VP6 and VP7 genes, and the team also saw gene swaps and shuffled segments. Growth of the virus pool stayed flat for decades, then rose slowly after about 2016. Pig vets and health staff gain a dated gene map for tracking spread.
pmc-13463606:
David Huang and a large team ask whether hormone-primed IVF cycles change the womb lining in ways that raise blood pressure risk in pregnancy. Clinics often prime the lining with hormones rather than relying on a natural cycle. The team built a single-cell map of lining tissue from both kinds of cycle.

Primed linings differed clearly at the gene level, with fewer uterine natural killer cells and weaker signals for embryo settling and blood vessel growth. Yet in 548 tracked pregnancies, primed-cycle conceptions showed no early imbalance in vessel growth markers and no extra cases of high blood pressure disorders. The womb, the authors argue, adapts well despite the early shifts.
pmc-13463806:
Yiheng Jiang and nine colleagues published this 2026 study developing a green ultrasound-assisted extraction for polysaccharides from Banqiao Codonopsis root, a prized Chinese medicine-food plant, and testing the product against ulcerative colitis. The standard hot-water method is slow, hot and wasteful, degrading the very compounds it extracts. The team optimised the ultrasound process statistically, probed how cavitation frees them, and compared yield and energy use against the conventional method.

At the optimum, 400 watts for 34 minutes, the ultrasound process yielded 21.31 percent polysaccharide, beating hot water by 42 percent, while cutting extraction time by 43.5 percent, energy use by 38.8 percent and carbon emissions by 56.9 percent, and stripping protein and nucleic acid waste more effectively. Ultrasound shrank the plant particles by about 22 percent and loosened the cellulose structure, easing their release. The authors present the method as the scalable, low-carbon route to producing this anti-inflammatory ingredient for functional foods and medicines.
pmc-13464506:
Gerlin and colleagues model the food fight between a bacterium and a tomato plant in this 2026 paper. The bacterium Ralstonia pseudosolanacearum causes bacterial wilt, a destructive crop disease. During infection the two organisms compete directly for nutrients. The team merged a genome scale metabolic model of the bacterium with one of the whole plant, then tuned it with experimental data.

Simulations predicted the flows of matter through the infected plant. The plant's photosynthesis limited bacterial growth more strongly than its mineral supply did. Falling water flow through the plant first slowed plant growth and later starved the bacteria. The bacterium also appeared to steal resources through the stem, though only to a limited degree. Gerlin highlights water flow as central to how this disease develops.
pmc-13465006:
Sang-Ho Jeong and three co-authors review bleeding care for gastric cancer, where tumor bleeding can kill quickly and stall all other treatment. Two decades of evidence feed a stepwise plan guided by how stable the patient's circulation is. Scope-based stopping of the bleed comes first in the plan.

For unstable patients or failed scope work, artery blocking through a catheter takes over. Palliative radiation offers a non-invasive route that can slow tumor bleeding over days. Surgery waits as the last resort when other routes fail. The review reframes success: halting the bleed only opens the gate, and survival turns on getting patients back to cancer therapy fast.
pmc-13465406:
Chatterjee and co-authors investigated a 2026 regulator of disc degeneration, the enzyme PHLPP1, in the nucleus pulposus, the gel centre of spinal discs. Degeneration there drives disc related low back pain through inflammation and matrix breakdown. Earlier work tied higher PHLPP1 levels to worse degeneration in patients.

In aged mice lacking the gene, age related disc degeneration and inflammation were blunted, most clearly in males, Chatterjee reports. Silencing the gene in degenerated human disc cells sharply suppressed inflammatory and signal recruiting genes such as IL1B, IL6, and several chemokines. Matrix building gene activity rose at the same time, shifting cells toward a less destructive, less tissue eating state overall. The authors position PHLPP1 as an upstream regulator of the disc's inflammatory networks and a candidate drug target for slowing degeneration.
pmc-13465606:
Charles Tremblay and co-authors report early work, published in 2026, on steering drug-loaded bacteria through tumors with magnets as a cancer treatment. The bacteria move on their own and can be guided, which sets the approach apart from a simple drug injection into a tumor. Reaching deep sites such as the pancreas and rectum needs image guidance inside a new magnetic setup.

The team lays out a full guided workflow, using endoscopic ultrasound or scans through the skin to place the bacteria. They frame the report as the first complete version of this delivery chain, built to settle the technical questions that a first trial in people would raise. Pancreatic and rectal cancers are the target diseases throughout.
pmc-13466406:
Jiangtao Hu, Byoung Ryong Jeong, and Qichang Yang introduce a journal special issue, writing in 2026. Now in its second edition, the issue covers how plants respond to light at the cell and molecule level. Light feeds plants through photosynthesis, yet it also acts as a rich signal that times flowering and shapes growth, chemistry, and stress defense.

Six papers in the collection range from small RNA signaling in maize to pigment metabolism, hormone shifts, antioxidant defense, and protection of the photosynthetic machinery. Together they show light quality acting at many control levels at once. One maize study found a small RNA's free levels changing with light through binding to a partner protein rather than through new production.
pmc-13466506:
Vladislav Kozák and Jiří Vala review local approaches for predicting how cracks start and grow inside structural materials, in a 2026 article. Rather than treating a part as uniform, these methods zoom into the stressed zone near a notch or flaw and let the tiny local structure speak. Modern statistics join the finite element calculations that engineers already use.

Three material families anchor the examples: metals where cracks begin around inclusions or grain boundary particles, fiber composites with strong interfaces, and hybrids of the two. Two-scale simulations, where small-scale behavior feeds a whole-part model, get the most attention. The review weighs hierarchical schemes, where scales pass results one way, against concurrent ones.
pmc-13466806:
Yachen Liu, Xi Liu, Hongmeng Ma, and Wenxin Li report a lung cancer that changed its tissue type during targeted treatment, an extremely rare switch, in a 2026 case report. The patient, a forty-five-year-old woman, had two years of cough, sputum, and breathlessness. Her cancer began as lung adenocarcinoma carrying an ALK gene rearrangement, treated with drugs that block that signal.

Under treatment the tumor transformed into pulmonary mucoepidermoid carcinoma, a type that normally arises on its own and makes up under one percent of lung cancers. Change into small cell cancer after such drugs is known, but this destination is almost unheard of. No shared guideline covers the mechanism or best care, which the report aims to start filling.
pmc-13467006:
Erin Tresselt Murray and colleagues study how heart-lung bypass during children's heart surgery splits two neutrophil weapons in opposite directions, in a 2026 study. Thirty-nine children from one day to four years old gave blood before bypass and a day after it. Bypass sent neutrophil counts soaring more than fourfold.

One weapon, the enzyme elastase, poured out more strongly after bypass yet did not forecast organ damage. The other, web-like traps the cells cast to snare germs, fell sharply after bypass. Children whose cells answered weakly to a gentle trap trigger before surgery carried the risk signal instead. The split matters because blocking inflammation wholesale could block a useful arm along with a harmful one.
pmc-13469206:
Martinelli and co-authors reviewed in 2026 evidence tying hearing loss in old age to cognitive decline and dementia, under the title the sound of silence. Cognitive impairment affects about 6.5 percent of people over 65, with no treatment reversing it. Hearing loss rises steeply with age, up to 40 percent past 65 and 75 percent past 80. The review covers ear-level damage and the brain's central processing of sound, plus screening tests from questionnaires to sound-booth audiometry.

Several paths may link the two: straining to hear loads the brain's thinking budget, and deafness breeds social isolation, itself a dementia risk. Central processing faults grow more important in later stages of age-related loss. The practical message is hopeful: hearing aids may delay decline, not just ease disability, and they lighten caregiver burden by restoring communication. Paired with cognitive training, correction of hearing is presented as one of the few levers available for prevention.
pmc-13469906:
Alsanousi and Prabhu review ways to measure mental workload from body signals in this 2026 paper. Cognitive load, the mental effort a task demands, affects safety and learning in jobs like flying and surgery. Self-reports miss quick changes during a task. So the authors assessed signals that sensors can track without entering the body. These included heart activity, brain waves, eye movements, and skin conductance.

The review drew on 37 sources published between 2021 and early 2026, including 25 original studies. Heart measures appeared most often, in 16 of the 25 studies, followed by brain-wave recording in 11. Brain signals linked most directly to mental effort but were hard to use outside labs, while wearable-friendly signals reflected general arousal instead. The authors propose pairing complementary signals rather than relying on any single one.
pmc-13471506:
Tian and colleagues built a finer-grained way to record skin damage in anti-MDA5-positive dermatomyositis, an autoimmune disease where skin ulcers can signal lung danger. Their 2026 retrospective study coded ulceration, itch, and scale across seven body regions in 339 patients, distilled from 513 screened at one center.

Simple presence of any ulcer already carried information: it was linked to depleted CD8 T cells with an odds ratio of 3.35 in the screening analysis, and each additional ulcer site added its own association at 1.43 per site. Location mattered too, since facial ulceration tied to pulmonary arterial hypertension with an odds ratio of 2.28, stronger than total site count. The authors stress the framework is exploratory, not yet a validated prediction tool.
pmc-13472206:
Kanchiralla and colleagues wrote this 2026 correspondence criticizing a life cycle assessment of ship exhaust scrubbers by Stathatou and co-authors. The original study used a well-to-wake analysis. It compared burning heavy fuel oil with a scrubber, a device that washes exhaust, against low-sulfur fuels. It concluded the scrubber option could match one clean fuel and beat another. These authors argue the conclusion downplays risks to the marine environment.

They point out that the original figures showed shipboard impacts for marine ecotoxicity and nutrient enrichment several times higher with scrubbers, yet those categories were set aside as too uncertain. The letter also challenges a dilution assumption used to lower those impacts, asking why dilution should apply there but not to carbon emissions. They warn the framing could sway ongoing International Maritime Organization debate about scrubbers.
pmc-13473406:
Bonilla and colleagues present a 2026 commentary arguing that Guatemala should tap its scientific diaspora, its trained citizens living abroad, to fix weak public governance.
