These expatriate professionals stay linked to Guatemala but work in richer systems abroad. At home, the authors describe an administration thinned by corruption, vested interests, and dysfunctional hiring that cannot attract scarce expertise.

The commentary calls the diaspora an undervalued, publicly unrecognized asset: brain linkage rather than brain drain. Structured ways to lend diaspora expertise, short missions, remote advising, and joint projects, could strengthen institutions without requiring permanent return. The barrier is partly design: government jobs pay poorly and hire opaquely, so even willing experts cannot plug in. Building clean channels for diaspora help is the authors' central plea for Guatemala's development.
pmc-13473506:
Villavicencio-Valero and Mondavi-Sobby simulated the early history of Saturn's moon Enceladus, asking how ammonia frozen into its south polar ice shell changes the moon's internal heating. Ammonia, detected in the moon's plumes at no more than 0.5% of their composition, lowers ice's melting point, and the authors tested two solid forms, ammonia monohydrate and dihydrate, across shell thicknesses and ice stiffnesses in 2026 numerical models.

The two hydrates behaved differently. Dihydrate widened the range of conditions allowing convection, the slow churning that redistributes heat, while monohydrate zones reacted more strongly to changes in ice stiffness and shell thickness. Both promoted pockets where melting temperatures could be reached without a globally molten shell. The authors argue that small chemical patches of this kind could explain Enceladus's lopsided activity.
pmc-13474606:
Minghui Yu and co-authors test lung washing as an add-on care in 2026 for hard-to-control allergic asthma. The wash, done through a scope, clears mucus and debris from airways. Patients treated from 2021 to 2024 got either standard inhaler-based care or the wash on top. Symptom scores, lung tests, and side effects were compared between groups.

The wash group gained more on symptom scores and on small airway measures. Gains were largest in patients whose lung scores started worst. A breath marker of airway inflammation did not differ between groups, and side effects stayed similar. Fluid from the wash also revealed which germs were present, guiding later care.
pmc-13477306:
Francesco Cribari and colleagues report in 2026 on heart muscle biopsies in cancer patients with suspected heart inflammation from immune checkpoint inhibitor drugs. The patients came from a prospective fast-track cohort for people with possible heart problems during this cancer treatment. Biopsy was used when the diagnosis stayed uncertain or when results would change cancer care decisions.

Forty-eight of 175 patients had a biopsy, with tissue samples read without knowledge of their clinical details. The team compared biopsy findings with symptoms, blood tests, heart tracings, and magnetic resonance scans. Most patients were women, and breast cancer was the most common cancer in the group. The study maps how definite inflammation on biopsy lines up with scan and clinical features, which may help doctors judge when biopsy adds real value.
pmc-13477406:
Hidetaka Suzuki and coauthors present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of quick stroke scales that ambulance crews use to spot large vessel blockages. These blockages need clot-removal treatment at specialized centers, so early field detection shapes where a patient is taken. The team searched English and Japanese literature from 2016 to 2024.

Forty-three studies qualified, and eight tools had enough data for pooled accuracy estimates. The Rapid Arterial Occlusion Evaluation scale caught about three quarters of blockages while correctly clearing about three quarters of other patients. A second scale, Field Assessment Stroke Triage for Emergency Destination, performed slightly lower on both counts. The authors also weighed how the tools would perform at different blockage rates, helping services judge the trade-off between missed cases and false alarms.
pmc-13478406:
Jepma and colleagues published a 2026 study on nursing assistants and end-of-life care planning. Advance care planning records what care a person wants near life's end. Certified nursing assistants know clients' daily wishes well, yet planning often skips them. The team interviewed fifteen assistants in Dutch home care and nursing homes.

Most assistants were not routinely part of planning talks with clients. Many wanted more knowledge and skill to join those talks well. Team culture could either open the door or close it to them. Close bonds with clients and families helped assistants speak up in planning. Time pressure worked against their taking part, the assistants reported. Training offers one clear fix for the knowledge gap found.
pmc-13478606:
Mivalt and colleagues created a pig model of hippocampal epilepsy in 2026, sized so that human brain implants can be tested in a freely moving large animal. Seven pigs received MRI-guided electrodes in both hippocampi and a thalamic target, then six were infused with kainic acid, a seizure-triggering chemical, and one with saline as a control. A fully implantable stimulator-recorder, built for humans, logged brain signals continuously alongside video.

Every kainic acid pig, six of six, entered prolonged seizure activity right after infusion, confirming the induction worked in all treated animals. Four pigs survived to long-term monitoring, and three of them developed spontaneous seizures, totaling 2,733 recorded seizures averaging 27.2 seconds each in the chronic phase. Tissue checks showed patchy neuron loss in the hippocampus, and epilepsy's global burden of 50 to 60 million people frames why such a testbed matters for new devices.
pmc-13479406:
Serhat Şen and Feyza Gülgel Şen published a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of platelet-rich plasma used during cesarean delivery. Wound problems follow up to 15 percent of cesareans worldwide. The plasma concentrate, made from the patient's own blood, carries growth factors that aid repair in other surgeries, yet cesarean trials had never been pooled.

Five databases were searched through March 2026 for randomized trials comparing plasma treatment with standard care. Outcomes covered scar quality on three rating scales, early wound inflammation scores, and the integrity of the uterine scar, including niche formation and remaining muscle thickness. Pain scores served as a secondary outcome. The synthesis gives obstetric teams a first quantitative read on whether this add-on step earns its place in the operating room.
pmc-13479706:
Rayan Saleh Moussa and a large team of coauthors published a 2026 qualitative study of why Arabic-speaking cancer patients in Australia rarely join clinical trials. Arabic is the country's third most spoken language, and trial underrepresentation deepens outcome inequities. Rather than asking patients alone, the team interviewed healthcare professionals about the barriers and enablers they observe.

The study deliberately looks upstream, at social determinants such as language services, transport, work, and family structures, instead of blaming individual hesitancy. Professionals described how these forces shape every step from referral to consent. Their accounts identify service-level fixes, including interpreter integration and culturally matched staff. The authors frame trial diversity as a system design problem with named owners, not a community deficit.
pmc-13480106:
Fernando Fernández-Aranda and co-authors introduce a 2026 report on a new live-in unit in Catalonia for adults with long-standing eating disorders. The unit opened in January 2024 inside the public health system. Eighteen patients with anorexia or a related diagnosis stayed three to four months on average and completed clinical interviews plus surveys on health, mood, quality of life, and satisfaction.

Patients had been ill for more than twelve years on average and had tried at least three prior treatments without lasting gain. Almost all were out of work despite varied schooling, and other mental health conditions were common. After treatment, quality of life and body mass index both improved by clear margins. Satisfaction averaged above eighty-five out of one hundred, with warm written feedback to match. Early results hint that dedicated long-stay care can help a group that standard services often miss.
pmc-13481106:
Lisandro Torre and co-authors report a 2026 trial of webinar training for vaccine advisory panels weighing a six-in-one child vaccine. National panels must judge proof across many angles before advising health ministries, and demand for coaching has surged as panels multiply. A five-part online series ran from January to June 2025 for panels weighing a switch from five-in-one plus polio shots to a combined six-in-one.

Panels from thirty-two countries joined at least one session, and nine joined three or more, mostly from the African region with support from the Gavi alliance. Surveys and interviews rated the sessions as useful, with peer stories from other countries prized most. Panels asked for more hands-on guidance on cost and feasibility angles plus pairing schemes between countries. Flexible online cohorts may scale expert coaching faster than site visits.
pmc-13482306:
Rathod and co-authors study a smart rubber in 2026 whose stiffness answers to both magnets and heat, a silicone filled with irregular flakes of electrolytic iron at 40 percent by weight. Unlike the round particles in standard magnetic elastomers, the flakes touch and grip more, which should sharpen the response to a magnetic field. The team swept temperature, strain, shaking frequency, and field strength across wide ranges to map the behavior.

Warming from 30 to 70 degrees Celsius softened plain silicone, dropping its storage stiffness 12.5 percent while its energy-absorbing loss measure climbed 67 percent over the same range. The filled rubber lost stiffness faster, down 18.9 percent, because heat loosened the grip that made the flakes reinforcing at cooler temperatures in the tests. The team also built a time-temperature master curve for the material and notes damping shifts with field strength too, pointing to vibration pads that can be tuned by temperature.
pmc-13483406:
Chen and team tracked which viruses sicken Shanghai children, comparing those treated in clinics with those admitted to hospital. Their 2026 surveillance study enrolled 3,533 children under 15 in Pudong over two years, testing swabs for nine respiratory viruses. The aim was to see whether hospital and clinic cases are really the same illness stream or two different ones.

Viruses were found far more often in outpatients, at about 34 percent, than in inpatients, at about 20 percent of those tested. Flu and the COVID virus dominated clinic cases, while RSV, a virus dangerous to infants, leaned toward hospital cases. Infants filled hospital beds, while teenagers filled clinic visits. Even RSV subtypes split by setting, with different variants leading in each group. Chen argues prevention plans should be tailored separately for clinics and wards.
pmc-13483606:
Yahao Li and co-authors pool published results on deep learning for diagnosing slipped lumbar discs from medical images. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis searched major databases through March 2026 and kept ten retrospective studies with usable accuracy data. Magnetic resonance imaging is the usual standard, but human readings vary between observers.

Pooled results showed sensitivity and specificity both near 0.94, with a summary curve area close to perfect. Variation between studies was very large, so the authors treat the averages as exploratory rather than settled. Models checked on outside data lost some specificity compared with same-center checks. Differences in what models were asked to output also drove variation. At typical pretest odds, a positive result sharply raised the chance of disease.
pmc-13486806:
Khushi Goda and co-workers gauge how much blood pressure spread comes from genes and daily life acting as a pair. Most past work treats the two as split forces. This 2026 study uses 24,000 people of mixed roots in the UK Biobank. It sets them against 23 daily-life traits. Spread is split three ways for three pressure marks: genes, daily life, and the pair effect.

Pair effects held 7 percent of spread for the lower pressure mark. They held 4 percent for the upper mark and 3 percent for pulse pressure. The 7 percent share ran near twice the rate from a white British-only check run the same way. Still, the gap fell short of firm proof. A genome-wide hunt for pair effects found no hit past the strict bar. Mixed-root groups may show pair effects that flat groups hide.
pmc-13487306:
Hui and team tested whether a data pipeline can sort university sports departments into meaningful governance types instead of grading them on one linear scale. Sports governance juggles money, fairness, efficiency, and sustainability, which rarely peak together. Their 2026 study generated 348 synthetic schools by model run, seeded with four archetypes from resource-focused to balanced, then checked whether clustering methods could recover those types from the numbers alone.

Both clustering approaches recovered the four planted archetypes, confirming the pipeline works under controlled conditions. Nonlinear performance patterns emerged between the types that a single weighted score would flatten away. The authors stress the patterns describe their model run design, not real schools, since no actual institutional data fed the test. Hui offers the design for future use once real governance data can be gathered, positioning configuration over ranking.
pmc-13487606:
Keston Mwiwa Sinkhonde maps where Malawian households with young children fall short on protein and two key amino acids. Published in 2026, the analysis reuses the national 2019 to 2020 household survey covering 5,952 children aged six to fifty-nine months. Food records are converted through composition tables and adult-equivalent scaling, then judged against international thresholds and plotted by district.

Shortfalls in usable lysine topped 40 percent in every Central Region district, with seven of thirteen Southern districts also above that line. Usable protein inadequacy followed the same central-then-southern geography. Total amounts looked better than usable amounts, since plant-heavy diets limit amino acid availability. District-level targeting beats national averages for nutrition programs, and lysine emerges as the quiet bottleneck nutrient.
pmc-13487906:
Zsolt Molnar and fellow specialists offer a 2026 position statement on hemoadsorption for septic shock, a severe form of sepsis where blood pressure falls dangerously. The treatment passes blood through a cartridge that removes cytokines and other signals driving harmful inflammation. The authors review why the idea is appealing, given the mix of excessive and suppressed immune activity in sepsis.

Evidence so far comes mostly from small studies, registries, and mixed patient groups, so firm guidance is still lacking. The statement stresses careful patient choice, timing, and treatment intensity rather than routine use for everyone. Readers get a clear map of what is known, what remains uncertain, and where larger trials are needed.
pmc-13488206:
Gabriela Reka and colleagues review chromosome microarray results in children with autism at a hospital in Lublin, Poland, in a 2026 retrospective study. The test finds tiny missing or extra DNA segments that standard chromosome views miss. Records covered 234 children diagnosed between 2012 and 2024, and the team grouped results by type, likely importance for development, and the genes involved.

About fifty-nine percent of children had a normal result on this test. Single extra segments and single deletions were the most common abnormal patterns, and several DNA changes together appeared in about thirteen percent. Clearly disease-causing findings explained roughly nine percent of cases. Certain regions recurred, including one tied to brain signaling genes. Clustering split the uncertain findings into distinct subgroups for follow-up.
pmc-13489206:
Zhu and a team in China traced in 2026 a chain that turns eye lining cells rogue and lays scar mats under the retina. The scar state is a grave snag of wet age linked macular disease, where sight fades fast. A fat signal dock, LPA1, sat high in scarred mouse eyes made by laser burns. The team raised or cut each link of the chain in cells and mice to test its pull.

More LPA1 drove the lining cells to shed their sheet form and crawl, the first steps of scar work. The dock acts through two aides: it lifts USP1, a tag stripper, which then shields ZEB1, a form switch, from the cell's shred bin. Cut either aide, and the rogue turn stalled. A drug that blocks LPA1, BMS-986278, curbed scar growth in mice more than it curbed leaky vessel growth.
pmc-13490506:
Maoudj and colleagues presented SPINDER, an open-source six-legged robot with eighteen movable joints built for reproducible insect-like locomotion research. Legged robot studies are hard to replicate when every lab builds its own machine. Their 2026 platform prints its body from plastic and drives legs with hobby servos. It senses the world with a depth camera, an inertial unit, and foot contact switches, while a pattern-generator controller coordinates the legs like a nervous system.

Hardware trials demonstrated stable tripod, ripple, and wave gaits, plus walking in any direction on command. The robot switched gaits smoothly, settling within about two gait cycles of each transition. It crossed structured uneven ground with height changes up to eighteen millimeters, completing every run with body pitch staying under five degrees. All designs and code are published for other labs.
pmc-13491806:
Yahao Li and five colleagues test in 2026 whether ordinary smartphone videos from clinic visits can reveal walking patterns tied to specific gene defects. The condition is osteogenesis imperfecta, a brittle bone disorder of childhood. Pose estimation software extracted step and posture measures from outpatient footage of children with IFITM5 or WNT1 gene changes, with a COL1 group kept as a comparison.

Step width and trunk lean measurements stayed consistent when the videos were artificially degraded, a check on reliability. Children with WNT1 changes walked with a wider stance and leaned their trunks further than the other groups, and the gaps survived adjustment for age, sex, medicines, and surgery. Their surgery-free survival also ended earlier. A trial classifier separated the genotypes fairly well, and the authors propose video gait checks as a low-burden monitoring tool.
pmc-13493806:
Chen and colleagues aim to speed up aircraft design by teaching a neural network to predict airflow over folding-wing aircraft. These planes change wing shape in flight to suit different missions. The usual tool, computational fluid dynamics, simulates air in fine detail but takes heavy computing time. The 2026 team generated training data with fluid simulations using moving meshes, then trained an improved PointNet++ model, a network that reads three-dimensional point clouds, to map wing shape onto surface pressure.

Once trained, the network produced pressure maps in seconds rather than the long runs full simulations need. Its predicted lift coefficient, the number describing how much upward force the wing generates, stayed within a small margin of the simulation results across test cases. The authors present the approach as a rapid screening tool that lets engineers test many wing shapes and reserve expensive simulations for the most promising designs.
pmc-13495306:
Yi Zhang and colleagues chart, in a 2026 study, multifocal germ cell tumors inside the skull, a rare form that strikes in two or more brain spots at once. Proof on this variant was thin, so the team reviewed 48 patients treated at one center across two decades. They logged symptoms, scans, tissue type, treatment, and survival.

Patients were mostly boys and young men, with a median age of thirteen. Excess thirst and urine from hormone failure was the top symptom, then weakness on one side. Two thirds had the germinoma tissue type, and over half got combined chemotherapy and radiation. Ten-year survival ran high, though freedom from return was lower, and worse than for single tumors. Germinoma type and combined treatment went with better outcomes, while immune cells inside the tumor marked worse ones. The authors back tissue-led, combined treatment for this rare disease.
pmc-13495506:
Temitayo Moyosore Adebisi and colleagues test, in a 2026 study in southwest Nigeria, whether a single teaching session can lift body and sexual functioning in women treated for cervical cancer. Care for survivors' daily quality of life lags behind prevention campaigns. Twenty women at a federal hospital's cancer unit took a researcher-built psychoeducation module, with functioning scored before and four weeks after.

Most women were in their late forties to mid fifties, none had had the HPV vaccine, and all were on chemotherapy. Scores nudged in the right direction across body, mind, and sexual domains, though none of those shifts cleared the proof bar. Overall quality of life did improve clearly. Pain and partner support stood out as the strongest social predictors of quality of life. The authors judge the session helpful and worth refining, while the single-group design and small numbers cap what can be claimed.
pmc-13495906:
Atul Verma, Esakkinaveen Dhanaraman, and Yen-Pei Fu build, in a 2026 materials study, a catalyst that splits water into hydrogen when shaken by sound waves. The method, called piezocatalysis, turns shaking motion into separated charges that drive chemistry, offering hydrogen without light or wires. Their catalyst grows from a bismuth framework into a bismuth-rich oxide, then couples with a flaky material called MXene.

The best blend produced hydrogen about thirty-six times faster than the starting framework and several times faster than either partner alone. Tracer tests revealed an unusual route through hydroxyl radicals rather than the standard electron path. The catalyst kept working in tap water and showed promise in seawater. Tests under shaking showed the motion turned into current with little loss. The authors present the blend as a step toward harvesting stray motion as fuel.
pmc-13498906:
Muñoz-Tafalla and colleagues mined the genomes of over eighteen thousand extremophile microorganisms for enzymes that digest PET plastic, in a 2026 study. Extremophiles are organisms living in extreme heat, salt, or acidity. Known PET-digesting enzymes belong to one enzyme family, while a different family, the true lipases, had been overlooked. The team combined genome scans with structural modeling, enzyme-substrate simulation, and validation.

Muñoz-Tafalla found two lipases, named LipBv and LipSh1, that hydrolyze PET, and related enzymes in their clusters shared the ability, supporting entire lipase lineages specialized for PET. Structural analysis pointed to differences in loop shape and active-site openness behind their activity and product patterns. These lipases clustered apart from more than thirteen hundred PETases found in the same genomes and from all known PET-digesters. That widens the search space for enzymes suited to mild, sustainable plastic recycling.
pmc-13500506:
Ganpat Singh Chauhan and co-authors build in 2026 a detector for fake online product reviews that reads sentiment toward specific product aspects rather than whole texts. Shoppers and manufacturers lean heavily on reviews, which invites fabricated praise or attacks. Their model embeds aspect-based sentiment into a graph neural network that maps how words, aspects, and feelings connect inside a review, exposing pairings that feel unnatural in invented text. The network also encodes links among users, reviews, and products.

Evaluated on 21,034 Amazon reviews spanning 30 product categories, the system reached accuracy in the low ninety percent range in the reported averages. It beat the strongest rival baseline on precision and recall by clear margins. Splits were stratified by product and reviewer to prevent leakage between training and test data, and the authors pitch the tool for real-time moderation duties.
pmc-13500606:
Seda Camalan and co-authors test in 2026 whether synthetic eardrum images generated by an artificial intelligence image maker can train better diagnostic classifiers. Examining the eardrum with an otoscope is central to spotting infections and perforations, yet labelled image sets are small and grading is subjective. The team created artificial and composite images with a StyleGAN3 generator and trained a deep image network. Comparisons ran against classic augmentation tricks such as flipping and rotating, and against no augmentation at all.

Synthetic augmentation lifted mean test accuracy into the mid-ninety percent range with a matching F1 score in the reported runs, ahead of classic augmentation and well ahead of the unaugmented baseline. The authors caution that their setup represents an optimistic upper bound, since generated images may leak information about the test distribution. The gap suggests machine-made training images can relieve the chronic data scarcity in ear imaging.
pmc-13501806:
Abdalla R Sulaiman and Ghassan E Bassit report a 2026 dental case involving implant treatment for a patient with primary hyperoxaluria type 1. The rare inherited disorder floods the body with oxalate. Crystals deposit in bone and damage the kidneys. This patient had received a combined liver and kidney transplant plus long-term immune suppression. Failing remaining teeth with external root resorption ruled out conventional dentures, so the team planned implant rehabilitation after clinical and radiographic assessment.

Resonance frequency analysis at six months showed firm secondary stability, with implant stability quotient values of 75 on the right and 74 on the left. At fourteen months the tissues around the implants remained stable, with no complications on examination or imaging. The authors present the case as evidence that implants can work in selected patients with this disease, while stressing that one case and short follow-up cannot settle long-term safety.
pmc-13503406:
Pereira Neto and colleagues tested whether a mouth gel carrying an iron phthalocyanine compound improves standard gum disease treatment. The compound is a pigment-like molecule with antimicrobial promise. Forty-seven people with periodontitis received scaling and root planing, the deep cleaning that anchors non-surgical therapy. They then received one of three gels: the active gel, a chlorhexidine gel as the established comparator, or the plain gel vehicle. The 2026 randomised trial re-measured pocket depths, bleeding, and plaque after 45 days.

No group beat another on any clinical measure at the follow-up. Within groups, deep pockets shrank significantly in the vehicle and active gel arms, and bleeding and plaque fell in all three, changes the authors attribute to the professional cleaning itself. The chlorhexidine arm did not separate from plain vehicle either. The team concludes the gel adds nothing measurable at this strength and suggests reformulation studies.
pmc-13504206:
Farshid Sarrafzadeh-Rezaei, editor-in-chief of Veterinary Research Forum, marks the journal's latest milestone in this 2026 editorial. The journal's impact factor rose to 1.4 in the newest Journal Citation Reports, a gain of 27 percent in one year. That keeps it in the second quartile and first among veterinary journals in Iran.

He traces the run from the first issue in 2010, through a shift from quarterly to monthly issues in 2023. No issue was ever late, he notes, except three held up during the recent war. He thanks the executive manager, board, reviewers, and authors for that record. The stated next goal is a first-quartile rank, with an open call for strong work from around the world.
pmc-13505106:
Keliang Liu leads a team studying how age and social standing jointly shape lung disease overlap in dust-scarred lungs, in a 2026 nationwide study in China. Pneumoconiosis, the fibrosis left by work dust, often arrives with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Age raises the odds, but how that rise differs across groups was untested.

The study drew nearly ten thousand patients from 27 provinces; about a quarter had the overlap. Each added year raised the odds slightly, and the rise steepened at older ages rather than running straight. City residents and those with work-injury insurance saw odds climb fast then level off in late life. Rural patients and the uninsured saw a steady climb with no plateau. Repeated checks confirmed the pattern, which the authors say should guide uneven, targeted screening.
pmc-13506106:
S S Etibarli and co-authors reviewed ninety-three patients treated in Azerbaijan for crushed vertebrae caused by osteoporosis, between 2015 and 2024. Most were women, and diagnoses rested on scans, bone density tests, and clinical examination. Seventy-six patients received percutaneous vertebroplasty, a procedure that injects cement through the skin to stabilise the broken bone.

Cement was placed at one level in most treated patients, though some needed two or more levels. Complete pain relief followed surgery in ninety-three percent of cases, with strong reduction in the rest. Five patients had minor complications, and none needed further surgery. The authors conclude the procedure is a safe and effective option that eases pain quickly, restores movement early, and cuts reliance on painkillers for this fracture type.
pmc-13507006:
Aase Marie Aurbakken Rusten leads a 2026 study of poor sleep after a heart artery procedure in Norway and partner centers. The cohort held 3417 patients treated with percutaneous coronary intervention, a balloon and stent method to open blocked arteries. Patients reported sleep and health at discharge and at two, six, and twelve months.

At discharge, insomnia signs affected 47 percent of women and 28 percent of men, and levels held steady over the year. Worse mental health linked to worse sleep in both sexes, while worse physical health linked in women. Early poor sleep also predicted later poor sleep. The authors urge early screening and targeted sleep help after the procedure.
pmc-13507106:
Nandita Menon, Tatiana D Mayorova, Adriano Senatore, and Anil Kishen model, in 2026 lab work, two-way nerve and immune talk relevant to apical periodontitis, a painful infection at a tooth root tip. Neuron-like cells were grown from gum ligament cells and placed with macrophages and ligament cells under bacterial toxin stress. Signals passed both through shared fluid and direct cell contact.

Nerve signals boosted inflammatory output when cells shared fluid only, raising macrophage markers and messengers such as IL-1β. With direct contact, the same signals calmed output instead. Fluid from inflamed mixes also retuned nerve sensors, favoring one pain messenger over another. Contact context decides whether nerve input fuels or brakes inflammation.
pmc-13507206:
Hongji Xu, Xuefeng Yang, Hang Luo, Liwei Zhang, and Chenglong Liu build, in 2026 work, an accuracy control system for installing supports of ultra-high-speed maglev tubes in China. The test platform targets speeds up to 1500 kilometers per hour inside tubes that can drop to near vacuum. Support placement sets track smoothness and tube sealing, with tolerances at millimeter scale or finer.

Their reverse method starts from support design accuracy and works backward through error spread math to set needed precision for control points and survey stations. A three-dimensional station model counts prior point errors, which softens their impact. Dense simulations mapped how station accuracy varies by position. Case checks support field use across tube and instrument setups.
pmc-13507306:
M Morfouace leads a 2026 report on Arcagen, a European study of molecular profiling and treatment access for rare adult solid cancers. Rare cancers are individually uncommon yet together strike hundreds of thousands yearly, and expert testing is unevenly available. The study enrolled 1235 patients with advanced disease across eleven cancer domains and thirteen countries, with 893 evaluable for profiling.

About seven in ten evaluable patients carried mutations that could guide therapy. Only 93 of those with actionable findings actually received matched targeted or immune treatment. Survival differed sharply by path: median survival was 1.1 years without adaptation and 3.3 years after switching to targeted therapy, while the immunotherapy group had not reached its median. Access gaps, not biology, limit benefit.
pmc-13507806:
Marcello Polenghi and six co-authors publish a dataset of images and power records for solar cells that were damaged on purpose, in 2026 work. Each cell started brand new and then faced soiling, impacts, cuts, bending, smashing, heat, or even flame. For every condition the team took three kinds of images. One used visible light, one used near-infrared light, and one used electroluminescence, which makes a powered cell glow so flaws show up.

Voltage and current were logged during the glow tests and again under a standard test light. Text notes describe each type of damage and how much power it cost. The set covers few cells from one solar design, so it suits matched comparison more than broad statistics. It gives image researchers paired views of the same damage, plus plain-language labels to train and test their tools.
pmc-13508006:
Chetan Patel, Ghanashyam Patel, and Nile Desai run a blinded trial of a natural oil-pulling rinse for mouth health, in work published in 2026. Oil pulling is a traditional practice now sold as a gentler choice than alcohol-based rinses, which can dry the mouth and alter taste. The trial enrolled 63 adults aged 18 to 50 with clear plaque and gum inflammation. People were assigned at random to the oil rinse, a store-bought alcohol rinse, or a placebo. Everyone used their rinse for 15 days.

The oil rinse cut one broad class of mouth bacteria far more than both rival groups, a gap that reached statistical meaning. Plaque scores fell by nearly one third, and gum scores improved slightly. Breath freshness and dryness measures also moved in its favor. The authors present the rinse as a workable natural option, with results close to the standard product overall.
pmc-13508206:
Courtney Van Houtven leads an eighteen-author trial testing two levels of support for rolling out a caregiver training program across Veterans Affairs sites, in 2026 work. The program, Caregivers FIRST, teaches family caregivers of veterans practical skills. A national mandate ordered it everywhere, yet few caregiver programs have scaled that far. The trial enrolled 25 sites that had not yet adopted the training six months after the mandate. Sites were assigned to basic support or to basic support plus group coaching from outside facilitators.

The main measures tracked how many referred caregivers attended at least one class, and how many classes each site delivered by twelve months. Faithfulness to the program and basic adoption were also scored. Surveys, interviews, and cost data added context. The study design shows how health systems can test rollout help itself, not just the program being rolled out.
pmc-13508806:
Boucherouite and colleagues built a 2026 automated system to spot early Parkinson's disease from brain scans called DaTSCAN images, which show dopamine activity. Visual reading of these scans can miss early disease. The team used 514 scans from a large Parkinson's research database, one per person.

Their pipeline processed each image, computed 23 features describing shape and tracer uptake, and classified scans with machine learning. A support vector machine reached about 97 percent accuracy, catching nearly all true cases while keeping false alarms low. It beat a deep learning baseline, which scored about 95 percent, and it trained much faster. The authors argue that careful feature design plus classical methods can suit clinics better when training data are limited.
pmc-13509006:
Leite and colleagues combined three computational approaches to sort drug candidates that switch the Abl kinase enzyme on or off through a side pocket. That distinction matters for leukemia and breast cancer drug design. Compounds binding the pocket called the myristoyl pocket either bend a regulatory helix to inhibit the enzyme or leave it straighter to activate it. Computer classification of the two classes has been unreliable.

Leite benchmarked molecular docking, structure co-folding prediction, and full molecular dynamics simulations against known compounds. Co-folding predicted the helix bending correctly and separated true modulators from decoys far better than docking, with discrimination scores approaching perfect for inhibitors. Docking still revealed stabilizing fluorine contacts deep in the pocket, while dynamics showed the helix sampling many shapes and linked its bending to long-range restraint of the activation loop. The combined protocol gives a validated route to function-specific Abl drug design.
pmc-13514906:
Veronica Vecchio, Rossella Cacciola, and Emma Cacciola report, in a 2026 study, early results for ropeginterferon alfa-2b in polycythemia vera. The disease is a blood cancer driven by a JAK2 mutation that thickens the blood and raises clot risk. The team instead reviewed thirteen high-risk patients who could not tolerate hydroxyurea, visiting them every two weeks while doses rose slowly from a low start.

Every patient reached a complete blood-count response within twenty-four weeks, at a mean of just over four months. The share of mutated JAK2 gene copies fell steadily to a much lower level at the durable-response point. Eleven patients achieved a partial molecular response and two a complete one, all patients saw their itching resolve, and no clots or adverse events occurred. Vecchio's team presents the close-monitoring schedule as a way to gain control well inside the usual year.
pmc-13515106:
Michele D'Alonzo and seven co-authors weigh surgical timing in acute aortic valve endocarditis, in a 2026 multicentre retrospective study. The study covered 203 patients whose surgery fell either within seven days of starting targeted antibiotics or between seven and thirty days, excluding emergency operations and infections of other valves.

Deaths in hospital were nearly identical, around fifteen to sixteen percent in both timing groups, and four-year survival did not differ significantly either. Relapse and reoperation rates matched closely as well. One outcome did separate the groups: permanent pacemaker implantation, needed when infection scars the heart's wiring, occurred in about eighteen percent of the delayed group against nine percent of the early group. D'Alonzo's team concludes that waiting buys no safety and may cost conduction tissue, supporting earlier operation once targeted antibiotics begin.
pmc-13516006:
Gene Yong-Kwang Ong leads a large author group, including the paediatric subcommittee of the Singapore Resuscitation and First Aid Council, in presenting the Singapore Paediatric Life Support Guidelines 2026. The document updates the 2021 edition for patients under eighteen, newborns excluded. Its makers reviewed the newest international task-force recommendations, American and European guidelines, and studies from 2021 to early 2026, then weighed them against local resources and practice.

Age bands are defined with care, from neonates in their first month through infants, children, and adolescents. Older adolescents may follow adult basic life support in community settings, and the council strongly urges willing responders to give breaths as part of CPR for children. Neonates still cared for in newborn units follow the newborn pathway instead. The guideline presents itself as evidence-based and patient-centred, tuned to Singapore's system.
pmc-13518506:
Giovanna Tassinari leads a ten-author study loading glioma cells with copper in a 2026 paper. Copper compounds tempt brain-tumour researchers because excess copper can poison cancer cells. Three glioma lines, two human and one rat, soaked in copper sulfate for a day across a wide dose range. The team read survival, the respiratory chain's working parts, membrane voltage, and the cell's damage and rebuilding signals.

Survival fell nearly everywhere. The mid-chain respiratory enzyme lost power in all three lines, and another fell in the rat line. Membrane voltage dropped across the board while PINK1, the damage tag that summons recycling, rose in every line. Two lines answered by switching on growth programmes for fresh mitochondria, each choosing a different master gene. Tassinari's team concludes copper kills glioma cells largely through their powerhouses, with the repair response varying by tumour line.
pmc-13518806:
Mohammadreza Mokhtari, Farkhondeh Amin Shokravi, Hasan Shahbazi, and Azam Saffar build and test a 2026 questionnaire on eco-driving beliefs among Tehran line taxi drivers. Vehicle exhaust drives much of the city's air pollution, yet no theory-based tool measured why drivers adopt fuel-saving habits. Their instrument rests on the Health Belief Model.

Starting from 96 draft items, validation steps with 401 drivers sampled across strata produced a final 57-item tool covering eight domains, from knowledge to self-confidence. Factor analysis supported the eight-part structure, and most scales proved reliable. Self-efficacy, knowledge, perceived benefits, and perceived risk predicted eco-driving behavior. Planners can use the tool to design cleaner-driving campaigns.
pmc-13518906:
Ravibala A. Patil and four colleagues simulate in 2026 how fluid flows past six square cylinders arranged in a line, all wobbling sideways together. Such arrays appear in heat exchangers, bridge piers, and offshore risers, where vibration and wake patterns decide safety and performance. The team used the lattice Boltzmann method at a modest flow speed.

Varying the wobble rate against the natural vortex shedding rate produced three regimes: clean lock-on, quasi-periodic lock-on, and non-lock-on behavior. The lock-on range was wider than for a single cylinder. One coherent wake wrapped the whole array, and higher wobble rates merged vortices downstream. The front cylinder felt the highest average drag, with values dipping then rising along the row.
pmc-13519006:
Xinchan Liu and four colleagues test in 2026 whether gum disease worsens fatty liver disease in mice fed a rich diet. Periodontitis is linked to metabolic liver disease in people, yet the connecting mechanism was unclear. Forty mice split into four groups crossing low- or high-fat feeding with induced gum disease.

After 12 weeks of diet and 4 weeks of ligature-induced periodontitis, mice with both burdens showed higher fasting glucose and much worse insulin resistance scores. Their liver disease activity scores also ran higher than high-fat controls. Fibrosis around liver cells also grew, and gut microbe balance shifted further, with Helicobacter enriched. Liu and co-authors read the pattern as gum inflammation aggravating liver disease through metabolic and microbial routes.
pmc-13520306:
Büşra Korkmaz and Ayse Aydın survey in 2026 how health literacy relates to confidence about breastfeeding among pregnant women in Türkiye. Health literacy means finding and using health information well, while self-efficacy means believing one can breastfeed successfully.

Interviews covered 292 women in late pregnancy at one hospital clinic between July and September 2020. About one third had limited health literacy, yet confidence scores were fairly high on average. Higher literacy scores went together with higher confidence scores across all subscales. The authors propose adding literacy-focused teaching to routine antenatal visits, so parents can judge feeding advice with more confidence.
pmc-13520406:
Arkaitz Cano and colleagues engineer in 2026 a new way to pair two unlike antibody halves. The method helps make bispecific antibodies. Such drugs can bind two targets at once. Wrong pairing pollutes the batch and slows clean-up.

The design moves a short strand from one heavy chain to the other. Added point changes then favour the right pairing. Purity neared 99 percent after a single clean-up step. That step matches standard antibody plants. Key immune jobs and blood life matched natural antibodies. Heat stability dipped a bit, yet the drugs stayed strong under stress tests. Trials on several pairs suggest wide plant use.
pmc-13522506:
Wen Luo and co-authors search for a genetic marker that predicts response to a depression drug in a 2026 study. The drug, liafensine, blocks reuptake of three brain chemicals and had failed to help unselected patients with treatment-resistant depression in earlier trials. DNA from blood specimens of trial participants was scanned genome-wide for variants tied to improvement.

One variant in the ANK3 gene was strongly linked to response in the discovery group and confirmed in a smaller replication group. The same variant did not predict response to two other antidepressants, suggesting a drug-specific effect. A later prospective study supported the finding. The authors present the marker as an example of precision medicine, where testing guides who should receive a particular drug.
pmc-13522606:
Tsovinar Harutyunyan and colleagues map patterns of COVID-19 protective behavior in Armenia in a 2026 survey study. Telephone interviews with nearly three thousand five hundred adults in 2021 covered mask wearing, hand washing, distancing, avoiding gatherings, and vaccination. Rather than scoring each behavior alone, the analysis grouped people by their overall pattern of compliance.

Hand washing was nearly universal, while keeping distance was least common, and only about twelve percent were vaccinated at the time. Two clusters emerged: a low-protection group covering about two fifths of respondents and a high-protection majority. Older age and being female raised the odds of high protection, while higher family spending lowered them. The authors urge targeted programs that lift several behaviors together in specific groups.
pmc-13523206:
Sridevi Saralaya and co-authors apply process mining and statistics to coffee harvesting in India in a 2026 study. Operations were examined in two Karnataka districts covering Arabica and Robusta coffee, including fifteen Robusta batches and three Arabica picking stages from early fly picking to final stripping. Workflow records were mined for patterns while statistical tests weighed productivity factors.

During fly picking, adding more workers was linked to less coffee picked per effort, showing that larger crews do not guarantee higher output. Labor efficiency, weather, and gender emerged as key influences on harvesting performance. Process mining revealed workflow variations that cause-and-effect analysis alone would miss. The authors present the combined approach as a data-driven model for managing harvest labor with human and environmental factors in view.
pmc-13523306:
Bandar Saad Alshreef pilots a hybrid feature selection method for mammogram analysis in a 2026 feasibility study. Breast imaging generates thousands of radiomic and deep learning features, and choosing a stable subset is difficult. Features were extracted for each lesion region from a public mammography dataset, combining standardized texture measures with deep features from a pretrained network. A hybrid algorithm pairing two nature-inspired search methods selected the subset.

On a very small pilot subset, the hybrid selected about half the features yet performed worse than using all features. On a synthetic dataset built to stress-test the scoring function, the proposed scoring clearly beat a legacy version. The collapse-prevention safeguard was never triggered. The author stresses that the results are exploratory and that the tiny real-data sample prevents any firm performance judgment.
pmc-13523406:
Wenqi Li, Chunting Zhao, and Mingya Liu describe rapid coronary disease progression in a genetic disorder in a 2026 case report. A forty-three-year-old man with classic Fabry disease developed exertional chest pain despite enzyme replacement therapy and well-controlled standard risk factors. Artery imaging showed severe disease in all three major coronary vessels, and ultrasound inside the arteries revealed several vulnerable plaques at risk of rupture.

Blood tests found autoantibodies and a raised inflammation marker, pointing to an active immune attack in the body. Treatment combined a catheter procedure, intensive cholesterol lowering, and the anti-inflammatory drug colchicine. The authors propose that Fabry disease itself strongly drives artery disease, with secondary inflammation speeding plaque growth beyond what standard risk scores capture. They urge close watching and inside-the-artery imaging in such patients.
pmc-13524606:
Nicholas T. Arredondo and colleagues report 2026 biochemical work on GDAP1, a mitochondrial protein from the GST family that is mutated in some forms of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, an inherited nerve disorder. GDAP1 was thought to bind a fatty acid called thapsic acid through an unusual side pocket, leaving the roles of its main active site and a nearby loop unclear.

The team mutated each region of the protein in turn and measured binding and protection of cells. Binding actually sat in the canonical active site, not the side pocket, and mutations there erased the protein's protective effect. Modeling suggested the loop and part of the site move together to reshape the pocket for the fatty acid. The authors map the residues involved and link binding to membrane integrity and redox balance.
pmc-13524806:
Carolin M. Lieber, Josef D. Wolf, Claire E. Ruckel, Lauren A. Harrison, and Richard K. Plemper test, in a 2026 ferret study, whether an antiviral drug can block transmission of a measles-like virus. With measles resurging amid vaccination hesitancy, drugs that stop spread could protect children. The candidate, GHP-88310, blocks the polymerase of a broad virus family and works by mouth.

Canine distemper virus, a measles relative that sickens ferrets, was spread by direct contact and by air in separate models. Preventive dosing eased illness in direct contacts and every sentinel survived. Twice-daily preventive dosing in air contacts prevented transmission outright, while once-daily dosing still gave complete survival. Treating air contacts after exposure saved them, while untreated air contacts died, and treating source animals shortened contagiousness by five days.
pmc-13525706:
Regragui and colleagues published a 2026 study on childhood blood cancers in a Moroccan hospital. Acute leukemias are the commonest childhood cancers, yet local data stay thin. The team reviewed 106 children diagnosed over two years in Rabat. They checked how a cell-sorting test, flow cytometry, sharpened each diagnosis.

Lymphoid leukemia made up about 81 percent of the cases overall. Myeloid leukemia accounted for 16 percent, with a rare mixed type behind. Boys outnumbered girls nearly two to one across the full group. Flow cytometry pinned down cell lineage where basic tests left doubt. The method proved vital where gene testing is not available locally. Odd antigen patterns were common, so panels must stay broad.
pmc-13527906:
Natalie Kleistnerova, Michal Tomcik, and Maja Spiritovic describe in a 2026 letter how a sensor glove measured hand therapy results in a child with juvenile systemic sclerosis. The rare disease stiffens skin and limits finger movement. Their patient was twelve years old. The child followed a six-month physiotherapy program with sessions twice a week.

The program mixed heat treatment, soft-tissue work, joint mobilization, and active exercises with therapy putty. The HandTutor glove recorded finger and wrist motion directly. It showed wider movement in most fingers, with the largest passive gains in the right thumb and left middle finger. Grip strength also rose, and skin scores improved. The child reported less stiffness and no more wrist pain under load. The authors argue such devices give clinics hard numbers alongside standard tests.
pmc-13528006:
Wen Zhu and three colleagues report a 2026 cohort study of drug-resistant gut bacteria at a secondary hospital in Shanghai, China. The bacteria, called CPE, make enzymes that defeat carbapenem antibiotics, a last-line drug family. The team studied isolates collected from January 2023 to September 2024. A rapid strip test identified which enzyme each strain carried.

All 131 strains tested positive for a carbapenemase enzyme. About seventy-five percent made the KPC type. Nineteen percent made metallo enzymes, and six percent made two enzymes at once. Double producers showed the most complex resistance patterns. Patients with more chronic illness fared worse. So did those needing ventilators or whose infection began in hospital. The authors urge enzyme-guided drug choice and tighter infection control in such hospitals.
pmc-13529906:
Chengcheng Ma and colleagues present 2026 real-world results for adding venetoclax to standard induction chemotherapy in younger adults with newly found acute myeloid leukemia. Venetoclax blocks a protein that helps leukemia cells survive. Its place beside strong chemotherapy for fit patients aged 18 to 60 has remained unsettled.

Clinicians at one center treated 28 patients between February 2023 and May 2024, split evenly between the standard drug pair and the venetoclax version. Response was checked by bone marrow testing after the first cycle, once blood counts recovered. Readers gain a careful comparison to weigh deeper responses against added toxicity.
pmc-13530706:
Sheean and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 11, a randomized trial of blood flow restriction therapy during the first twelve weeks of rehabilitation after knee ligament reconstruction. The therapy trains muscles with a cuff that partly limits blood flow, aiming to build muscle at low loads. Weak thigh muscles dog recovery, and the technique promised a shortcut.

Patients receiving a quadriceps tendon graft were randomized after surgery to identical work-matched exercise programs with or without the cuff for twelve weeks. Strength plus MRI-measured thigh muscle volume were then compared. Forty-five patients were randomized and thirty-eight completed the program. There were no differences between the groups in isometric or isokinetic thigh strength, and none in quadriceps or hamstring muscle volume at twelve weeks. The authors call it the largest such trial with a standardized surgical approach.
pmc-13531806:
Yingying Shen, Peiqing Zheng, and Jiaxu Zheng test in 2026 whether two gene variants raise lung cancer risk in a Chinese population. A case-control study genotyped 500 patients with non-small cell lung cancer and 500 matched controls on a mass-spectrometry platform. Smoking, sex, and age were handled in adjusted models.

One variant in TP63, a damage-response gene, and one in CIR1, tied to a growth pathway, each raised the odds of lung adenocarcinoma by roughly 40 percent after strict correction. The TP63 signal looked stronger in people who had smoked, though the interaction itself stayed unproven. Larger groups must confirm the findings.
pmc-13531906:
Hong-cheng Xing leads a 2026 mouse study uncovering a brake that protects jawbone from inflammatory breakdown in gum disease. A receptor called ROR2 in jaw stem cells normally traps a signaling partner and mutes production of an inflammatory messenger. Without that brake, mice lost more bone as bone-eating cells multiplied.

Removing the trapped partner gene rescued the bone balance in deficient mice. The team then built a temperature-sensitive gel carrying antibodies that neutralize the messenger. The gel eased gum disease bone loss in living animals, preserving bone-building capacity while trimming bone-eating coverage.
pmc-13532006:
Guanghui Shen and co-authors study in 2026 how mismatched distress between parents and teenagers relates to self-injury without suicidal intent. A total of 147 parent-teen pairs joined, with teens treated for depression or bipolar disorder. Both sides completed a standard distress scale, while teens reported self-injury frequency for surface-style analysis.

Teen distress alone tracked more self-injury across depression, anxiety, and stress measures. Mismatch itself predicted higher self-injury for all three dimensions, whichever side felt worse. For anxiety the harm curved upward at extremes in either direction. Family work on shared emotional understanding is the authors prescription.
pmc-13536706:
Can Wang and co-authors investigate a gene regulator called ATAD2 in womb lining cancer in a 2026 laboratory study. High levels of the regulator track with worse survival and faster cancer growth, so the team raised and lowered its levels in cancer cells and tested its partners. Animal tests also checked whether blocking the regulator slows tumors. The work links cell aging, immune escape, and tumor growth in one pathway.

ATAD2 was found to stabilize a second protein, SIRT7, which quiets a tumor guard pathway involving p53 and p21. With aging signals suppressed, cancer cells avoided an aged state and released fewer warning signals, while the tumor surroundings became less hostile to growth. Blocking ATAD2 restored those signals and slowed tumor growth and spread in animals. The authors propose ATAD2 as a drug target worth further testing.
pmc-13537106:
Ostermeier and colleagues reported that people with HIV on antiretroviral therapy carry many platelet-natural killer cell complexes in their blood, in a 2026 study. These are pairings of clotting fragments with antiviral immune cells. Natural killer cells are central to controlling HIV, yet they malfunction during infection. Platelets are activated under treatment, sticking to immune cells through a protein called P-selectin.

Ostermeier found the complexes more frequent in treated HIV patients than in uninfected controls. The killer cells inside complexes looked different: more activation markers and interferon production, but less of an activating receptor. Growing killer cells alongside platelets in the laboratory pushed them toward the activated profile. In macaques, complex levels tracked viral loads in blood and spinal fluid, and the link weakened after treatment with an antibody that blocks the platelet-gluing interaction. The authors propose platelet activation gluing to killer cells contributes to their dysfunction.
pmc-13537906:
Serin Lee, Eunju Jang, and Jun Chang compare two flu vaccine targets for lung-resident killer T cells in a 2026 mouse study. Universal flu vaccines aim for lasting T cells in the lungs that attack shared viral parts. Nose-delivered virus carriers carrying either nucleoprotein or polymerase basic protein 1 produced similar cell counts in airways. Survival after a lethal flu dose and cell quality measures then separated the two vaccines sharply.

Only the nucleoprotein vaccine gave full survival. Its cells favored a surface pattern linked to stronger killing, showed far higher sensitivity to tiny viral signals, and killed more strongly inside lungs. Polymerase cells favored a different surface pattern with weaker performance. The authors argue that target choice should prize cell quality over cell count alone.
pmc-13538706:
Wenlai Cui and colleagues compare warm-up priming plans for tennis serve play in a 2026 test. Players primed upper limbs, lower limbs, or the full body with either ballistic or heavy work, then served at set gaps up to fifteen minutes later. Serve speed and accuracy were tracked across every setup and time point.

Serve speed rose after priming in all setups. Ballistic work beat heavy work overall, with its edge focused in the first nine minutes and strongest for upper limb and full body routines. Accuracy shifted over time but never differed clearly between setups at matching times. The authors advise ballistic upper or full body priming shortly before serving.
pmc-13539806:
Yuxiang He and four colleagues describe, in a 2026 case report, a stroke that followed stent placement in a neck artery. The patient, a 51-year-old man, had severe narrowing with a tear in the left vertebral artery and received a stent to hold it open.

After the procedure he became confused and lost memory, signs pointing to damage in the thalamus on both sides. Scans confirmed that pattern, caused by blockage of a variant vessel called the artery of Percheron, which feeds that region in some people. He recovered well with supportive care and rehabilitation. The authors warn intervention teams to watch for this rare clot complication.
pmc-13539906:
Ender Eren Ozcelik and seven colleagues map, in a 2026 bibliometric study, how research on immune treatment for solid tumors grew over twenty-five years. Their source was a title-based search of the Web of Science collection, checked against a high-impact subset from Scopus.

More than fifty thousand documents appeared between 2000 and 2025, with output climbing steeply after the first checkpoint drug approval in 2011. China now publishes more than the United States, though American papers gather more citations and wider collaboration. Topic maps shift from an early cytokine period to checkpoint drugs, then toward the tumor surroundings and treatment given before surgery.
pmc-13540206:
Fatemeh Navab and six colleagues examine, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, how swapping one protein food for another relates to the acid load of the diet in people on haemodialysis. Failing kidneys handle acid poorly, and protein choice is one lever patients can adjust.

Across several centres, 307 patients completed a long food frequency questionnaire, and blood albumin gauged nutritional state. Statistical swaps that kept calories equal produced counterintuitive results: replacing red or processed meat with dairy, legume, or nut protein tracked with higher odds of a heavy acid load. Directions reversed for several meat-for-plant swaps. Albumin levels strongly modified these patterns, the authors report.
pmc-13540406:
Kılınç Oktay and colleagues published a 2026 letter on a new gene fault behind low platelets from birth. A gene called MPIG6B helps build platelets, the blood bits that stop bleeding. Faults in it cause low platelets plus slow spleen and marrow changes. Their patient, a nine-year-old boy in Türkiye, carried a variant never reported before.

His platelet counts stayed low from his third day of life onward. At age four, anemia and a swollen spleen joined the picture. His sister and cousin also carried low platelet counts in the family. The same fault played out unevenly across the children in the family. The case widens the known range of this rare disorder. His parents were first cousins, a pattern tied to recessive inheritance.
pmc-13541806:
Catarina Coelho, René Bobe, and Susana Carvalho review wild neighbours in 2026. Their subject is primates and hoofed animals living side by side. Ecologists long noticed this pairing. Few studies treated it head-on. Sharing space and food raises basic questions. How do species persist together over time?

The authors gathered the published evidence on these pairs. They mapped where associations occur. They also mapped which species pair up. Gains and losses for each side were weighed. African studies dominate the record. Baboons beside small to medium antelope lead the list. Help with foraging is a common gain. Early warning against predators is another.
pmc-13542106:
Elham Bagheri and Yalda Mohsenzadeh model image memory in a 2026 study. They asked what makes some images stick after one viewing. Their tool is an autoencoder. That network squeezes an image into a compact code. It then rebuilds the image from the code. Memorability is a measurable property of images.

Images the network rebuilt badly tended to be memorable. The distinctiveness of each code also tracked memorability. A small prediction network read the codes. It forecast memorability scores robustly. Heat maps highlighted the visual features behind the forecasts. The authors argue this learned space mirrors human memory. Hard-to-rebuild images linger, much as odd scenes linger for people.
pmc-13543506:
Yusaku Yokotani and colleagues published a 2026 case report of a small gallbladder polyp that slowly grew into a precancerous tumour called intracholecystic papillary neoplasm. Such growths are rare, and small polyps are usually watched rather than removed. A 56-year-old woman's polyp measured 7.6 millimetres at discovery and reached 11.2 millimetres over two years and eight months. Enhanced scans showed a papillary lesion that took up contrast dye, and the gallbladder was removed by keyhole surgery.

Under the microscope the lesion proved to be the pyloric gland type of the neoplasm, with low-grade dysplasia and no invasive cancer. Staining for mucin proteins supported a gastric-type identity. No recurrence appeared during follow-up. Steady growth, a frond-like shape, and enhancement, the authors argue, can mark a neoplasm even below the usual ten-millimetre action threshold, so watchful waiting should not become neglect.
pmc-13543606:
Ha Thu Dinh's team validated a short questionnaire in 2026 for borderline personality features in Vietnamese adolescents, traits of emotional, relationship, and identity instability that connect to maltreatment and depression. No locally checked tool existed in Vietnam. The eleven-item scale was given, in Vietnamese, to 2,326 grade seven and nine students from eight randomly chosen northern schools. It sat alongside measures of maltreatment and depressive symptoms, and its structure was tested on split halves of the sample.

The scale proved consistent and single-factor, and it scored boys and girls on the same footing. Girls scored clearly higher than boys. Scores tracked closely with both maltreatment and depression, exactly as theory predicts. Schools and clinics in Vietnam now have a brief, locally checked screen for a high-risk trait pattern, the authors conclude, suitable for spotting teenagers who need fuller review.
pmc-13546706:
Mohammed Babatunde Sadiq and colleagues ran a 2026 pilot study on whether routine hoof trimming stresses dairy cows that are not lame. Twenty healthy cows with normal gait and no hoof lesions were split into a group trimmed by the standard five-step Dutch method. A control group was only restrained as if trimmed. Blood cortisol, walking scores, time spent lying, feeding, and standing, plus milk yield, were tracked over two days.

Cortisol rose in both groups right after handling, showing restraint alone is stressful, yet trimmed cows kept higher cortisol and lay down more on the following two days. Walking scores and milk yield did not differ. The authors conclude that preventive trimming itself can cause short-term stress, and that letting cows rest matters for recovery.
pmc-13547206:
Xue Zhang and colleagues reported in 2026 a rare eye infection caused by Nocardia brasiliensis, a soil bacterium, that was first mistaken for ordinary eye inflammation. A 67-year-old man had two months of recurring pain and redness in his right eye before his vision collapsed quickly and pus appeared inside the eye. He had no known immune weakness, though testing found previously unrecognized diabetes.

Fluid from the eye plus gene sequencing identified the bacterium. Antibiotics given into the eye and by vein, followed by surgery to remove the eye's gel and fill the space with silicone oil, still could not stop the damage. The cornea clouded and his final vision in that eye was only light perception. The authors urge early microbe testing in stubborn eye inflammation.
pmc-13548706:
Stanslas Avaga and colleagues measure how often chemotherapy damages the nerves of cancer patients at a Ugandan regional center, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Nerve injury from platinum drugs, vinca alkaloids, and taxanes can progress to weakness and disability. Over two months, the team enrolled 235 adults on chemotherapy at Mbarara Regional Cancer Centre, interviewing patients, reviewing files, and scoring symptoms with a standard twenty-item tool.

Nearly a third of patients had chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy. Odds rose with age past sixty, with a past episode of nerve trouble that had resolved before chemotherapy, and with taking other nerve-toxic medicines alongside. Only about thirty percent of affected patients received any treatment, usually nerve pain drugs or vitamins, while guidelines recommend a specific antidepressant the center rarely used. The authors urge closer monitoring of high-risk patients so treatment starts promptly.
pmc-13550306:
Guang Zhang and colleagues dissect how the oyster mushroom defends itself against heat, in a 2026 molecular study. Heat waves bottleneck commercial production of Pleurotus ostreatus, ruining yield and quality. The team studied a gene for glutathione peroxidase, an antioxidant enzyme, and found it quiet during mushroom formation but switched on by stresses, heat above all.

Silencing the gene produced a surprise: the fungus grew faster, branched more, and suffered less heat damage, with lower chemical scarring from oxidation and a muted heat shock protein response. The silenced strains stockpiled more trehalose, a protective sugar, and a scavenger that mops up reactive oxygen erased that buildup, tying the effect to oxygen signaling. Blocking trehalose production restored heat sensitivity. The authors name the gene a breeding target for heat-hardy mushrooms.
pmc-13550406:
Ilaria Stanisci and colleagues gather the recent European evidence on air pollution and death from specific causes, in a 2026 review combining meta-analysis and meta-regression. Thirty-one studies from 2020 to 2025, including two large Italian projects, were screened, with pooled analysis possible for the fine particle studies. The team graded bias risk with an international tool.

Fine particles showed the clearest toll. Each added increment raised overall mortality by about a tenth in pooled terms. Cardiovascular and respiratory deaths also rose. Long-term exposure hurt more than brief spikes. Nitrogen dioxide tracked with the same three outcomes under long exposure, while coarse particles looked weaker and ozone evidence was mixed. Heavy differences between studies temper the numbers. The authors back tighter standards aligned with world health guidance.
pmc-13551306:
Bíró and colleagues present a 2026 longitudinal case study of how dreams changed during one year of psychotherapy with a 28-year-old patient. The patient had anxiety and depressive symptoms alongside ulcerative colitis, a chronic bowel inflammation. Five dreams judged clinically important were analyzed together with session notes and the patient's own associations.

Three themes ran through the dreams: vulnerability and loss of control, threat perception with emotional overwhelm, and emerging control and agency. Early dreams showed helplessness and sharp sensitivity to danger. Later dreams cast the dreamer as able to notice danger and respond in a more adaptive way. The authors suggest dream content can act as a sensitive window on improving emotion regulation during therapy, especially in psychosomatic care.
pmc-13551706:
Liyuan Zhang, leading six colleagues, published a 2026 retrospective study linking a simple insulin resistance marker to death after bleeding in the basal ganglia, a deep brain region. The triglyceride-glucose index had no established relation to prognosis in this stroke type. The single-center study followed 282 patients for one year, confirming deaths by standardized phone follow-up and modeling risk with survival methods.

Forty-nine patients, about one in six, died within the year. Each standard deviation rise in the index carried a notably higher mortality risk in the reported model, with risk climbing roughly linearly past a cutoff value the authors identified. Adding the index to a basic model improved some accuracy measures but not others, a mixed result the authors report plainly alongside robustness checks.
pmc-13551906:
Pengfei Zhang, Wanning Huang, Qiang Li, and Xiuyun Wu published a 2026 study of men's curling at the 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics. The team compared China with the medal-winning teams across 34 matches. They logged shot types and takeout moves. They compared tactical range and success rates. They then modeled which signs predicted a win.

China leaned on attacking shots such as draws and hit-and-rolls. Medal teams mixed attack and defense with wider range. Medalists also landed key shots more often. One takeout type predicted winning strongly in the models. Sweeping success predicted losing, oddly. The team reads sweeping as a rescue move used under pressure, not a cause of defeat.
pmc-13553506:
Dan Qi and six colleagues target nucleolin-driven cancer stemness in high-risk neuroblastoma. Neuroblastoma is the most common solid tumor outside the brain in children, arising from developing nerve-lineage cells. High-risk disease makes up about half of cases and drives most deaths. Event-free survival for high-risk disease stays near 40 to 50 percent, and relapse is typically fatal.

Cancer stem cells in neuroblastoma renew themselves, seed tumors, and fuel spread, treatment resistance, and return of disease. The team's earlier work tied nucleolin to upkeep of CD34-positive stem cells. Their 2027 paper reports that targeting nucleolin-driven stemness suppresses high-risk neuroblastoma in living models. The work points to nucleolin as a lever against relapse and resistance.
pmc-13555906:
Abdirezak Mawlid Abdi and three colleagues analyse what Somalia needs to fold chronic disease and mental health care into basic clinics in a 2026 review. Somalia's coverage index sits very low, and clinicians number barely a tenth per thousand people. Chronic diseases already drive about two fifths of deaths. The team drew on national plans, disease burden estimates, and health accounts, then costed expansion toward eighty percent coverage by 2030.

Households pay nearly half of health costs from their own pockets, above the danger line for catastrophic spending. Medicines and supplies form the largest cost driver in the expansion model, reflecting years of chronic care. Gaps in financing and service delivery remain structural. The authors judge integration workable and frame it as the route toward universal coverage.
pmc-13556006:
Pelin Kiyat and Melis Palamar studied 524 healthy volunteers in 2026 to see how eye dominance lines up with hand dominance and eye structure. Participants aged 20 to 60 took a hole-in-card test for eye dominance and a standard handedness inventory. Detailed scans measured the cornea, retina, and choroid, while a separate device measured the length of each eye.

About six in ten volunteers were right-eye dominant. A striking crossed pattern appeared: people with a dominant left eye were far more often right-handed than people with a dominant right eye. Dominant eyes also showed a thicker central cornea once strict statistical corrections were applied, with some retinal measures trending the same way. Choroid measures did not differ. The findings matter for clinicians who plan surgery or interpret scans one eye at a time.
pmc-13556106:
Xiaoyong Xiao and thirteen colleagues identified in 2026 a protein, tenascin C, that helps drive abdominal aortic aneurysm, the dangerous ballooning of the body's main artery. A burst aneurysm kills most patients, and disordered artery wall muscle cells sit at the disease's core. The team combined single-cell sequencing of patient tissue, public data, clinical samples, and mouse experiments to trace the protein's role.

Tenascin C signals ran high in aneurysm tissue, and blood levels of the protein predicted the condition in patients. Mice engineered to lack the protein only in artery muscle cells formed fewer aneurysms under chemical provocation, with calmer muscle cell behaviour. Mechanistic work showed the protein pushes an inflammatory switch into the cell nucleus through a surface receptor. The pathway gives drug developers a defined target chain to interrupt.
pmc-13558306:
Asha K. Rajan and twelve colleagues reviewed in 2026 how to dose the last-resort antibiotic polymyxin B in patients whose kidneys are failing. Drug-resistant Gram-negative infections leave few options, and this drug's behaviour in damaged kidneys, with or without dialysis-like support, is hard to predict. The systematic review gathered population pharmacokinetic studies of adults with renal impairment published up to May 2025 and appraised their quality with a validated tool.

Eleven studies covering 603 patients qualified. Clearance and distribution volume varied widely between individuals. Kidney function, the type of continuous replacement therapy, and illness severity were the main forces moving drug exposure, with flow-driven replacement methods clearing the drug faster. The authors advise against dosing by kidney numbers alone and outline a loading approach plus individual adjustment built on all three factors.
pmc-13558506:
Augustin and colleagues report in 2026 early results from AD-REAL, a multinational study of adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. The study follows them as they start oral systemic treatments in routine care for this chronic itchy skin disease. How long patients stay on these drugs was poorly documented.

The cohort began with 313 patients starting either older conventional drugs, the drug baricitinib, or other drugs from the same Janus kinase inhibitor family. By week 24, about half of the conventional group had stopped their first treatment. Under a third of the baricitinib group and under a fifth of the other inhibitor group had stopped. Ineffectiveness was the main reason for stopping the newer drugs. Far more patients on the newer drugs also reached mild disease levels on a standard eczema severity score.
pmc-13559106:
Ting Zhou and Feng Xiong published a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis on how childhood weight status relates to the timing of puberty. Heavier children have been reported to enter puberty earlier, especially girls, though findings vary between studies. The pair searched five databases, including Chinese sources, for observational work using weight or body mass index as the exposure.

Forty-one studies covering 416,789 participants from 18 countries or regions entered the review. Pooled estimates put the risk of early puberty about 56 percent higher in overweight or obese children than in normal-weight peers. The risk climbed step by step from overweight through obesity to severe obesity, showing a dose-response pattern. Effects were strongest for menarche timing among the markers examined. The authors call for shared definitions of exposure and outcome so future studies compare more cleanly.
pmc-13560206:
Hayat Topçu and eight colleagues dissect drought responses in two contrasting strawberry cultivars. Drought limits strawberry yields worldwide, yet cultivar tolerance mechanisms stay poorly understood.
