Their 2026 study compares drought-tolerant Kara with drought-sensitive E22 under water deficit and PEG-induced osmotic stress. It joins body, chemical, and gene analyses.

E22 lost chlorophyll and photosystem power while Kara held or raised chlorophyll and kept higher power. Proline, a key stress shield, rose much higher in Kara at peak stress. E22 rewrote over 22,500 transcripts under PEG, shutting photosynthesis paths and firing stress signals, while Kara changed under 900 transcripts per stress. Osmotic sensing thus drives large-scale gene control under drought.
pmc-13560706:
Baodi Shang and colleagues report the complete genome of an Acinetobacter strain taken from a sick hybrid sturgeon at a fish farm in Guizhou Province, China. Their 2026 genome announcement describes strain BZX-2, cultured from mucus on ulcerated skin of the hybrid fish in April 2024. Relatives of this bacterium have already sickened farmed sturgeon, disturbing organs and gut communities.

Hybrid long- and short-read sequencing assembled one chromosome of about 3.82 million bases carrying 3,566 predicted protein-coding genes. The team catalogued the strain's antibiotic resistance genes as part of the characterization. The isolate now rests in a national culture collection for other researchers. The authors frame the genome as groundwork for preventing and controlling sturgeon disease in aquaculture, where Acinetobacter outbreaks threaten a valuable farmed fish.
pmc-13561606:
Haodong Guo and colleagues map twenty-five years of research on imaging-guided localization in breast cancer surgery, the techniques that help surgeons find tumors that cannot be felt. Their 2026 bibliometric analysis searches the Web of Science in November 2025 and keeps 366 publications from 2000 to 2025. Network and keyword tools chart who publishes, who cites, and how themes move.

Output climbed steadily after 2011, signaling growing interest, while average citations per article drifted downward in recent years. The United States dominates output, citation impact, and international collaboration in the country analysis. Themes shifted visibly from wire-guided localization and basic imaging toward precision approaches tied to chemotherapy before surgery. The most cited work is clinical, showing guidance improving surgical precision and margin control. The authors call for rigorous comparative trials and wider collaboration to standardize the new methods.
pmc-13561706:
Ling Du and Lei Wang present this 2026 case report on a rare kidney cancer, primary renal squamous cell carcinoma. It makes up under one percent of kidney tumors and has no standard treatment path. Their patient was a fifty-six year old man whose cancer returned soon after kidney removal.

The recurrence appeared one month after surgery for a large, locally advanced tumor. Doctors treated it with sunitinib, a targeted drug that blocks tumor blood vessel signals, combined with precise radiotherapy aimed at the returning mass. The tumor shrank in a partial response, his strength score rose sharply, he gained weight, and his anemia cleared. No spread appeared during follow-up. The authors suggest this pairing deserves study for similar relapses.
pmc-13569106:
Geovana Rocha Marzochi and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether essential oils from orange and citronella can act as natural weed killers, as herbicide-resistant weeds push farmers to seek alternatives. Oils made by two extraction methods were applied at several doses to seeds of four major weeds, and sprouting and early growth were measured.

Citronella oils nearly stopped seedlings from the middle dose upward, driven by compounds such as citronellol and geraniol. Orange oils weakened germination more gently and unevenly across weed species. The contrast positions citronella oil as a strong bioherbicide candidate and orange oil as a supporting tool in greener weed control.
pmc-13569206:
Javier Caviedes-Bucheli and colleagues review a little-studied brake on tooth pain: neuropeptide Y, a signalling molecule inside the dental pulp. The pulp is a densely wired, rigid tissue where inflammation can quickly raise pressure, choke blood flow, and cause pain. While two excitatory messengers, substance P and CGRP, are well known drivers of that spiral, neuropeptide Y's counterbalancing role has been underexplored. Their 2026 review synthesised 92 studies.

Across models, neuropeptide Y emerged as a master regulator that damps excitation, constricts vessels, and quiets pain-sensing nerves, partly by suppressing CGRP release. In decayed teeth its levels shift with disease stage, hinting at an early protective program that fails as damage advances. The authors frame pulp outcomes as a balance between excitatory and inhibitory signals, with neuropeptide Y as a potential therapeutic lever.
pmc-13569606:
Xiao Wu, Duo Jiang, and Bin Li build, in a 2026 retrospective study, prediction models for complete tumor disappearance after immune therapy given before lung cancer surgery. Two established markers, a tumor protein level and the number of tumor mutations, were combined with clinical features in 232 surgical patients, then checked in 115 later patients at the same hospital.

Combined immune therapy with chemotherapy strongly raised the odds of complete response, as did higher marker levels, while nodal spread lowered them. A paper chart and a machine-learning model were both built and graded for accuracy and calibration. Such tools could help surgeons and patients judge who gains most from pre-surgery immune treatment.
pmc-13571806:
Patrik Šimják and colleagues report, in a 2026 prenatal case, blocked nasal passages on both sides spotted in the first trimester. The finding was the first sign of a severe new syndrome in one twin. The pregnancy was a naturally conceived twin pair. Screening at thirteen weeks was normal for both, yet one fetus showed a gap at the upper jaw that prompted a closer look.

Three-dimensional imaging showed both nasal cavities symmetrically widened with clean bony edges and a prominent central bone, suggesting choanal atresia, a blockage never before reported this early. Genetic testing later found a new harmful variant in the KMT2D gene, giving the first prenatal diagnosis of BCAHH syndrome. Early nasal imaging may flag this condition before birth.
pmc-13572206:
Xiaoyu Zhao and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, whether curcumin, the yellow compound in turmeric, protects chick livers against a common plasticizer called DEHP that leaks from plastics into the environment. Cell experiments and live chick exposures traced damage through oxidative stress, energy production, and a mixed cell-death program.

In cells, curcumin restored mitochondrial power, calmed calcium imbalance, and eased internal stress while suppressing a sugar-burning pathway that the plasticizer switched on. Blocking that pathway lowered death markers too. In live chicks, the plasticizer shrank body weight and swelled and scarred the liver, while curcumin feeding largely reversed those changes. The findings support turmeric compounds as a feed defense where plastic contamination reaches poultry.
pmc-13572406:
Somayeh BeyranvandRaad, with two colleagues, presents a 2026 computer study of a nano sheet that might carry the gut drug mesalazine. The drug calms swelling in the bowel, but poor delivery can blunt its effect and raise side effects. The carrier in focus is graphitic carbon nitride, a flat sheet of carbon and nitrogen.

Quantum chemistry calculations compared the drug on the sheet in gas and in water. Binding was favourable in both, at about minus 19.68 and minus 21.50 kilocalories per mole for the most stable pose. Weak forces, not strong bonds, held the pair, which should let the drug come off at the target. Charge flowed from the drug to the sheet. Light absorption peaks shifted in each medium. The authors rate the sheet as a strong carrier prospect.
pmc-13575106:
Nate Christensen sets out a 2026 physics paper linking stability boundaries across fields, from quantum systems to the expanding universe. His organising idea is a damping ratio, a unit-free number that marks where a system's behaviour changes class. At a value of one, the system reaches a special boundary called an exceptional point.

Christensen shows an exact algebraic link between the start of cosmic acceleration and a critical damping point for the growth of structure. He is clear that the link restates known equations rather than adding a new law. Its value, he argues, lies in a testable forecast: models beyond the standard flat cosmology should show a small offset that the standard model lacks. Particle lifetimes are also sorted into stability bands under his scheme.
pmc-13576106:
Mia L Barron leads a 2026 scoping review of communication between clinicians and African American adults living with lupus. Lupus is an autoimmune disease that damages many organs, and outcomes run worse for African American patients. Weak communication and missed screening for changeable risks add to that gap.

Searches of four databases covering 2012 to mid-2025 yielded 214 papers, of which 20 met the review's rules. Helpful habits included involving family, speaking more slowly, and showing empathy. Several papers pushed for decision aids with communication built in. None tested a communication tool aimed at cutting changeable risks or improving outcomes in this group. The authors flag that absence as the key gap for future work.
pmc-13576206:
Chang-Zhu He and five colleagues test whether combining structural and blood flow eye scans improves spotting normal-tension glaucoma in very short-sighted eyes, in a 2026 diagnostic study. High myopia and this glaucoma type can look alike, making diagnosis tricky. Structural scans map tissue layers, while a related scan maps tiny vessels.

The study enrolled 87 patients, 42 with high myopia alone and 45 with glaucoma added. Structural measures beat vessel measures overall. One layer measure at the lower macula scored best, at 0.85 on the ranking accuracy scale, while the best vessel measure sat lower. Machine learning and standard regression models were built from the chosen features and checked with resampling and calibration tests. Explanation tools showed how each feature pushed individual predictions. The authors see combined data as useful support for a hard distinction.
pmc-13576306:
Giuseppe Migliaretti and Paolo Giacomo Arduino test whether entrance exam scores forecast success in dental school, in a 2026 study from the University of Turin. Italy long admitted dental students by national exam, and a recent reform scrapped that route. The team looked back at 431 students enrolled between 2009 and 2018.

Higher admission scores tracked with earning credits on schedule and graduating on time. The test predicted first-year performance with a ranking score of 0.71, and degree completion at 0.70 in the same units. A cut-off of 40 out of 90 separated strugglers: students below it had five times the odds of falling behind on first-year credits. The authors argue the findings should inform the debate on removing the exam, given the risks for dropout rates and wasted resources.
pmc-13576606:
Chiu and colleagues published a 2026 trial on a magnetic tracer for breast cancer surgery. Surgeons check the first lymph node, the sentinel node, to stage early breast cancer. The standard method pairs a radioactive tracer with a blue dye. The trial tested iron oxide particles that a magnet probe can find instead.

Nearly 300 patients were split between the magnetic tracer and the standard pair. The magnetic method found the sentinel node in over 99 percent of cases. The standard pair scored a perfect rate, a gap within the set limit. One failure occurred in the magnetic group across 153 procedures. The authors back the magnetic tracer as a sound stand-in option. The trial ran from 2021 to 2024 across several hospital centers.
pmc-13580006:
Yuteng Wang and a large team of co-authors link social isolation and loneliness to early menopause and death in women, in a 2026 study of the UK Biobank. Nearly eighty thousand women were classed by when menopause came, early at forty to forty five or in the normal band after that. Isolation was scored from living setup, contact, and group life; loneliness from felt loneliness and having someone to confide in.

Both hardships tied to higher odds of early menopause, modestly but steadily. The survival penalty hit far harder in the early group: high isolation raised death risk by over half there, against a far smaller lift in the normal group. Survival curves split wider as hardship rose. The authors urge menopause care to screen for social strain.
pmc-13587106:
Adelie YS Tan and a large team map decay in the striatum, a deep brain hub for movement, in X-linked dystonia parkinsonism. The inherited disease, first described in 1976 and rooted on the Philippine island of Panay, mixes twisting movements with Parkinson-like slowness. Its brain signature stayed murky because so few cases have been studied. The team stained post-mortem tissue from 18 patients and 10 people without brain disease.

Decay ran in a gradient from top to bottom of the striatum, and one inner compartment, the matrix, wore away faster than its partner patches. The pattern tracked how long the disease had run more than the length of the gene repeat that causes it, though that repeat did set the age when symptoms began. The authors read the damage as the slow breakup of a wider movement circuit over the course of the illness.
pmc-13588206:
Ryan Meachen and colleagues review spiritual care in serious illness across low- and middle-income countries. Most research on spiritual care comes from rich countries, yet most seriously ill people live in poorer ones, where faith often plays a larger public role. Their narrative review drew 46 qualifying studies out of a large parent review, spanning Asia, Latin America, the Middle East and North Africa, and sub-Saharan Africa.

Across those settings, stronger spiritual wellbeing and positive religious coping traveled with better quality of life, less distress, and stronger family outcomes, while spiritual struggle tracked worse mental health. Care itself came mostly from family and faith communities rather than clinicians. Most studies used questionnaires built in rich countries, though tools from Thailand, Iran, and Nigeria caught local paths the imports missed. The authors propose keeping the global tools while adding local ones.
pmc-13590406:
Charles J Gomez, writing alone in 2026, asks whose ideas steer world science. He built networks from close to 240 million works published between 1990 and 2023, drawn from the OpenAlex database. His focus is what he calls discursive influence: which topics and claims a field treats as worth chasing. That kind of sway, he finds, sits heavily with a small set of rich nations.

The United States, Canada, and parts of Western Europe and East Asia hold a growing share of that sway, Gomez reports. Credit for work spreads more widely than topic setting power does. He warns that such narrowing can breed echo chambers and shut out fresh views from poorer lands. His remedy is a broader, more open world research effort.
pmc-13591006:
Martin Wilson and two colleagues examine a hidden bias in functional MRS, a scan method that tracks brain chemicals while the brain works. When an area wakes up, blood flow shifts, an effect known as BOLD, and that shift slightly narrows spectral lines. Narrower lines can masquerade as a true rise in a chemical. The team used synthetic scan data to test fitting tools at two scanner strengths.

Both standard tools showed a bias near one percent for glutamate, matching earlier lab work, and newer 2D tools fared no better. Adding a step that matches line width to the BOLD state cut the bias to under a fifth of a percent. Wilson and the team urge that step for all such studies at 3 Tesla and above.
pmc-13591706:
Faezeh Ghorbani and five colleagues ask, in 2026, what helps or hinders teenagers asked to wear a brace for a curved spine. Braces can halt worsening curves before bones mature, yet teens often skip wearing them. The team interviewed 74 people: adolescents with scoliosis or a hunched upper back, their parents, and the clinicians who fit and oversee braces. Talks ran over eight months at spine centers.

Responses sorted into four big themes and dozens of smaller factors, from brace comfort and looks to family support and follow up care. Each teen's path differed in detail, the team found. They advise personal plans, steady follow up, teaching videos, and rewards to lift wear time. Success stories from peers may also build a hopeful outlook.
pmc-13592406:
Kyoung-Yong Chun and three colleagues build, in 2026, an artificial skin sensor that splits touch into steady pressure and quick vibration, much as human skin does. Their stack pairs a magnetic rubber loaded with iron oxide, which answers fast shakes, with an ion conducting gel that reports steady load. The rubber's own voltage drives the gel, so the pair runs self powered in one layered unit.

Read together, the two channels drew tactile fingerprints that sorted surface textures, caught slips, and flagged grooves of differing width. The fast channel reached a kilohertz of vibration range. Chun and the team offer the hybrid as a scalable recipe for robot hands and human machine interfaces that need rich touch, not just force readings.
pmc-13592506:
Annie Prasad and six colleagues blend glowing lanthanide complexes into room temperature ionic liquids for anti counterfeit tagging. Lanthanides emit razor sharp color lines, each metal with its own fingerprint, while ionic liquids flow, mix freely, and barely evaporate. Their salts pair a bulky phosphonium cation with complexes of europium, terbium, dysprosium, or samarium. Each liquid kept its metal's signature glow.

Because the emitters are liquids, simple volume mixing built two, three, and four metal blends with dense, layered spectra and no new synthesis. Heat tests confirmed stable liquid behavior suited to printing. Prasad and the team argue that decoupling spectral richness from synthetic effort opens a scalable route to security inks and optical tags.
pmc-13594906:
Valerie Oberhardt heads a large team tracking the virus-specific killer T cells of patients with chronic hepatitis D during treatment with bulevirtide, the first approved drug for this severe liver infection. Twenty-eight patients with cirrhosis were followed for up to about two years in their 2026 study, with detailed immune profiling along the way.

Detectable responses existed in about four of ten patients at the start and did not grow much on treatment. Most responses aimed at viral fragments the virus had already mutated, evidence of past escape. One target region stayed unchanged and was attacked throughout therapy, and the cells attacking it looked worn out at first but gradually shifted toward a memory-like state as viral levels fell. The authors suggest treatment can partially revive exhausted immunity, though escape limits how much good that does.
pmc-13595506:
Jeannette Weber and co-authors revisited a German randomized trial of psychotherapeutic consultation offered at the workplace. The trial served employees with common mental health symptoms. The team asked whether the sessions changed how people experienced their jobs. About five hundred fifty employees were randomized to up to sixteen work-focused sessions or routine care. Working conditions were rated again two years later.

In data from 231 participants, the consultation group reported somewhat lower emotional demands. Work and private life also blurred less at follow-up. The differences were modest. After adjustment for multiple comparisons they no longer cleared the usual significance bar. The authors state that caution plainly. These outcomes had not been pre-specified in the trial plan. Resources such as decision freedom and social support showed no clear shift. The analysis is exploratory, hinting that workplace therapy may ease felt job strain without redesigning the job itself.
pmc-13595606:
Florian Richter argues that autonomy, properly layered, is the concept that makes invasive brain-computer interfaces ethically describable. Such implants blur the line between person and device so deeply that saying who decided what becomes genuinely hard, yet clear authorship of decisions is exactly what responsibility and privacy judgments need.

Richter separates autonomy into three levels: operational, strategic, and moral. Machines, he contends, can act on the first two, since their behavior follows built-in dispositions about what is possible. Humans alone occupy the moral level, because human agency rests on norms, on attitudes about what ought to be done, which cannot be flattened into mere possibility. That asymmetry, he proposes, gives ethicists a workable method. They can judge where a device's action ends and a patient's own decision begins. This matters even as implants gain therapeutic ground in conditions such as Parkinson's disease.
pmc-13595806:
M. von Cossel published a correction to a 2026 article on the twin limits of soil carbon storage. One limit is the physical ceiling on how much carbon soils can hold. The other is the practical capacity of farmers to build it. The corrections adjust wording in the abstract and introduction of the Global Challenges article.

Where the text had described soil carbon as the largest actively managed terrestrial reservoir, the wording changed. Soil carbon is now called the biggest land store of organic carbon, one that land management substantially shapes. The authors call that a softer and more defensible claim. A paragraph about agriculture's footprint was trimmed. The argument now rests on the carbon stock itself, about 1500 billion tonnes in the top meter and more below. Smaller edits sharpen terminology, such as specifying declining soil organic carbon stocks. The stock figures themselves stand unchanged.
pmc-13597106:
Mark A Eckert and co-authors scanned older adults doing word recognition in noise and sorted their mistakes by type, asking whether different errors carry different brain signatures. Two people can earn the same score while failing differently. One swaps a word's final sound. Another loses the whole word. Their 2026 trial-level analysis used data from two imaging experiments. The experiments had forty-five and forty participants.

Swapping the first or last consonant came with distinct activity patterns across hearing and monitoring networks. Dropping a word entirely happened when the hearing network ran quiet while monitoring and default mode networks ran high, a profile suggesting weak signal plus disengagement. Other errors paired with stronger monitoring activity, as if the brain noticed trouble. The authors argue these patterns could explain why a listener struggles in ways a single score never reveals.
pmc-13598106:
Johannes Lauer and co-authors tested a drug that selectively boosts one subtype of NMDA receptor. The subtype is the GluN2A type. It is implicated in the thinking problems of many brain disorders. The drug was tested across mouse tests of working memory and flexibility. Their 2026 study asked whether help depends on how the impairment was caused and on the animal's starting point.

The drug did nothing for average performers yet lifted mice whose baseline working memory was naturally poor. It rescued deficits caused by amphetamine and by scopolamine, two drugs that disturb chemical modulation while leaving the receptor usable. It failed completely against MK-801, which physically plugs the receptor's pore, exactly as its mechanism predicts. Effects ran stronger in females, and mental flexibility did not improve at all. The authors describe a state-dependent profile: the booster helps only when the system is underperforming yet still reachable.
pmc-13598406:
E Carrillo and colleagues tested baby garter snakes that had never seen prey, asking whether their hunting preferences are born rather than learned. Two species were compared in their 2026 study. One was the Lake Chapala garter snake, an aquatic specialist. The other was the checkered garter snake, a generalist. Scent extracts, tongue flicks, and attacks served as measures of interest.

The naive snakes' preferences matched the diets reported for wild adults: the specialist committed to aquatic prey while the generalist stayed flexible. In shallow water the specialist struck forward with wider gape and better accuracy and speed, aided by sharper vision, while the generalist struck sideways. In deeper water both species converged, striking forward, opening wider, taking longer, and swallowing underwater. Head shape tracked the styles, with the specialist narrower and shorter. The authors read the results as hardwired specialization plus flexible adjustment.
pmc-13600306:
Jiajin Li and three colleagues build a scoring framework to help China choose which metabolic disease drugs its national medical insurance should cover. Metabolic diseases such as diabetes and high blood pressure affect huge numbers in China, yet picking medicines for the insurance catalog has leaned on personal judgment. The team wanted an open method weighing clinical value, patient needs, cost-effectiveness, and budget limits.

They combined a hierarchy method that ranks criteria, a three-round structured expert consultation, and a light health technology assessment. Criteria were drawn from essential medicine lists from the World Health Organization, India, and Kenya, plus Chinese policy sources. The finished framework holds 14 main indicators and 42 sub-indicators. Seven experts from clinical, pharmacy, and insurance backgrounds reached solid agreement on the weights. The authors offer it as a transparent starting point, noting it still needs a real-world pilot.
pmc-13616306:
Shibo Liu, Xiangling Li, and Wei Ouyang review the road toward sensors that can sit inside the body and report chemical levels nonstop for weeks, using aptamer-based electrochemistry. Aptamers are crafted strands that fold around a chosen molecule and change shape, turning binding into an electric signal. Such live data could reshape how doctors dose drugs and catch disease shifts early, yet most sensors still fade or fail within days.

Recent studies have reached week-long runs inside the body, proving the idea can work. Remaining blocks include the sensor surface fouling, the aptamer wearing out, and the lack of a fully packaged device that patients can live with. The review sorts the fixes now being tried, from protective coatings to self-calibrating designs, and judges what stands between the lab and the ward.
pmc-13617106:
Yuping Shan and four colleagues grade the quality of short online videos about precancerous cervical lesions, the cell changes that can precede cervical cancer. They collected one thousand eight hundred forty-two videos from four major Chinese platforms: TikTok, Bilibili, Kwai, and Xiaohongshu. Five established scoring tools judged quality, reliability, transparency, and how usable the health guidance was.

TikTok videos scored highest across nearly every tool, while the other platforms varied widely. Videos made by medical professionals, especially gynecologists, outscored those from lay creators, and basic disease explainers taught more than prevention or after-treatment clips. Popularity signals such as likes did not reliably match quality. The authors suggest platforms can be useful health channels if quality checks improve and more clinicians take part in making videos.
pmc-13617906:
Hanyu Li and four colleagues report a 2026 study of the mouth's microbial ecosystem in heart failure, comparing dental plaque from sixty-three patients with thirty-one healthy controls. Bacteria and fungi were profiled by gene sequencing, and the team looked for community patterns tied to severity grades. An oral-heart axis has been proposed before, yet severity-linked evidence has been thin.

Heart failure status and severity class were among the strongest explanations for how plaque communities varied. Over one hundred bacterial and nearly seventy fungal variants differed between groups. A combined six-marker score separated patients from controls well and flagged advanced disease even better. Predicted microbial pathways shifted too: energy-cycle pathways rose with severity while a butyrate-making fermentation pathway, typical of plaque, faded. The authors say the pattern shows functional uncoupling of the plaque ecosystem in severe disease and call for multi-omics validation.
pmc-13618406:
Janine P. M. Faessen and five colleagues compare how Dutch women experience food during pregnancy and after birth, in a cross-sectional online survey recruited through social media. One thousand six hundred nineteen women answered, eight hundred forty-two pregnant and seven hundred seventy-seven postpartum, mostly educated with a mean age of thirty-two. Both groups rated nutrition as important.

Pregnant women enjoyed food least and rated their diets worst in the first trimester, eating mainly for the child's health, while postpartum women ate mainly from hunger. After birth, phase-specific knowledge and time for preparing and eating food dropped sharply, yet eagerness to learn rose and confidence in cooking grew. Websites were the top information source, then professionals, then apps. App use plunged from ninety-one percent in pregnancy to fifty-nine percent postpartum, with many women unaware such apps exist, a gap the authors flag for designers.
pmc-13618906:
Ioannis Vasilikos and seventeen colleagues test borrowed eye surgery chemistry on the dura mater, the tough membrane wrapping the brain and spinal cord, whose defects challenge neurosurgeons. Riboflavin plus ultraviolet-A light crosslinks collagen in the cornea. Here the team applied it to forty specimens of cow dura outside the body, varying vitamin concentration and light intensity. They measured stiffness with an atomic force microscope before and after in matched spots.

Ultraviolet light alone stiffened the tissue modestly, two to three fold. Adding riboflavin produced a dramatic, concentration-dependent effect: the strongest recipe raised the elastic modulus about one hundred fifty fold. Post-treatment stiffness rose in a nearly perfect straight line with riboflavin dose, making the effect precisely adjustable. The authors call it proof of concept for biochemical reinforcement of dural tissue, with human tissue testing, macroscopic strength checks, penetration depth, and safety work still to come.
pmc-13619006:
Milena Marie Santo and nine colleagues compare the microbial chemistry along the gut under four feeding regimes. The options were round-the-clock pasture, hay freely available, or hay plus oats at two starch doses. After feeding, the horses were dissected and digesta sampled from successive sections, analyzed for dry matter, acidity, short-chain fatty acids, ammonia, and lactate, the fingerprints of microbial fermentation.

Gut section dominated: each measure differed between sections, with a clean divide between foregut and hindgut, and within the hindgut. Diet still mattered. Pasture-fed horses showed the highest fatty acid levels, signaling vigorous fermentation. In the far hindgut, pasture raised markers of amino acid breakdown, suggesting microbes there fermented more protein. Oat supplementation changed chemistry in the stomach, pointing to higher protein-splitting activity upstream. The map explains how feeding shifts where fermentation happens in the horse gut, relevant to gut health and disorder risk.
pmc-13619706:
Niklas Amann and thirteen colleagues reviewed how often women with breast cancer and an inherited BRCA mutation chose preventive removal of the ovaries and fallopian tubes. Such surgery is the only proven way to cut the raised ovarian cancer risk these mutations bring. The team studied 148 patients treated at a German university center between 2012 and 2024.

About sixty percent carried a BRCA1 change and the rest a BRCA2 change. Just over two thirds of the group went on to have the preventive surgery, and most of those operations happened within two years of the breast cancer diagnosis. Hidden ovarian cancer turned up in three women at the time of surgery, while four women without the surgery later developed ovarian cancer. The authors argue the operation should keep being offered and discussed under current guidelines.
pmc-13621806:
Cécile De Cat and five co-authors ask how much exposure multilingual children need before their school language skills match those of monolingual classmates. Children who grow up with several languages are often judged against one-language norms, which can hide real support needs. The study covers children aged five to nine learning English, French, or Dutch as the language of school.

The team tested sentence repetition and word knowledge, then used statistical models that allow for turning points instead of fixed cut-offs. For grammar, group scores entered the monolingual range after roughly fifty-nine months of added-up exposure, with gains levelling off near that point. Word knowledge showed no clear threshold, and thinking skills plus rich language experience mattered more than exposure alone. The authors advise steady language support through primary school rather than early withdrawal.
pmc-13624706:
Suguru Miida and colleagues chart how thigh-level muscle, measured at the third lumbar level on CT scans, wastes away over five years in people with cirrhosis. Their review covered 175 patients scanned once a year between 2010 and 2022 at Japanese centers. Muscle loss, called sarcopenia, is common in this liver disease and predicts poor outcomes, so the team asked which routine facts foretell faster decline.

Muscle shrank steadily each year, and patients whose livers scored worst on the Child-Pugh scale at the start lost muscle far faster than those with mild disease. A trial model guessed year-five muscle mostly from the starting scan, yet only five patients had the worst liver score, so the authors urge caution. Early muscle checks may still flag who needs help first.
pmc-13625306:
Di Wu and four colleagues, publishing in 2026, report the first use of remimazolam to sedate a newborn for an MRI scan. Newborns must lie still in a loud scanner for many minutes, yet their small airways and fast drug handling make sedation risky. Their patient, born just shy of term and weighing under three kilograms, first resisted settling methods and then a nose-spray sedative.

A small vein dose of remimazolam, a short-acting sedative known for gentle effects on heart and breathing in adults, settled the baby within a minute. The seventeen-minute scan finished with heart and breathing steady throughout. One case cannot prove safety, so the authors call for larger multi-center studies, while offering remimazolam as a rescue option when standard sedation fails.
pmc-13627206:
Carlo Lai and co-authors follow women through the first month after breast cancer surgery, when body and mood are both raw. The prospective study enrolled 101 women and measured quality of life, anxiety, and depression in the first days after surgery and again one month later. Alongside, it tracked perceived pain, arm and shoulder disability on the operated side, and acceptance of the disease, using standard scales at both visits.

Quality of life rose and distress eased across the month. Once pain, arm disability, and acceptance entered the models, the calendar itself explained nothing more, which means recovery rides on those three levers. Pain and a stiff arm dragged quality of life down, arm trouble also fed depression, and acceptance shielded against both anxiety and low mood. Early, team-based rehabilitation is the clear implication.
pmc-13629306:
Dandu Anitha and seven colleagues review how to make dense, high-energy green jet fuel. The prized fuels are rich in cycloparaffins, ring-shaped hydrocarbons with high energy per litre. Their survey covers approved green fuel methods and their limits. It then turns to fresh feedstocks. Those include terpenes, terpenoids, and plant oils rich in cineole.

Unlike chemistry suits each feedstock. Terpenoids pass through drying, oxygen removal, and reshaping steps. Terpenes are treated with hydrogen, paired up, or given extra rings. The review compares catalysts for activity and for picking the right products. It then checks the fuels against flight standards to judge drop-in readiness. The authors present these green routes as a sound path. Fully renewable jet fuel blends with lower emissions could follow.
pmc-13629806:
Kyra E. Verboon and five colleagues followed a mother and her fourteen-year-old daughter through five weeks of trauma therapy. They asked whether a parent's protective behaviour helps, or unwittingly keeps the teen's stress symptoms alive. The pair combined surveys with phone prompts four times a day. Direct watching and interviews joined the mix.

The phone data showed wide day-to-day swings. The mother's shielding swung, and so did the daughter's symptoms. The two moved together in both directions. The standard surveys missed that pattern entirely. Watching and interviews added the mother's aims and the pair's clashing views. The authors argue this multi-method approach, though more demanding, reveals useful dynamics. Standard tools flatten those dynamics away.
pmc-13630006:
James Rufus John and forty colleagues describe the plan for STARS for Kids. This Australian trial tests a co-designed, tiered support model for families in the first years of life. The model aims to spot problems earlier. Targets include child development issues and parent mental health strain. Family social needs count too. Support intensity matches need across three unlike sites.

The trial will recruit parents of children aged six months to three years. Each site takes 140 families. Sites sit in multicultural southwestern Sydney, a regional area with an Aboriginal community, and a low-income Perth district. Side phases will study rollout on the ground. They will also model costs and lifetime gains. A nested trial tests a video programme for toddlers showing poor emotional control.
pmc-13630306:
Anastasia Rousaki and three colleagues mapped what patients and carers think of technology-based appointment reminders, the texts, calls, and app nudges meant to cut missed appointments. Their scoping review searched six databases in autumn 2025 for studies from 2010 onward and included forty-five.

Text messages were the most studied format, and satisfaction ran high overall. Recurring problems clustered around equity: digital exclusion, language barriers, confidentiality worries, and cost all limited who could engage, and most studies recorded social characteristics without testing whether they changed engagement. The authors call for reminder systems designed with users and judged explicitly on fairness, so they narrow rather than widen healthcare gaps.
pmc-13630506:
Hanna Särkilä and seven colleagues followed 48,124 Finns who started benzodiazepines or related sleeping drugs in 2006, tracking deaths over five years against the doses actually dispensed. Published in 2026, the nationwide cohort study models use as it changes over time rather than as a single yes-or-no exposure.

Any use period carried somewhat higher mortality than non-use, but the risk concentrated at higher doses. Medium-to-high dosing raised all-cause mortality clearly, very high dosing raised it far more, and low dosing showed no elevation at all. The steepest risks were for the most preventable deaths: overdoses, suicides, and accidents. The authors stress that danger scales with dose and with juggling several of these drugs at once.
pmc-13630806:
Lattimore and Johnson reflected in 2026 on local treatment for occult breast cancer with advanced lymph node spread. Occult breast cancer means cancer found in armpit nodes with no tumour detectable in the breast itself. Mastectomy, removal of the breast, was the historic default, since doctors assumed a hidden tumour remained.

Their linked study found that nearly all such patients had MRI and drug therapy before surgery, and most kept the breast with whole-breast radiation. No cancer returned in the breast or chest wall despite rare mastectomy in their centre's cohort. In a national database cohort, survival was high in both the radiation and mastectomy groups, even with advanced nodal disease. The authors argue that selected patients can safely skip mastectomy after team review and shared decision-making.
pmc-13633406:
Aqeel Abbas and eight colleagues report the case of a young woman whose kidney crisis exposed an undiagnosed inherited syndrome. The twenty-seven-year-old arrived with sudden kidney injury after a bout of stomach and bowel infection. Doctors found her kidneys had in fact been failing quietly for years. The wider picture pointed to Bardet-Biedl syndrome, a recessive condition marked by obesity, an eye disease that erodes vision, extra fingers or toes, and learning difficulties.

Kidney damage is the syndrome's most dangerous feature, yet it hides for years without regular checks. Where resources are limited, the condition may go unnamed until adulthood, as happened here. The authors urge doctors to suspect the syndrome when eye disease, obesity, extra digits, and kidney trouble appear together, especially in families where parents are related. Early naming allows monitoring that can delay lasting damage and improve daily life.
pmc-13634306:
Jiexun Cai and eight colleagues built a blood score meant to capture the body-wide inflammation behind COPD, a chronic lung disease. Breathing test results often fail to match how burdened patients feel. The team measured eleven cytokines, small immune signaling proteins, in the blood of sixty-two patients with stable disease. They combined the readings into one score using an automated selection method that kept only the most useful markers.

The final score rests on three cytokines. It tracked breathing-based severity better than any single cytokine and separated severity grades reasonably well. Breathing scores still explained effort-related symptoms such as breathlessness more strongly. The new score leaned toward sleep and energy complaints, though those links stayed short of firm statistical ground. The authors present the score as a companion to breathing tests, not a replacement, and call for outside validation in larger, longer studies.
pmc-13637106:
Demet Çelik and Orkun Erkayiran published this 2026 interview study on how hemodialysis reshapes family life in Türkiye. Dialysis patients spend long hours tied to a machine several days a week, and the treatment reorganizes the whole household around it. The pair interviewed fifteen patients at a hospital in Central Anatolia during mid 2025. They analyzed the conversations with a mix of ready-made family-systems themes and new themes drawn from the interviews themselves.

Six themes emerged. Families pulled closer in solidarity, yet roles and care burdens shifted onto particular members. Exhaustion and rest formed a repeating cycle, and daily routine bent around dialysis appointments. A line appeared between emotional loyalty and practical help. Faith-based acceptance helped long-term patients normalize their situation, a theme stronger in veterans of treatment than in newcomers. The authors recommend family-centered planning that builds rest into daily life and fixes transport headaches.
pmc-13638906:
Stefano Cacciatore and ten colleagues published a 2026 network analysis of intrinsic capacity and death in very old adults in Italy. Intrinsic capacity combines five areas of healthy aging: movement, thinking, vitality, mood, and the senses.

The study used the ilSIRENTE cohort of 319 people aged eighty and over living at home. Vitality, mood, and thinking clustered closely together, while hearing and vision sat at the edges and connected through movement. Better movement scores and higher overall capacity each predicted lower death rates over four and seven years. The authors suggest routine assessments could flag older people most at risk.
pmc-13639206:
Lisa Dasen and eight colleagues published a 2026 study of stress and mental health among forcibly displaced people living in Switzerland. Earlier work treated trauma exposure as a single scale, which can hide very different individual patterns.

Survey data from 437 people were sorted into five profiles, from very high stress with very high symptoms down to low stress with none. Men, people with stronger social support, and people with secure visa status were more likely to sit in lower-symptom groups. The authors say such profiles can help services spot both vulnerable and resilient people and tailor support accordingly.
pmc-13639606:
The GBD 2023 Tetanus Collaborators report a systematic analysis of tetanus burden across 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023. Tetanus is deadly yet vaccine-preventable, and global campaigns have cut it sharply without eliminating it.

Standardized incidence fell from about eleven cases per hundred thousand people in 1990 to under one per hundred thousand in 2023. The remaining burden concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, while wealthy regions approached zero. Burden tracked closely with a social development index, falling as development rose. The group presents the estimates as a guide for closing the last gaps in vaccination.
pmc-13642306:
Zhongming Chen and two colleagues present a 2026 method for reading the past paths of migrating cells inside living tissue. Watching cells move deep in the body over long periods is nearly impossible with ordinary live imaging.

Their trick is to engineer cells to release fluorescent protein fused to collagen, leaving glowing trails in the tissue as they travel. In mice, the team found trails in healthy organs, primary tumors, and sites where cancer had spread. Some trails ran together along blood vessel walls, hinting at group travel. Reading the trails after death reconstructs migration history that cameras could never capture.
pmc-13647906:
Linna Ma and seven colleagues chart the conversation between switch genes and defense genes in rice under attack by the blast fungus, in a 2026 study. Rice blast is among the most destructive crop diseases on Earth. Drawing on the rice pan-genome and gene activity measured across an infection time course, the team built interaction networks with two independent methods. One switch family, the bHLH factors, lit up across the response.

To test the network, the team knocked out three bHLH genes in rice lines. Each knockout left the plants clearly more susceptible to the fungus, which confirms the family defends rather than merely watches. Two of the genes are entirely new candidates for blast resistance. The authors present the first pan-genome-based map of its kind for this disease. Breeders gain both a wiring diagram of rice immunity and fresh genetic material for resistant varieties.
pmc-13650606:
Xingxing Wang and thirteen colleagues build a way to read pancreatic cancer's makeup from scans instead of surgery. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma mixes tumor cells with supporting stroma in widely varying proportions. That ratio shapes recurrence and drug response, yet it has only been measurable on tissue removed in an operation.

Using enhanced magnetic resonance images from 737 patients across several centers, the team trained a scoring model. It predicted the tissue-measured ratio with strong accuracy in training and solid accuracy in outside validation. The score separated patients by recurrence risk on its own and sharpened early recurrence forecasts when combined with clinical facts. Tumors scoring high on stroma fared better under standard systemic therapy and under immune-based combinations. Gene and single-cell analyses tied low-stroma tumors to matrix remodeling pathways and distinct immune cell states, giving the scan score a biological footing.
pmc-13651106:
Guiomar Mendieta and eleven co-authors interview doctors across six European countries about inflammation's place in cardiovascular care. Evidence more and more ties smoldering inflammation to the progression of artery disease combined with kidney disease or heart failure, yet nobody knew whether front-line physicians believe it or act on it.

Sixty-two cardiologists, kidney specialists, and general doctors with substantial experience joined hour-long interviews in early 2024. Most accepted inflammation's importance in theory, but only about a quarter routinely ordered the sensitive blood test that measures it. The barriers were practical: unclear meaning of a result and no proven treatment to offer when the value runs high, leaving doctors feeling unable to change management. The authors conclude that inflammation remains a neglected target for want of evidence-backed treatments and clearer guidance, not for want of awareness among physicians.
pmc-13651706:
Mario González-Gutiérrez and ten co-authors fix a subtle artifact in fluorescence lifetime imaging, a microscopy method that maps molecular settings by how long fluorophores glow. Because the microscope's blur spot mixes light from neighboring molecules into one pixel, blended decay curves masquerade as intermediate environments that do not exist.

Their workflow sharpens the raw intensity image with a mean-shift super-resolution method first, building spatial masks that keep each pixel's photons honest. Only then does it run the lifetime analysis, leaving the timing data untouched. In human cells carrying two overlapping dyes, the phantom in-between group sat exactly at blur interfaces and vanished under masking, while each dye's true signature survived. Simulations showed blending persists at separations ordinary resolution rules call safe. A three-dye test also separated cleanly. The authors argue spatial refinement, not temporal tinkering, is the honest cure.
pmc-13651806:
Peng Qin and four colleagues speed up ions trapped inside nanoporous crystals by applying a sideways gate voltage, a trick borrowed from transistor thinking. Ion mobility inside porous electrode materials limits batteries and supercapacitors, and the team used ionic liquids inside metal-organic framework films as a clean model system.

Conductivity rose by up to about a third when the gate field was switched on. Simulations explained why: the field sorts ions into parallel layers of higher and lower concentration running along the transport direction. Ions inside the favorable layers moved up to two and a half times faster than in the bulk liquid. The authors dub these strata ion highways. A general link between local concentration and mobility emerged from the data. The study offers both insight into confined ion dynamics and a practical method for squeezing more speed from porous devices.
pmc-13659106:
Yoon Shin and five colleagues compare two hepatitis B drugs on the outcome patients fear most: liver cancer. Besifovir is a newer option for chronic hepatitis B, while tenofovir has a long track record, and besifovir's long-term effect on cancer risk was unproven. Using Korean national insurance records covering more than thirty thousand patients, the team matched besifovir users with similar tenofovir users to make the comparison fair.

Liver cancer developed less often in the besifovir group, with cirrhosis tracked as a second outcome. Because the data come from routine care nationwide rather than a selected trial population, the result carries real-world weight, though records-based studies cannot erase every difference between groups. For doctors choosing between two daily antivirals meant to be taken for years, cancer risk is exactly the kind of long-horizon evidence that should steer the choice.
pmc-1629006:
Staff of the United States Food and Drug Administration issue draft guidance on patient-reported outcome measures. Such measures capture how patients feel and function, as reported by patients themselves. Drug makers may use them as endpoints in trials to support claims on product labels.

The guidance explains how the agency judges these tools and what it currently expects from sponsors. It covers how a measure should be built and how trial results may back a label claim. Clear rules help firms design trials that truly reflect patient experience, not only lab values.
pmc-2270306:
Mossong, Hens, Jit, and co-authors measure social contacts that matter for spreading infectious disease. Models of diseases passed by breath or close contact, such as pandemic flu, guide choices about vaccines and closures. Contact patterns are known to drive what those models predict.

The team gathered real data on who meets whom, by age and setting, across everyday life. Such data replace guesses in models with observed mixing. Better contact data lead to better forecasts of how fast an outbreak grows, which groups drive spread, and which interventions help most.
pmc-3111406:
Boulkedid, Abdoul, Loustau, and co-authors review how the Delphi method is used and reported for choosing healthcare quality indicators. The Delphi technique is a structured process in which experts answer rounds of questions until views converge. It is commonly used to build quality indicators, yet guidance for users was thin.

The authors describe how studies report their Delphi work and discuss its strengths and gaps. Inconsistent reporting makes indicator sets hard to judge or copy. Their review pushes for clearer standards, so measures used to grade hospitals rest on a sound process.
pmc-3995906:
Assarsson and co-authors reported a new protein test in 2014 that can measure many targets at once. Care that is tailored to each patient needs large amounts of high-quality data on markers in blood and tissue. Older tests often measured one protein at a time, which was slow and costly.

Their proximity extension assay measures ninety-six proteins in a single run, all in one format. The method uses pairs of probes that must bind side by side, which keeps the signal specific. Tests showed high sensitivity and good scaling to large sample sets. Such panels can speed the search for marker patterns that warn of disease early.
pmc-4086106:
Robert and Gouet presented a new version of ENDscript in 2014, a web server for studying protein structure. Proteins have levels of structure, from their amino acid chain up to folded units and complexes. Pulling all that information together by hand is slow and error prone.

ENDscript two gathers and draws a full analysis in an automated way, from the basic sequence to the assembled form. The upgrade was rebuilt to improve speed, accuracy, and ease of use. It also adds interactive three-dimensional viewing. Structural biologists use such views to spot the features that govern how a protein works.
pmc-4987906:
Afgan, Baker, van den Beek, and their colleagues updated the Galaxy platform in 2016. High-throughput technologies, above all next-generation DNA sequencing, had brought disruptive change to biomedical research. Reading the huge datasets they produce takes sophisticated statistical and computing tools.

Galaxy offers those tools through a web platform designed to be accessible, reproducible, and collaborative. Users run complex analyses without programming, and every step is recorded so others can repeat it. Sharing workflows helps teams check and build on each other's work. Galaxy brought data-heavy biology within reach of labs without dedicated computing staff.
pmc-5081106:
The NCD Risk Factor Collaboration pooled data in 2016 on worldwide trends in diabetes since 1980. One global target for non-communicable diseases is to halt the rise in adult diabetes prevalence by 2025 at its 2010 level. The team estimated trends and judged how likely countries are to meet that target.

Their pooled analysis covered hundreds of population-based studies with millions of participants. Such scale reveals which regions drive the global rise and where progress stalls. The results show the scale of change needed in diet, activity, and care. Governments use these trend estimates to set and check national diabetes plans.
pmc-517706:
Edgar presented MUSCLE in full in 2004, a program for multiple sequence alignment of proteins. Aligning many protein sequences side by side reveals which parts are conserved and how proteins are related. In an earlier paper, Edgar had shown MUSCLE reaching the highest scores then reported on four accuracy benchmarks.

This paper presents the algorithm in more detail. MUSCLE was designed to cut both the time and the memory that alignment takes, without losing accuracy. Faster alignment matters because sequence collections were already growing quickly. MUSCLE became one of the most used alignment tools in biology, a base step for trees, structure work, and gene family studies.
pmc-5491406:
Roth, Johnson, Abajobir, and many colleagues measured the global burden of cardiovascular diseases in 2017 for the GBD 2015 study. In many world regions, the true burden of these diseases was still murky. The team merged data on new cases, total cases, and deaths into consistent, current estimates.

Cardiovascular diseases cover heart attacks, stroke, heart failure, and other causes, ten of which the team tracked from 1990 to 2015. Their estimates show where death rates fall with treatment and prevention and where they still climb. Consistent methods across countries make the comparisons meaningful. Health ministries use such figures to plan cardiac and stroke services.
pmc-549606:
Pao, Miller, Politi, and their team reported in 2005 on why some lung tumors stop responding to targeted drugs. The drugs gefitinib and erlotinib block EGFR, a growth switch. Tumors that respond at first tend to carry changes in the EGFR gene that make the switch easy to block.

Most such tumors grow back in time as resistance sets in. The team found that tumors which had become resistant often carried a second change in the same part of EGFR. That second change lets the switch dodge the drug. The find explained a chief route of resistance and pushed the design of new EGFR drugs built to beat it.
pmc-5642006:
Stephen Burgess, Dylan Small, and Simon Thompson wrote this methods review in 2015. Their topic is Mendelian randomization, a way to test cause and effect using genes as stand-ins for a risk factor. The review compares the main statistical tools researchers use for that job.

Each method rests on assumptions about the gene variants, and the authors explain when those assumptions can fail. They weigh strengths and limits side by side so readers can pick a tool that fits their data. For anyone using genetic data to judge whether a habit or trait truly causes disease, the guidance here helps avoid false claims.
pmc-5753206:
Daniel Zerbino and a large team at Ensembl published the 2018 update of the Ensembl genome resource. Ensembl has collected and shared genome data since the first draft of the human genome. Its aim is to speed research by giving public data away fast and free.

The update reports new genomes, richer gene annotation, and better tools for comparing species. Users can browse genes, variants, and regulation data in a web browser or pull data in bulk. Most genomics papers rely on Ensembl at some step. The yearly updates keep the resource matched to fast-growing data volumes.
pmc-6227606:
The GBD 2017 Causes of Death Collaborators published this mortality analysis in 2018. Countries need cause-of-death figures they can compare to judge their own progress. The study estimates deaths by age and sex for a long list of causes.

Coverage spans nearly two hundred countries and territories over almost four decades. Heart disease and stroke lead the global totals, while child deaths from infection keep falling. The authors flag places where death records are weak and estimates lean on models. Even with those limits, the release is the standard yardstick for global mortality.
pmc-6441206:
Yang Mou, Jun Wang, Jinchun Wu, and coauthors reviewed ferroptosis in cancer in 2019. Ferroptosis is a recently named form of cell death driven by iron and fat oxidation. It looks and behaves quite unlike the classic apoptosis pathway.

Fast-growing work links ferroptosis to many cancers. Some tumors resist standard drugs yet stay sensitive to ferroptosis triggers. The review gathers the core machinery, from iron handling to lipid repair failure. It also lists the hard problems, such as finding markers in patients. The field hopes this death route can kill cancers that evade other treatments.
pmc-7182206:
Bui Quang Minh, Heiko Schmidt, Olga Chernomor, and coauthors presented IQ-TREE 2 in 2020. IQ-TREE builds evolutionary trees by maximum likelihood and is popular for its speed and ease of use. The first version had gathered many features since its release years earlier.

The second version adds new models, including ones for mixed and partitioned data, and faster search methods. It handles the huge alignments of the genomic era without special hardware. Benchmarks show accuracy on par with or better than rival tools. Phylogenetics courses and labs worldwide treat it as a default choice.
pmc-7719906:
Fiona Bull and co-authors set out the World Health Organization's 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behavior. The guidelines were built following the organization's standard process, with an expert group reviewing the evidence. That evidence covered how activity and sitting time relate to health in children, teenagers, adults, and older people.

The document states how much activity each age group should aim for each week, and advises cutting down long stretches of sitting. It also speaks to people living with chronic conditions and disabilities, groups often left out of such advice. National health agencies around the world base their own recommendations on these guidelines, so the numbers chosen here shape public advice for years.
pmc-7764106:
Zeinab Breijyeh and Rafik Karaman wrote a comprehensive review in 2020 on Alzheimer's disease, the main cause of dementia worldwide. The disease slowly breaks down brain cells, and with them a person's thinking, memory, and independence in daily life. It is understood as a condition with many contributing causes rather than a single one.

The review lays out the leading explanations for how the disease begins and advances, including the long debated roles of abnormal protein deposits in the brain. It then surveys the treatments in use and under study, and what each can and cannot do. For readers seeking one clear account of a complex illness, the review gathers causes, symptoms, and therapy in a single place.
pmc-8010506:
Laith Alzubaidi and colleagues wrote a broad review in 2021 of deep learning, the approach that had come to dominate machine learning. Deep learning trains layered networks on large amounts of data, and it had recently produced standout results in fields from image recognition to language. The authors set out to give newcomers and specialists one shared map of the field.

They explain the core concepts, then compare the main network designs built around convolutional networks for images. They also take stock of open problems, survey real applications, and sketch where the field may head next. A review of this scope serves as an entry point for students and as a checkpoint for researchers measuring how fast the ground is shifting.
pmc-8617206:
Xiaojia Hu and co-authors reviewed in 2021 the JAK/STAT signaling pathway, a fast route by which cells pass messages from their surface to their nucleus. The pathway was discovered more than twenty-five years ago and has since proved central to many vital processes, including immunity and blood formation. It works as a rapid module: a signal at the membrane switches on transcription factors that head straight for the genes.

The review traces the pathway from laboratory discovery to the clinic, where drugs blocking its Janus kinase enzymes now treat several diseases. The authors also cover what goes wrong when the pathway is overactive or broken. Few signaling routes have traveled so completely from basic biology to the pharmacy shelf.
pothier-obligations-contracts-1806:
Robert Pothier, a French judge and scholar, wrote his Treatise on Obligations in the 1760s. William Evans's English translation of 1806 is the version here, with notes on English law. Pothier's book is the French civilian foundation of modern contract law.

He defines contracts, consent, error, and fault in clear, ordered chapters. His rules passed almost whole into the French civil code and from there worldwide. English and American judges cited the translation in court for decades. Anyone tracing where modern contract ideas came from will land on Pothier, the quiet professor from Orléans who organized a whole field.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-159-19:
October 6, 1920, in Punch, volume 159, opens with Charivaria, the standing column of short jokes on the news. Motors, servants, and literary quarrels supply this week's material.

A London magistrate rules that motorists cannot go about knocking people down every day, and the column agrees once should be enough for any walker. A Kensington lady hires a parlourmaid three feet seven inches tall, a sign of the servant shortage. A play called The Man Who Went to Work is treated as a farce by its title alone, an Ealing sergeant has summoned six hundred motorists since March, and Mr. H. G. Wells and Mr. Henry Arthur Jones agree to shake hands and stay enemies.
ramusio-navigationi-et-viaggi-vol-3-1606:
Giovanni Battista Ramusio's Delle Navigationi et Viaggi closes with volume three, here in the Venetian printing of 1606. The collection itself dates to 1550 through 1559, when Ramusio issued its volumes in Italian at Venice. He worked from reports sent home by travelers, merchants, and ambassadors of many nations.

Ramusio's three volumes formed the first great voyage collection, the pattern for Hakluyt's and Purchas's later English sets. Marco Polo's travels found their first complete printed home in its pages. Voyages to Africa and Asia fill out the survey. With volume three, the work that taught Europe to read the world as one map stands complete.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: A publisher's header, and a publisher's header only, fronts volume six of Constant's Private Life of Napoleon Bonaparte in these pages. From it a reader gathers the title, the author Constant, and that the work is in English. No page of the valet's account of his master follows in what is shown: neither an opening chapter nor a contents page is present. Which years or scenes of Napoleon's life this sixth volume holds is therefore a question these pages leave unanswered.
richard-carvel-volume-06:
Winston Churchill's Richard Carvel opens its sixth volume with His Grace Makes Advances, as Richard casts about for his next move. Jack Comyn blows in like a gust of wind, rating him for moping and ignoring his calls. Comyn swears Dorothy loves him, for there were no tears when Comyn made his own avowal.

Mr. Manners, Comyn holds, had appealed to Dorothy to save him, and her tears point one way only. Richard laughs and recalls Comyn's earlier counsel, spoken when he got Richard out of the sponging-house. The volume's list runs from Lord Baltimore and a glimpse of Mr. Garrick to Holland House and Vauxhall.
rivers-the-todas-1906:
W. H. R. Rivers went to the Nilgiri Hills of southern India to study the Toda people, and his 1906 book reports what he found. The Todas were few in number, pastoral, and organized around the buffalo in a way no outsider had fully recorded.

At the center stands the sacred dairy, where buffalo milk is handled as a ritual by priest-dairymen under strict rules. Rivers also documents polyandry, in which brothers share a wife, and works out Toda kinship with new care. His genealogical method, built for this study, changed fieldwork itself. The book launched British social anthropology's classic period.
san-francisco-during-the-eventful-days-o:
James B. Stetson wrote San Francisco During the Eventful Days of April 1906 as personal recollections, written in June 1906. A note adds that, the first edition being used up and a new one required, he has included some events that occurred later, without changing the original date. Stetson says the earthquake and great fire of 1906 were events of such unusual interest that he jotted down incidents he personally observed while they were fresh. He laid the notes away so he could refer to them later with some assurance of their accuracy, knowing how faulty memory grows after time passes.

On the morning of April 18, 1906, at 5:13, in his residence at 1801 Van Ness Avenue, Stetson was awakened by a very severe shock. The shaking nearly threw him out of bed.
santayana-life-reason-vol-5-1906:
Reason in Science, published in 1906, closes The Life of Reason as its fifth and crowning volume. Santayana turns last to science, the pursuit his whole system had to honor without worshiping.

He treats science as reason's most disciplined form: a method for mapping nature's order, powerful exactly because it describes rather than consoles. Against it he sets the claims of history and of the inner life, which science cannot replace. The volume rounds the five books into one vision: reason as man's one guide in every sphere. Santayana was thirty-nine when he finished; few systems begin so complete.
scheible-das-kloster-vol06:
Johann Scheible closed the year 1846 with band six of Das Kloster, cells twenty-one through twenty-four. Halfway through the set, the shape of his work stood clear. He meant to save the whole range of German folk print, high claims and low alike, in full reprints.

The grimoire shelf stays heavy here: spell books, Faust books, and Höllenzwänge in their full, stark text. Beside them sit folk charms and popular chapbooks, the small books that passed from hand to hand. A modern reader meets magic here as it was sold, not as later ages cleaned it. That plain honesty gives the band its lasting use.
schlussel-zu-dem-cabinet-der-geheimen-sc: A 1706 German key unlocked nature's secret treasure chamber. The cabinet of hidden riches. The natural secrets. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care for all readers. Scholars prize such firsthand sources from long ago.
serapis-volume-06:
Georg Ebers wrote this historical novel of Alexandria; volume six opens at chapter twenty-five in the vast Hippodrome. Thousands fill the seats on race eve, though a night storm and fear have kept many home. Word spreads that the statue of Serapis came through the siege of his shrine unharmed.

Imperial legate Cynegius and city prefect Evagrius enter with great pomp, followed by senators and ranked ladies and men. Christians, heathen, and Jews sit together as the games, put off by panic, begin at last. This closing volume stages a city's relief and dread in one bright, tense public scene.
shahnama-warner-vol-2-1906:
Arthur George Warner and Edmond Warner published Volume 2 of their Shahnama of Firdausi in 1906. The Shahnama, or Book of Kings, is the Persian national epic, written by Firdausi around the year 1000. The Warner brothers set out to give English readers the whole poem, in nine volumes.

Volume 2 carries the epic's early kings and heroes onward, through wars, hunts, and court tales told in verse. Their translation kept the poem's shape while making its stories plain to English readers. No full English Shahnama existed before theirs. The volume continues a vast record of Persian myth and memory, where legend and early history flow together without a clear break.
shahnameh-warner-vol2-1906:
Ferdowsi wrote the Shahnama, the Book of Kings, the great epic poem of Persia. Arthur George Warner and Edmond Warner turned it into English verse. Theirs was the first full English verse version of the whole poem. Book two of their set came out in 1906.

Kings rise and fall in long tales of war, love, and fate. Heroes fight beasts and rival lords while wise men warn of pride. The Warners kept the sweep of the tale in plain, strong verse. For most English readers, this set was the first door into Persia's best loved book.
shaku-sermons-buddhist-abbot-1906:
Soyen Shaku was the Zen abbot who spoke for Buddhism at the Chicago Parliament of Religions in 1893. His Sermons of a Buddhist Abbot, published in 1906, gathers the addresses he gave on his American tour of 1905 and 1906. His student Suzuki translated them into English.

Shaku explains karma, rebirth, and the Buddha's enlightenment in a calm, gracious voice shaped for Western hearers. He presents Buddhism as a way of waking, not a set of dogmas to be believed on command. The sermons mark the moment Zen first addressed America through one of its own masters. His dignity did much to win Buddhism a fair hearing in America.
sherrington-integrative-action-1906:
Charles Sherrington was a British physiologist whose lab work mapped how nerves join muscles into working systems. His 1906 book The Integrative Action of the Nervous System sums up years of trials on reflexes. It is often named the founding text of modern neuroscience.

Sherrington names the synapse, the tiny junction where one nerve cell hands its signal to the next. He shows how reflex arcs combine, compete, and yield so that an animal acts as one whole. Later brain science built directly on his terms, his maps, and his careful method. He coined much of the language that nerve science still speaks.
sinclair-jungle-1906:
Upton Sinclair went undercover in Chicago's stockyards in 1904, living among the packinghouse workers for seven weeks. He published The Jungle in 1906, intending a socialist indictment of wage slavery. Sinclair later joked that he aimed at the public's heart and hit its stomach instead.

Jurgis Rudkus, a Lithuanian immigrant, arrives strong and hopeful, then is ground down by injury, layoffs, and the loss of his family. Around his story Sinclair documents the meatpacking industry in revolting detail: spoiled meat, filth, and worse sold as food. Congress rushed through the Pure Food and Drug Act and meat inspection within months. The Jungle remains the most consequential protest novel in American history.
spr-proceedings-vol20-1906:
Volume twenty of the Proceedings, from 1906, consists of part fifty three alone. The Society for Psychical Research often filled a whole part with one great report. Telepathy and trance work dominate the society's business in this period. Long sittings with mediums appear in near verbatim form.

Investigators weigh the Piper material and its rivals with care. Spontaneous cases of apparitions arrive in smaller numbers, well documented. The volume's single part format suits readers who want depth over range. It forms one brick in the archive wall built between 1882 and 1930. The society's standards, set early, hold firm here. Evidence first remains the rule.
suess-face-of-earth-vol2-sollas-1906:
Volume 2 of Sollas's translation of Suess's Face of the Earth appeared in 1906. Eduard Suess turned in this volume to the oceans, their history and their floors. The work surveys the Atlantic and other seas as archives of the Earth's past.

Suess traced marine transgressions, the long advances of sea over land recorded in layered rocks. He compared coastlines and fossil seas across continents to rebuild vanished oceans. One of them, the Tethys, became a lasting term of geology from his pages. Sollas's translation kept pace with the German original's ambition. The volume shows geology thinking at planetary scale a generation before plate tectonics gave it a new engine.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-vol:
The Magick Cup stands alone in the sixth volume of La Fontaine's Tales and Novels. It tells of a husband who tests his wife's faith with an enchanted cup. The cup spills on the unfaithful. Jealousy is the volume's whole subject.

The poet begins by calling jealousy the worst of ills, beside which all other torments are trifling. He pictures the jealous fool as suspicion's easy tool, finding no repose by night or day, forever dreaming that his forehead sprouts, and never doubting the truth of his dreams. Against that portrait the tale sets its test: a cup that promises certainty, and the misery certainty brings. La Fontaine treats the green-eyed passion with pity and mockery in equal measure.
tales-and-novels-volume-06:
Volume VI of Maria Edgeworth's Tales and Novels holds The Absentee, her novel of an Irish landlord's son who comes home from London fashion to face the estate his family has drained. The tale opens in the crush-room of the opera-house, where carriages are waited for and gossip does the work of news.

Lady Langdale and Mrs Dareville trade word of Lady Clonbrony's coming gala. The rooms are to be furnished at prodigious expense. The style will be most magnificent. Colonel Heathcock marvels at the rate the Clonbronies are dashing on. Then her grace asks a simple question. Who are these Clonbronies, that one hears of so much of late? The novel's question is set by it. New money apes old rank here. The Irish tenants pay for the show.
the-amateur-cracksman-pg706:
Eight linked tales by E. W. Hornung make up this volume, all circling Raffles, a gentleman thief at ease in smart London rooms. Its contents run from The Ides of March and A Costume Piece through Gentlemen and Players and Wilful Murder to The Return Match and The Gift of the Emperor.

The opening story finds the narrator back at the Albany after midnight, facing a table strewn with baccarat counters and glasses. Raffles, now in a blazer, raises his brows at the late visit. The younger man admits he barely knows his host, yet reminds him they met at school and asks to be heard.
the-bride-of-the-nile-volume-06:
Volume 6 of The Bride of the Nile, by Georg Ebers, opens at Chapter XXII with a girl in swift change. Till a few days back Katharina was a docile child. She held it a point of honor to obey at once her mother's lightest word, Dame Neforis, and even the sour Eudoxia. She hid nothing, and could not rest till, before evening prayer, she had confessed each small fault and been forgiven. Night after night the Water-wagtail slept with a conscience as white as her whitest dove.

The change came after Orion's kiss among the flowering trees. Since then each hour has waked new hopes and new views in her. A barrier, too, stands between her and Paula. Paula, she is sure, is that other one of whom Orion spoke. With the governor's house shut to her, Katharina has no one left to trust.
the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume-06:
The sixth part of The Caxtons keeps the son, Pisistratus, as its teller. Readers hear the family from inside, in his own words. At the center sits his father, learned, retiring, and fond of a good argument after tea.

Mr. Trevanion sits in the family drawing room on a warm night, at ease after two cups of tea. With him comes Sir Sedley Beaudesert, a college friend his father has not seen for years. Talk turns on whether happiness is the end and aim of human life. The narrator's father answers the common claim with plain doubt, and the talk sets the tone for the part.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau:
Book VI of Jean Jacques Rousseau's Confessions stands here as volume VI of the twelve-book set, privately printed for members of the Aldus Society at London in 1903.
